20082-warrior-gap-a-story-of-the-sioux-o:
Warrior Gap tells a story of the Sioux outbreak of 1868, on the western frontier. A young lieutenant leads his column toward home after hard service. Barely two years an officer, he rides with a light heart. Each mile brings him closer to the home he longs for.

He had spent one hard year as a plebe at the military academy. At twenty-five, most of his years had seemed bright and glad. War on the plains will test that bright outlook soon enough. Readers get a frontier tale of troops, Sioux resistance, and a young man's trial.
antony-and-cleopatra-pg2268: Enobarbus describes the barge in this edition: Cleopatra on the Cydnus, "the barge she sat in, like a burnished throne, burned on the water." The serpent of old Nile beguiles Antony to ruin. The richest love tragedy ever written.
arxiv-2512-00068:
Turbulence is the chaotic swirling motion seen in fast-moving fluids, from air over a wing to water in a pipe. Marcial Sanchis-Agudo and Ricardo Vinuesa offer a geometric foundation for its universal laws in a 2025 study. They ask where the small dissipative structures of turbulence come from.

Their framework treats tiny fluid parcels as random tracers whose paths carry some uncertainty. From that picture, the viscous term of the Navier-Stokes equations appears as a natural smoothing operator tied to microscopic diffusion. If the approach holds, it links everyday fluid equations to deeper variational principles and may guide new models of turbulent flow.
arxiv-2512-00168:
Deep neural networks show crackling, avalanche-like activity whose origin has lacked a clear explanation. Arsham Ghavasieh develops a stochastic theory of information propagation in such networks in a 2025 study. The theory builds in fluctuations at the level of the central limit theorem.

Four effective couplings characterize the dynamics, leading to a Landau-style description of the static exponents. The activity cascades take a directed percolation structure, a pattern known from statistical physics. Ghavasieh argues this framing can tune universality in network behavior, linking machine learning to ideas long used for phase transitions in physical systems. Avalanche language comes from physics, where crackling systems share the same mathematics. The work speaks to two crowds at once. Folks who build these nets, and folks who study how crowds of small parts act when they link up.
arxiv-2512-00268:
Teams of autonomous agents often need to agree on a shared solution while talking only to neighbors. Hong Wang studies decentralized optimization with explicit consensus penalties in 2025. Classical decentralized gradient descent is appealing for its minimal state, yet it fails to reach exact agreement with fixed step sizes.

Usual fixes add trackers or dual variables, which complicate each agent. Wang explores penalty terms that enforce consensus directly while keeping the method lean. Exact agreement matters in sensor networks and robot swarms, where a nearly shared answer can still mean inconsistent actions across the team. Exactness matters most at the end of optimization, when small disagreements become visible errors.
arxiv-2512-00468:
Radio waves bounce off building walls in messy patterns that network planners must predict. Tongjia Zhang and co-authors measure diffuse scattering from three typical building surfaces in 2025, at three frequencies including two in the new FR3 range. They also analyze the mechanisms behind the scattering.

The team proposes a three-dimensional measurement procedure that captures the full spatial character of the scattering. Its accuracy gains were verified with measurements at the highest frequency studied. Better scattering models improve coverage predictions for next-generation wireless networks, where walls are part of the channel, not just obstacles. Millimeter-wave and mid-band frequencies scatter differently, so measuring all three anchors the model. For folks who plan the next wave of cell sites, the gain is fewer blind spots. They can say how walls bend the waves long past the line of sight.
arxiv-2512-00568:
Zero cycles are formal combinations of points on an algebraic variety, and their equivalence classes form the Chow group. Alejandro De Las Peñas Castaño studies zero cycles on products of two elliptic curves over local fields in 2025. The curves have good supersingular reduction.

For such a product over a p-adic field, the author produces infinitely many rational equivalences in the Chow group. The construction uses genus two covers of the two elliptic curves. Chow groups encode deep arithmetic information, and explicit infinite families are rare enough to be valuable in themselves. Supersingular reduction is the extreme case, where the elliptic curve's arithmetic is most rigid. Genus two covers provide the extra room the construction needs.
arxiv-2512-00668:
Two-sample tests ask whether two groups come from the same distribution, and permutation tests answer by shuffling labels. Jungwoo Ho studies a restricted block permutation scheme for such testing in 2025. Permutations are limited to single cross-swaps between block-selected representatives.

The analysis yields three main results, beginning with an exact validity construction that applies to any fixed restricted permutation set. Restricting permutations slashes computation, which matters for huge modern datasets. Proving validity anyway keeps the statistical guarantee intact, so speed does not come at the price of untrustworthy p-values. Blocks keep related observations together, respecting structure that naive shuffling would destroy. Exact validity means the test's error rates are what they claim to be.
arxiv-2512-00968:
Ziyang Zeng and a large team improve search ranking at Xiaohongshu in a 2025 paper. Search engines must rank items by relevance to a user query. Traditional relevance models output a single score or a direct label. That limits how much reasoning they can show and how complex signals they can use.

Their generative ranking approach produces richer outputs, and reinforcement learning optimizes the relevance it achieves. Generative models can weigh many signals and explain their picks in words. Reinforcement learning then tunes them toward rankings users judge relevant. Better ranking relevance means users find what they meant faster, a core gain for a large social search platform.
arxiv-2512-01268:
Jongwon Sohn, Juhyeon Moon, Hyunjoon Jung, and Jaewook Nam present ViscNet in a 2025 engineering paper. Viscosity, how thick a fluid is, must be measured for process monitoring and for autonomous laboratories. Conventional viscometers are invasive: they must touch the fluid and need controlled lab conditions unlike real process settings.

ViscNet is a vision-based viscometer that works in line, inside the process. It watches a fixed background pattern through the fluid's surface. Mixing deforms that surface, and refraction distorts the pattern in ways tied to viscosity. Reading thickness from a camera could let mixing processes self-monitor continuously without probes.
arxiv-2512-01368:
Klaus Thomsen gives a new proof of a classic result on sofic shifts. A sofic shift is a set of symbol strings made by a labeled graph. Its future cover is a canonical graph built from what can follow each past. Krieger showed that cover is canonical.

Thomsen proves that claim by a fresh path. He also shows how to make new canonical covers from a given one. The new covers link to the future cover but tend to differ from it. Extra covers give scholars more tools to sort and compare symbol systems.
arxiv-2512-01468:
Ya-Wen Pan, Ming-Zhu Liu, and Li-Sheng Geng probe three-body forces in hadron systems. Such forces act when three particles meet at once. They are widely used in nuclear work. Whether they are truly needed is still hotly debated.

The trio focus on three-hadron systems with set charge parity. For those systems, they argue the need for a three-body force is certain. Charge parity here acts as a strict filter. A firm case in one class of systems would settle part of the debate. It would guide how nuclear forces are built from now on.
arxiv-2512-01568:
Sandro Andric asks if language models act on the values they claim. He tests whether their gut links and stated views predict real altruistic acts. Two dozen frontier models faced three test types drawn from human psychology. One test gauged implicit links to altruism.

Other tests asked the models to report their own views. A third set watched what the models did in choice tasks. Gaps between talk and acts would warn users not to trust stated values alone. The work gives a template for checks of model character. The three-way gap test can be reused for other traits like honesty or care, giving labs a shared audit for model character claims.
arxiv-2512-01768:
Ruiqi Bao and co-authors propose hybrid skin-topological states in exciton polariton lattices. The non-Hermitian skin effect piles bulk states at edges. That piling breaks the usual bulk-boundary rules. Polaritons mix light and matter, which makes them a rich test bed.

Their honeycomb lattice adds sublattice-dependent gain and loss. That non-Hermiticity couples to built-in topological edge modes. Edge modes then relocate in new ways. Hybrid states could yield light tools whose edge flow is both protected and tunable by gain settings. Gain and loss are tunable in polariton systems by pump shape, so the hybrid states can be dialed in during an experiment, not just predicted.
arxiv-2512-01968:
Cubic fourfolds are shapes cut out by a cubic equation in higher-dimensional space, and sorting them into families is a subtle art. Simone Billi and Lucas Li Bassi study in 2025 when two such shapes count as the same under a relation called L-equivalence, a weakening of being truly identical.

They prove that for very general cubic fourfolds, L-equivalence forces the shapes to be isomorphic after all, genuinely the same. Yet special examples exist that are L-equivalent without being isomorphic, so the relation is not empty of surprises. In special families tied to Hassett divisors, L-equivalence also implies the shapes are Fourier-Mukai partners, a deep kinship between their geometries.
arxiv-2512-02068:
Neutrinos change flavor as they travel, oscillating between types in a rhythm set by quantum mechanics. Bipin Singh Koranga, Parnav Kumar, and Baktiar Wasir Farooq ask in 2025 whether faint corrections from quantum gravity would leave a fingerprint in the entanglement carried by two-flavor neutrino oscillations.

They track the entanglement with the von Neumann entropy, a standard measure of quantum correlation, across successive oscillation cycles. The gravity-inspired changes enter through the neutrinos' dispersion relation, suppressed by the Planck scale and therefore tiny. Even so, the study shows how entanglement measures could, in principle, register effects far beyond direct experimental reach.
arxiv-2512-02268:
Emulating the climate with generative models promises fast forecasts at many scales, but earlier methods crawl forward weather-step by weather-step, too slow for century horizons. Jeremy Irvin and a large Stanford team present in 2025 a spatiotemporal pyramid flow matching approach built for climate emulation.

Autoregression at weather scale is inherently slow over long horizons and has yet to stay stable when the forcing driving the climate keeps changing. Flow matching sidesteps stepwise generation by learning the whole evolution at once, across a pyramid of scales. Stable, fast emulation under shifting conditions would sharpen long-range climate projections used in planning.
arxiv-2512-02568:
Matteo Capoferri and Matthias Täufer study waves in materials made of stiff matter dotted with soft balls. The soft spherical inclusions have random sizes, scattered through the stiff matrix. Operators of this kind model composite materials with strong contrast between their parts.

The pair examines the spectrum of these operators, the set of allowed vibration patterns and energies. Random high contrast media also arise in stochastic homogenization, which replaces fine detail with average behavior. Understanding when waves stay trapped, called Anderson localization, helps predict how real composites carry sound, heat, or light. The same math can guide the design of foams and gels built to block sound or shake in a planned way.
arxiv-2512-03068:
Bias inside AI systems can lead to real harm. Nicoleta Tantalaki, Sophia Vei, and Athena Vakali wrote this 2025 study on that risk. AI tools now help make choices in key fields, yet bias can enter at many stages of their life cycle.

The authors note that past work often lists bias and harm apart. Their plan links each type of bias to the harm it may cause, using both human judgment and large language models. That link could help teams spot risks early. It also gives builders a clearer map for checks before a tool goes live. For policy teams, linked bias and harm maps could shape safer rules for AI use.
arxiv-2512-03168:
Galaxies near us drift in a shared flow. Richard Watkins and Hume Feldman ask where that bulk flow comes from in this 2025 work. They use the CosmicFlows-4 catalog, a large list of galaxy motions.

The authors split the flow into parts made inside a set volume and parts from structures beyond it. That split shows how much of the drift is local and how much is pulled by distant mass. The answer tests models of cosmic structure. It also helps map dark matter that cannot be seen directly. Peculiar motions are direct signs of gravity at work, so their sources matter greatly.
arxiv-2512-03268:
A note in pure math extends old results to a wider setting. J. Beckmann generalizes work by Magnar Dale in this 2025 paper. Dale studied secant varieties of curves and proved facts using Terracini's lemma.

Beckmann shows that nearly all of Dale's proofs carry over to embedded joins of varieties. Joins are a broader construction that includes secants as a special case. As an application, he computes the degree of a canonical map between joins. Such extensions let one proof serve many cases in algebraic geometry. Join results unify older theorems, showing they were shadows of one broader fact.
arxiv-2512-03568:
Usability walkthroughs are useful but costly to run with people. Ruican Zhong, David McDonald, and Gary Hsieh test whether language models can simulate them in this 2025 work. A cognitive walkthrough steps through an interface as a new user would.

The authors compared walkthroughs by GPT-4 and Gemini against human participants. They asked how closely model performance aligns with human behavior in the task. Synthetic walkthroughs could give design teams cheap early feedback. They would not replace human testing, but could triage issues sooner. Alignment with human walkthroughs is the test, since a synthetic user must stumble where people stumble, not where models find code paths.
arxiv-2601-06668:
Vishal Ganesan and co-authors measure microwave losses in niobium oxide in 2026. Two-level systems in amorphous oxides limit superconducting qubits and cavities. These tiny defects absorb microwave energy and shorten coherence times.

Niobium resonators are widely used in quantum science experiments today. Niobium's natural oxide layer contains various types of oxides mixed together. Their relative contributions to loss had not been clearly distinguished. The team studies chemically pure bulk niobium oxide samples to separate them. Pure samples let one oxide type speak at a time. Quantum hardware builders need exactly this attribution of loss sources. Reducing the worst oxide could extend qubit lifetimes in future devices.
arxiv-2601-06968:
Research by D. Schaerer and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with nitrogen abundances in star-forming galaxies 2.2 gyr after the big bang are not. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Using deep medium-resolution JWST rest-optical spectra of a sample of typical star-forming galaxies (Lyman break galaxies and Lyman- α emitters). From the LyC22 survey at z 3 z 3.

We determined the nebular abundances of N. O, and Ne relative to H for a subsample of 25 objects with the direct method, based on auroral [O. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07168:
Loren Spice and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with jordan decompositions in lie algebras and their duals. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. We provide a discussion of Jordan decompositions in the Lie algebra, and the dual Lie algebra. Of a reductive group in as uniform a way as possible.

We give a counterexample to the claim that Jordan decompositions on the dual Lie algebra are unique. And state an upper bound on how non-unique they can be. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07668:
Shiro Kuriwaki and Cory McCartan reassess ecological inference, a classic problem in social science. Scholars often have only aggregate averages, like district-level results, but want group-level behavior. Estimating conditional means from marginal means is exactly that problem. Their 2026 preprint gives a new formalization of when the problem can be solved at all.

The authors show how the needed identification conditions fail in common cases. They also examine the roles of confounders and linearity assumptions. Ecological inference is widely used with election and census data, where individual records stay private. A clear statement of when it fails protects scholars from confident but wrong conclusions. Political scientists and statisticians are the natural readers. The reassessment urges more care before drawing group claims from totals.
arxiv-2601-07768:
Akshay Karthik and Alex Huang present THETA, a low-cost way to track hands for controlling robotic hands. Teleoperation usually needs depth cameras or sensor gloves to estimate finger joint positions. Both are expensive. THETA instead uses three ordinary webcams. Triangulation across the cameras approximates the relative joint angles of human fingers. Their 2026 preprint describes the system.

Cheap hand tracking could widen access to robot teleoperation research. Schools and small labs often cannot afford glove-based setups. Three webcams are easy to buy and replace. The trade-off is accuracy, which the system must show is good enough for control. The paper targets robotics scholars who teach robots by demonstration. It also suits automation tasks where a human guides a robotic hand remotely.
arxiv-2601-08168: Syue-Cian Lin, Wei-Yu Chiu, and Chien-Feng Wu attack bilinear matrix inequality problems in control design. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that such problems are fundamental to control systems yet hard to solve. Their nonconvex form defeats many standard solvers. The team adapts a memetic covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy for the task. The memetic version adds a local refinement phase built on a (1+1) variant. Combining global search with local polish aims at reliable designs for controllers that must meet strict matrix constraints.
arxiv-2601-08268: Hoang Minh Nguyen, Hoang An Nguyen, and Cong Trinh Le optimize maximal quantum f-divergences along unitary orbits. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats a class of distinguishability measures for quantum states. These divergences are defined through the commutant Radon-Nikodym derivative and operator convex functions. The authors study how the measures change as states move along unitary orbits. Optimization results clarify the best and worst cases for telling two quantum states apart. Such bounds matter for quantum information tasks that rest on state discrimination.
arxiv-2601-08468: JudgeRLVR reorders reasoning training by teaching the model to judge first and generate second. The 2026 arXiv paper addresses reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, now a standard reasoning paradigm. Training only for final-answer correctness can push models into verbose, aimless exploration. Models then rely on exhaustive trial and error rather than structured planning. Judging first aims to build evaluation skill before generation. If a model can spot a good path early, training may waste fewer tokens on blind search.
arxiv-2601-08568:
K. Sai Mineesh Reddy and Navin Kashyap construct quantum error-correcting codes with transversal Clifford gates. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces a framework for Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes. The codes must support fault-tolerant logical Z-rotations applied transversally, gate by gate across physical qubits.

Using the framework, the authors obtain asymptotically good CSS codes. Those codes fault-tolerantly realize the full logical transversal Clifford group. Transversal gates are prized because they stop errors from spreading within a code block. Good codes with this property bring fault-tolerant quantum computing closer, since Clifford gates form the backbone of most quantum circuits.
arxiv-2601-08668: Kyuri Im, Shuzhou Yuan, and Michael Farber analyze bias in false refusals during hate speech detoxification. Their 2026 arXiv paper warns that it contains examples of hate speech. Language models are increasingly applied to rewrite toxic text into safer forms. Prompts for this task often trigger safety alerts, causing models to refuse outright. The authors study that false refusal behavior and its biases across groups. Uneven refusals can leave some communities unprotected while over-blocking others, a fairness problem for moderation tools.
arxiv-2601-08768:
Cody Kommers and Ari Holtzman argue that much AI use is play, not work. Most talk about AI says it will raise work output and do hard mind tasks for us. Yet many users open these tools to chat, joke, make art, and pass time. The authors say that use is not a side case. It is a main case.

They set out what it means to design AI for fun. Fun use has its own goals, risks, and tests of good work. A tool built for work may fail as a toy, and a toy may be judged by the wrong scale. A reader who builds or rates AI gets a new lens. It asks what users seek when no task must be done.
arxiv-2601-08968:
Nikolas Claussen, Fridtjof Brauns, and Boris Shraiman ask what takes the place of stretch rules in live stuff. Dead stuff obeys a law that ties push to stretch from a rest form. Live stuff is not like that. Its push comes from tiny motors that burn fuel and pull. There is no fixed rest form to stretch from.

The team studies nets of such pull lines, called active tension nets. They seek a new base law for how these nets bear load and change shape. Cells and tissues may obey that law, not the dead stuff law. A reader in bio physics gets a fresh frame. It may explain how a cell sheet can be both soft and tough at once.
arxiv-2601-09368:
F. J. Polanco-Rodríguez, C. Krafft, and P. Savoini study how solar radio bursts turn plasma waves into escaping radio waves. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses particle-in-cell simulations of beam-driven Langmuir and Z-mode waves. Type III bursts occur when electron beams excite turbulence near the plasma frequency.

The team compares two routes that convert the waves into electromagnetic emissions. One is nonlinear decay of the waves; the other is linear transformation on random density fluctuations, including mode conversion at fixed frequency. Sorting out which route dominates helps explain the bright radio flashes seen from the Sun. The results feed models of space weather near Earth.
arxiv-2601-09768:
Lorenzo Monti and six co-authors build a clustering tool that stays alert for the unknown. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents CLiMB, a domain-informed framework for novelty detection in scientific data. Science needs methods that sort known phenomena while flagging true anomalies.

Semi-supervised clustering often fails that dual task. It may force rigid rules that crush unexpected patterns, or demand the number of clusters in advance. CLiMB uses domain knowledge to guide grouping without closing the door on surprises. Such tools help surveys of the sky and other big datasets surface real discoveries.
arxiv-2601-09868:
Ali Taani studies the slow swing of binary pulsar orbits and what drives it. His 2026 arXiv paper treats apsidal motion in non-synchronous binary pulsars, where spin and orbit are not locked. Such motion probes relativistic gravity, star structure, and the dynamics of close binaries.

The author weighs three effects together: tidal interaction, the stars' oblateness, and general relativity. Three systems are examined: J0621+1002, the double pulsar J0737-3039, and the Hulse-Taylor binary 1913+16. Splitting the observed swing among its causes tests gravity where fields are strong. It also reveals how tidally stressed neutron stars are built.
arxiv-2601-10368:
Lukas Hückmann, Jonathon Cottom, Jörg Meyer, and Emilia Olsson explain how a key chip stuff picks its form. The stuff is TiSi2, a mix of titanium and silicon. It has low drag for current and stands up well in use. Chips use it at metal and semiconductor joins.

But the stuff has many crystal forms. Which form grows rests on fine shape facts. The team tie its growth to the shape of the base. On a silicon face of set cut, one rare form wins. Their claim rests on topology, the math of shapes and joins. It may help fabs pick the form they want.
arxiv-2601-10468:
Daniyaal Farooqi, Gavin Pu, Shreyasha Paudel, Sharifa Sultana, and Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed study job fears in computer science students as AI spreads. Firms now use AI to do work fast and lift gains. That shift can push staff out of roles. New grads feel that risk as they near the job hunt.

CS students may feel it most, since AI now writes code. The team ask how wide and deep that fear runs. They also ask what shapes it, from news to course work. The work gives schools a read on a fear that can shape study picks and health.
arxiv-2601-10568:
Gabriel S. Nahum works on a question from the theory of interacting particles. Such systems pair up single particles that push on each other, and their large-scale behavior is often described by a diffusion equation. The spread in that equation is set by a coefficient. Nahum asks which functions can play that role.

He shows that any positive, continuous, and bounded function can arise as the diffusion coefficient of such an equation. The proof builds a suitable particle model and then uses the entropy method. The result links a wide class of smooth spread profiles to concrete particle systems. It gives researchers a firm bridge between small-scale rules and large-scale flow.
arxiv-2601-10968:
Jing-Ze Xia, Hong-Xuan Jiang, Yosuke Mizuno, Antonios Nathanail, and Christian M. Fromm study plasmoid formation in black hole accretion flows. Magnetic reconnection and plasmoids, blobs of magnetized plasma, are thought to power flares from black holes. The flows they model are threaded by magnetic fields with multiple loops. Radiative cooling, the loss of energy as light, is the factor under test.

The team aims to learn how cooling changes plasmoid birth in such flows. Cooling can thin current sheets and speed reconnection, or drain the energy that flares need. The balance shapes the bright outbursts telescopes see from galactic centers. The work links plasma physics at small scales to the flicker of the largest engines in the sky.
arxiv-2601-11068:
Weiyang Liu and co-authors portrait the history of cosmic reionization inside the early dark energy model. JWST observations of Lyman-alpha light from galaxies at redshifts near eleven to six show rapid reionization. The intergalactic medium cleared within the first 700 million years or so. Early dark energy is a proposed extra ingredient in the young universe.

The authors ask what reionization history that model implies. Reionization timing ties to the first stars and to the expansion history at once. A model that changes early expansion must still clear the fog on schedule. The work tests early dark energy against one of JWST's sharpest new constraints on the young cosmos.
arxiv-2601-11168:
Askar Dzhumadil'daev and Nurlan Ismailov study a branch of pure algebra here. Their 2026 preprint deals with free Novikov algebras. The core move is to symmetrize the Novikov product, that is, to add both orders of a pair. They ask which elements act as null Lagrangians in that world.

To answer, they embed the free algebra in a differential one. The ground field has characteristic zero, a mild base case. Euler operators, also called variational derivatives, do the key work. The team shows the null set is just the set closed under the paired product. They also give a full account of its module structure over the symmetric group.
arxiv-2601-11268:
Christopher Ingenhutt and six coauthors built a mobile star instrument. Their 2026 preprint names it MI2SO, for stellar intensity work. Intensity interferometry times the flicker of starlight at two sites. From that flicker, the size and shape of a star can be read.

The method has found new life at Cherenkov telescope arrays. Those arrays do such work when the Moon is too bright for gamma rays. MI2SO was built as a proof of concept from scratch. It is made just for intensity work, not as a side use. A mobile unit can be set where and when it is needed. That freedom helps tests that fixed arrays cannot easily run.
arxiv-2601-11368:
Ishraq Tashdid, Tasnuva Farheen, and Sazadur Rahman secure chiplet systems in this work. Their 2026 preprint is named InterPUF, on distributed authentication. Modern packages mix chiplets from many vendors on one interposer. Reconfigurable interposers let users plug parts in and swap them.

That freedom brings sharp trust problems to the package. Old security tools do not scale to so open a setup. They also fail to adapt after fabrication is done. The team uses physically unclonable functions, or PUFs, for trust. A PUF gives each chip a unique, hard-to-copy fingerprint. Multi-party computation lets vendors check each other in joint form. No single side must be trusted with the whole check.
arxiv-2601-11568:
Quang-Hung Bui and Anh Son Ta cut the memory cost of training LLMs. Their 2026 preprint is named AdaFRUGAL, on adaptive training. Models like GPT-4, LLaMA, and BLOOM reshaped language tech. Their immense scale brings a heavy training bill with it.

Memory for training is the exorbitant part named here. Weights, gradients, and optimizer states all pile up. AdaFRUGAL controls memory use dynamically as training runs. Adaptive control can spend memory where it helps most. Frugal steps may let smaller labs train bigger models. The work joins a push for efficient large model training. Lower memory walls widen who can build frontier systems.
arxiv-2601-11668:
Houda Yaqine and Christiane Fuchs add households to outbreak models. Their 2026 preprint uses random change equations in an SIR frame. Disease spread is a critical public health challenge for all. Household dynamics and community spread interplay in real outbreaks.

Traditional models often treat populations as homogeneous. That simplification misses crucial household-level interactions. Infections inside a home move faster and cluster more. The team builds an SDE approach on the SIR framework. SIR sorts people as susceptible, infectious, or recovered. Household structure enters the random dynamics of the model. Such models can guide policy that targets homes, not just crowds.
arxiv-2601-11868:
Mike A. Merrill, Alexander G. Shaw, Nicholas Carlini, and a large team built a hard test for AI agents in the terminal. Agents may soon do long, real jobs on their own. Old tests are too easy or too fake to grade top models well.

Their test, Terminal-Bench 2.0, holds 89 tasks in real terminal setups. The tasks come from real work flows. Each task is picked to be hard yet fair to grade. The set gives a shared scale for how far agents have come at real computer work.  Their work shows where AI screens need checks for blind users.
arxiv-2601-11968:
Qihao Zhao, Yunqi Cao, Yangyu Huang, and their co-authors build a tool that can talk with users about music scores and played audio. Broad multimodal models still grasp music poorly. Music needs grounded thought over both the written score and the sound of a played piece.

Their system, named in the work, joins those two streams. Users can ask about a score and hear links to the audio. Such grounded tools could aid music study and practice. The work tests how well the system ties signs on the page to sound.
arxiv-2601-12168:
Elif Cüce, Saeed A. Khan, Boris Mesits, Michael Hatridge, and Hakan E. Türeci classify quantum states in one shot via nonlinear amplification. Quantum amplifiers are nonlinear by nature, and quantum laws set their limits. In most work, amps are run in the linear range to lift signal-to-noise.

That aim suits gauge tasks, but not the task of telling states apart. The team use the nonlinear range on purpose for state calls. A one-shot call that is firm would speed quantum readout. The work reframes amp design for that task.
arxiv-2601-12568:
Maximilian Ammer and Stephan Durr compute a key coefficient for lattice fermion simulations. The coefficient is called c SW, an improvement term for Wilson and Brillouin fermions. Improvement terms cancel errors that come from putting space time on a grid. The team work at one loop order, the first quantum correction level.

They cover fermions treated with stout smearing or Wilson flow. Both tricks smooth the gauge fields to tame noise in the simulation. The glue side can use Wilson or Symanzik actions, and each pairing is covered. Exact one loop values let large scale lattice QCD runs start from a better base. That saves costly tuning on supercomputers later.
arxiv-2601-12868:
Shiyue Hu, Ruizhe Li, and Yanjun Gao study bias tied to race and ethnicity in large language models. These models now operate in high stakes settings, including healthcare and medicine. Demographic traits may be stated outright in text, or inferred by the model itself. Past studies mostly document disparities in final outcomes.

Outcome level evidence gives limited insight into internal mechanisms, though. The team aim to look inside at how such effects arise. Knowing the mechanism matters for any serious fix. A patch on outputs may fail if the inner bias stays. Their work serves fair deployment of models in medicine and beyond.
arxiv-2601-13068:
Pu Lin, Haonan Yang, Bin Ma, and a large team share first data from a new Antarctic scope. The tool is an infrared binocular telescope set at Dome A in Antarctica. Dome A is one of the driest spots on Earth, and that dry air opens a rare window.

Most ground sites lose the band near 1.4 micro metres to water vapour in the air. The team made a new filter that spans 1.34 micro metres up into that band. Their release gives early views taken through it. For star watchers, the data show what a dry polar site can do in a band that is shut from most of the world. The release also tests the scope and its tools in harsh cold.
arxiv-2601-13268:
Zainab Ghafoor and co-authors use a loop of agent checks to make medical AI more safe. Large language models see more use in care work. Yet proof that they meet ethics and safety rules is still a top block to real use in clinics.

Their frame loops in rounds. Two maker models draft and fix text. Two judge agents score the drafts in each round. The loop aims to catch flaws that a one pass check would miss. It also keeps a trace of why a draft changed. For care teams, the work offers a way to lift trust with no loss of the speed that makes such models apt.
arxiv-2601-13468:
Deep Ghoshal does time series tests with no resample, by way of kernel space embeds. Time data that is multi part or curve valued breaks stock tests. Tasks at stake span good fit tests, hunt for a change point in spread, and tests if two series move free of each other.

Resample tools for such tasks are slow and can be shaky. Ghoshal maps each series into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, a space where sense marks turn into spans. Tests then run on those spans in closed form. No boot strap rounds are need. For stats teams with long series, a fast firm test is a clear gain.
arxiv-2601-13668:
Ying Li, En Wang, Li-Sheng Geng, and Ju-Jun Xie study a rare particle decay in theory in 2026. The decay turns a charmed baryon, Lambda-c plus, into a proton, an anti-kaon, and a neutral pion. The team works within the chiral unitary approach, a method for how light particles interact. Their focus is the N(1535) resonance, a short-lived excited state of the nucleon.

They treat N(1535) as dynamically generated, born from the interplay of other particles. That view differs from seeing it as a simple three-quark state. The decay gives a clean test of which view holds. Tests like this sharpen the map of excited baryons.
arxiv-2601-13768:
Wenzhen Yue and co-authors present a lean linear model for forecasting many time series at once in 2026. Their model, vLinear, targets multivariate series, where many values move together. Top forecasters often use self-attention to catch links between series. That step can cost in line with the square of the series count.

vLinear has two parts: a vecTrans module and a WFMLoss objective. The design aims for strong forecasts with linear, not quadratic, cost. Many series arise in energy, traffic, and finance work. A fast, true forecaster for them has broad daily use.
arxiv-2601-13868:
Michi Shinozaki, Masao Mori, Yuka Kaneda, and Kohei Hayashi study the inner shape of dark matter haloes in 2026. Nearby galaxies, mainly dwarfs, show inner mass profiles that depart from cold dark matter norms. A cusp is a sharp inner peak, while a core is a flat center. Baryonic feedback, from normal matter, seems to drive the shift.

The team updates an analytic cusp-core transition model. They add the effect of supernova-driven mass loss, where blasts push gas out. They find a characteristic mass and an energy conversion efficiency for the shift. Those values feed scaling relations that link galaxy traits.
arxiv-2601-13968:
Nguyen Van Thu studies wetting in a mix of three ultracold gases in 2026. The system is a dilute ternary Bose-Einstein condensate, with three components. Wetting here means one component spreads along the border of an other. Thu asks how intraspecies interactions shape the wetting phase diagram.

The work uses the GP formalism, the Gross-Pitaevskii model of condensates. A double-parabola approximation describes the interfacial properties. The case in view has strong segregation between two components. Phase diagrams map which wetting states can exist, guiding lab tests of quantum fluids. The map of states can help labs pick the right mix for their tests. It shows which knobs change the wetting most.
arxiv-2601-14068:
Philippe Heim and Rayna Dimitrova speed up solving games with unbounded data in 2026. Infinite-state games frame the synthesis of reactive systems with unbounded domains. Solving them relies on symbolic fixpoints, mainly symbolic attractors. These computations may not terminate, which blocks synthesis.

Recent acceleration techniques try to force termination. They often rely on acceleration arguments of limited expressiveness. The team's modular attractor acceleration aims for broader power. Systems like controllers and protocols need synthesis that finishes with a proof. Fast, sound games work is key for safe code in planes, cars, and grids. A method that ends more often can widen what teams dare to check.
arxiv-2601-14768:
M. N. Mazziotta and nine co-authors work on precise particle timing in this 2026 paper. Dedicated research and development efforts are underway to couple a thin Cherenkov radiator to Silicon Photomultiplier arrays. The goal is precise charged particle Time-of-Flight measurements. Time-of-flight tells how long a particle took to cross a known distance, which reveals its speed and identity.

Cherenkov radiation is prompt: it is emitted the instant a fast particle passes. That prompt nature makes it an ideal candidate for ultimate timing performance in a time-of-flight detector. The paper presents an efficient and precise Cherenkov-based timing approach using SiPMs. Speed is the whole game. A fast flash, caught at the right tick, names the thing that made it. Readers get detector research aimed at the sharpest possible time stamps.
arxiv-2601-14968:
Mingyue Cheng, Xiaoyu Tao, and co-authors rethink how to sort time series data into classes. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with tasks such as labeling sensor or signal records. Most methods map an input sequence straight onto a single class label.

That direct route has two flaws, the authors say. It uses context poorly, and a one-hot label hides how classes relate in meaning. Their InstructTime++ uses multimodal language modeling instead. It adds an implicit feature enhancement step to bring out richer cues from the series before the class is chosen.
arxiv-2601-15268:
Jesse Jääsaari counts the real zeroes of a special family of modular forms. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with half-integral weight Hecke cusp forms. The forms live in the Kohnen plus subspace, a chosen part of the full space of forms.

He bounds their weight by a large parameter and lets it grow. For a large share of these forms, the count of real zeroes grows at the rate one expects. The paper is a sequel, marked II in its title. It extends an earlier count of the same kind to this wider family.
arxiv-2601-15868:
S. Zhu describes real-time data handling for a major physics detector in a 2026 arXiv paper. The ALICE Time Projection Chamber was upgraded for LHC Run 3. It now runs in continuous readout mode. Lead-lead collisions arrive at rates up to 50 kilohertz. Those collisions produce over three terabytes of raw data per second. No storage system can simply keep that flood. Processing must happen in real time.

The paper details the FPGA pipeline that does this work. FPGAs are chips programmed for one fast, fixed task. The pipeline compresses and filters data as it streams. ALICE studies quark-gluon plasma in heavy-ion collisions. Its physics depends on catching rare events in the flood. A pipeline that keeps up at full rate is an engineering result in its own right.
arxiv-2601-16068:
Chaohua Liang, Xingliang Peng and Jun Matsushima apply neural nets to sound waves in rock that lose strength. Their 2026 preprint sits in earth wave maths. Wave runs help teams read deep rock and find stores or risks. Grid based ways to run waves can be slow. They need step by step runs for each new guess of the ground.

The team uses nets that learn from the laws of wave move. Such nets can run waves forth and also work back to the ground form. The authors test how the grid step size in training shapes the result. Care with steps should keep the net true to real waves. The work aims for fast, sound earth wave tools.
arxiv-2601-16168:
Sehovic, Fossez and Hergert extend a big maths tool to wide nucleus states. Their 2026 preprint deals with first rule maths for nuclei. Reach has grown much in past years of work. Yet the drip lines, where nuclei fall apart, stay hard to place. Hard parts stem from force doubt and from open system acts. Wide states that leak parts act as open systems.

The team joins the Gamow form to a large scale group maths tool. That join lets the tool treat wide states with care. Wide states set the true edge of which nuclei can live. A tool for them sharpens drip line maps. The work pushes first rule maths to that edge.
arxiv-2601-16268:
Christopher Layden and a large team set out a fast, low noise cam on a big scope. Their 2026 preprint names the cam proto-Lightspeed. The cam sits on the Magellan Clay scope at a side port. It takes pics at high speed with very low read noise. Low noise at speed suits brief sky acts like flares and passes.

First runs test if the cam meets its design marks in real use. Sharp, fast pics can catch short acts that slow cams blur. The team built the cam as a test bed for a full build. A good test bed de risks the full cam cost. The work serves teams who watch fast sky change.
arxiv-2601-16768:
The BESIII team in China reports fresh work on charmed mesons. These are short-lived bits of matter with a charm quark. The team has built a huge set of such pairs near a set energy. Pairs born there share a linked quantum state. That link makes the set a rare lab tool. Their 2026 preprint sums what the set can gauge.

The linked state lets the team gauge phase gaps in decays. Those gaps are key to maps of how charm bits change. Fine gauges feed tests of the base theory of matter. They also aid hunts for new effects in charm decays. The set holds twenty inverse femtobarns of data.
arxiv-2601-16868:
Anna Abbatiello, Miroslav Bulíček, and Petr Kaplický test the firmness of flow laws for thick fluids. Their fluid fills a 3D zone and bears heat as it flows. It is thick in a non-Newton way, like glue or blood. Wall heat is set, and the walls grip the flow. No push from the back acts on it. Their 2026 preprint asks if the flow's path stays firm under small shifts.

The stress law in view spans power-law and Ladyzhenskaya forms. For a span of powers, no one knew if paths stay unique. Nor was the energy count on firm ground. Firmness proofs would put such flow codes on safe feet. Thick heat flows sit in plants, food lines, and care gear.
arxiv-2601-17168:
Judy Zhu, Dhari Gandh, Himanshu Joshi, Ahmad Rezaie Mianroodi, Sedef Akinli Kocak, and Dhanesh Ramachandran argue that agent checks must rise a level. Chatbot agents now plan in steps and act in the world. A lone model's word for its acts won't do. Their 2026 preprint calls for system-level checks in place of model tales. The whole chain of steps, tools, and acts must face review.

Such checks trace who set each act in train. They show where blame sits when an act goes wrong. Firms that field agents need that trace for law. It also helps teams fix flaws at the right joint.
arxiv-2601-17268:
Jaideep Pathak and twelve co-authors work on very short-term storm forecasts. Good forecasts of clouds and rain save lives and time. They guide severe weather warnings. They help planes fly safe and solar farms plan output. At storm scale, though, the best tools have clear limits. Math weather models can be slow or coarse. Simple track-forward methods fade fast.

The team learns storm growth straight from observed data. That path aims for sharp forecasts at the scale of single storms. Better short-range skill means warnings can come with more lead time. It also means fewer false calls. For weather teams, a data-led method could sit beside classic models and lift both.
arxiv-2601-17368:
Shuning Zhang and seven co-authors review how privacy policies are shown to users. Policies are the base of informed consent online. Yet most users do not grasp them. Decades of design research have proposed charts, icons, and layered views. Few of those designs spread in real products. The team scopes that body of work from a human-computer interaction view.

They draw guidelines from what the record shows. Good display must fit law's needs and human limits at once. The gap between intent and use is the core problem. Their guidelines can help teams design policy views people read. That would make consent more than a click through a wall of text.
arxiv-2601-17468:
Chia-Ming Lee and five co-authors present ReflexSplit, a method to split reflections from photos. A shot through glass mixes two layers. One is the scene behind the glass. The other is the reflected scene. Past methods confuse the two, mostly in deep decoder layers. Weak fusion and poor scale coordination cause much of that mix-up.

ReflexSplit uses a dual-stream design with three key changes. The streams handle the two layers with more care. Clean splits help photo tools, drivers, and store cameras. Glass is common in all those settings. The work aims at hard mixes, not just faint glare. It gives vision systems a clearer view through real windows.
arxiv-2601-17568:
Amritha Premkumar and Christian Herglotz speed up encoding of 360-degree video. Immersive video must stream at many quality levels. Each level needs its own encode at set resolution and quality steps. For 8K panoramic content, that work is huge. The team works in OMAF streaming workflows, the standard for such media. They propose fast multirate encoding.

Shared work across versions can cut total encode time. Streaming firms pay for each version they compute. Faster prep means fresher live and on-demand content. It also cuts energy per stream. The work targets ultra-high-resolution content, where costs bite most. Gains there scale to the whole catalog.
arxiv-2601-17768:
Raja Gond, Aditya K Kamath, Ramachandran Ramjee, and Ashish Panwar of Microsoft Research study a quirk of large language models. The same prompt can give a different reply each time the model runs. Their 2026 preprint traces the cause to math inside the machine. Adding numbers in a changed order can change the final sum, and batch sizes shift that order.

One fix is to turn off dynamic batching, but that slows the system down a lot. The team instead works on a way to keep results stable while the speed stays high. Their title calls the method verified speculation. Steady output matters for tests, audits, and any use where the same input must give the same output.
arxiv-2601-17868:
Zhihao He and co-authors present VidLaDA, a video language model built on diffusion rather than step-by-step writing. Their 2026 preprint targets video understanding. Most video models read frames with a vision encoder, then let an autoregressive model talk about them. That style has two costs. One-way attention limits how well the model can pool events across time and space. Serial decoding also slows output down.

A bidirectional diffusion design attacks both costs at once. Each part of the reply can draw on the whole video context. Steps can also be refined in parallel rather than one token at a time. The aim is faster, more global video understanding. Such models serve search, summary, and monitoring tasks.
arxiv-2601-18368:
Caterina Fuster-Barceló and six colleagues built a tool that reads MRI scans of the inner ear with no help from a human hand. The scans show a fault where fluid in the ear swells past its right share. Doctors call that fault endolymphatic hydrops, and its size helps them judge ear disease.

Their tool, named OREHAS, runs in three steps. First it sorts the scan slices by type. Next it finds the inner ear in each slice. Last it marks the fluid zones and works out how much of the ear space they fill, ear by ear. Since the whole flow runs on its own, clinics could get the same clear count each time. There would be no slow hand work to slow the count down.
arxiv-2601-18468:
Daniel Hier and Tayo Obafemi-Ajayi ask why some facts stick in a language model and some do not. After first training, a model holds facts with quite unlike strength. Some facts sit in its weights but stay hid when it writes in its plain mode. Some facts are barely there at all.

The pair fine-tune a model on fact pairs from two big maps of body and gene terms. Those maps link each term to a code used in health work. The team then check if the strength of a fact before the tune-up tells how fast the model learns it in the tune-up. A firm link would help teams plan how to teach a model new facts. It would also show which facts need more drill to stick.
arxiv-2601-18568:
Sanu Kumar Gangwar and five colleagues chart the waves that can run through a cloud of cold atoms with a twist. The cloud is a rare state in which many atoms act as one. Its atoms can point in three ways, and a twist in the lab makes spin and path trade push. That trade can let the cloud form stripes that act both as a stiff solid and as a free fluid.

The team work out the full set of waves the cloud can hold, across a wide range of pull strengths. Their maths shows which waves stay calm and which ones grow wild. Wild waves mark where the cloud would break or shift phase. A firm chart helps labs pick set-ups that hold the rare state still. It also guides the hunt for new phases in such clouds.
arxiv-2601-18768:
Nizar El Idrissi and Hicham Zoubeir prove two new claims in the maths of gaps and lengths in spaces with a dot rule. One claim ties the four sides of a four-point form: the long side can't beat the sum set by the rest in a set way. Claims of that kind are old and prized, since they bind how far points can sit from each other. The next claim uses a table of dot scores for a set of points.

That table, called a Gram table, holds the cos-like scores of all pairs. From it, the pair draw fresh bounds on joint gaps. Such bounds feed work in shape maths, in codes, and in the tests that prove a set of points must act in a set way. Pure claims like these are tools that next work can lift whole.
arxiv-2601-19068:
Chaoliang Tang, Hehui Wu, and Junchi Zhang pin down a Turán type bound for sparse hypergraphs. A linear 3-graph links triples of points so that any two links share at most one point. The question: how many links can such a graph hold with no path of length five hiding inside?

The team proves the count stays under a fixed share of the point count, and they name the only graph that hits the bound exactly. It is built from copies of one small graph with eleven points. Sharp bounds with a named extremal case close a problem fully, a prized outcome in combinatorics.
arxiv-2601-19168:
Brianna L. Wimer and seven co-authors help blind students grasp data structures through touch and sound, not pictures. Blind and visually impaired students face built in barriers when learning how data is organized. Most aids just turn diagrams into alt text, which tells how a picture looks, not how the structure works.

Richer aids often fail to scale in complexity or cost. The team builds nonvisual support aimed at the structure itself, so students can reason about links and order directly. Their work was shared at the CHI conference on human factors in computing systems.
arxiv-2601-19468:
N. M. Zubarev and E. A. Kochurin simulate what a charged liquid surface does when an electric field pushes it hard. A non conducting liquid with charge on its free surface, set in a field along the surface normal, grows unstable. The team follows the strongly nonlinear stages of that growth by direct simulation.

Two stages stand out: first, dimples form on the surface; then the pattern develops into sharper structures. Knowing the stages helps read real systems, from inks and sprays to liquid metal devices, where charged surfaces meet strong fields.
arxiv-2601-19568:
Ke Xu and eight colleagues work on a slow step in automated software development: finding the right code. Before an agent can fix or extend a program, it must locate the files and lines that matter. Running search tools one by one is slow. Running them in parallel could help, but agents often call the same tools again and again, wasting the gain.

The team reports that current agents repeat a large share of their tool calls. Their method, FuseSearch, plans parallel searches as a joint problem of quality and efficiency. Calls that add nothing are cut before they run. The goal is fast discovery with less waste. Better code localization speeds up every repair and feature task built on top of it.
arxiv-2601-19668:
Luis Amorim and four colleagues build fake time series that behave like real ones. Forecasting models, especially deep learning ones, need large training sets to generalise well. Real datasets are often small, so data augmentation creates extra examples. Many existing tricks transform the data in ways that break its key properties.

Their method, Grasynda, generates synthetic series using graphs. The graph view is meant to preserve the structure that matters for forecasting. Synthetic series that keep the right properties can train models without leaking real records. The approach targets settings where data is scarce but decisions depend on forecasts. Better augmentation could lift forecast quality in energy, retail, and beyond.
arxiv-2601-19768:
Shir Rozenfeld and five colleagues build a safety monitor for large language models. Activation monitoring watches a model's inner signals, not just its words, to catch harmful behaviour. Existing monitors are trained on broad misuse data. They often suffer from poor precision, little flexibility, and no clear explanation of their alarms.

Their system, GAVEL, moves toward rule-based safety through activation monitoring. Rules let operators define exactly which behaviours to flag. That promises clearer control and more interpretable alerts. A monitor that explains itself is easier to trust and to fix. The work addresses a growing need as language models take on sensitive roles.
arxiv-2601-19868:
Shrajal Bajpai and Lakshmi Kanta Patra work on estimating variances that are known to come in a fixed order. Their data model mixes two normal distributions at different scales. Component-wise estimation asks for each variance separately while respecting the order. Two loss functions frame the problem: squared error loss and entropy loss.

The authors derive general results on when one estimator improves on another. From those results they construct estimators that beat the standard best affine equivariant estimator. Ordered parameters arise wherever theory fixes a ranking in advance. Better estimators sharpen tests and intervals in such problems. The work is a careful piece of decision theory with practical statistical payoff.
arxiv-2601-19968: Youngwoong Cho asks what artificial general intelligence would mean for offensive security work. The essay splits the question in two. First, can every offensive security task be reduced to manipulating symbolic language, meaning representation plus reasoning? Second, are powerful language models enough to handle any such manipulation? The answers decide whether general AI would transform cyber offence. The paper is a position piece, mapping the debate rather than reporting experiments.
arxiv-2601-20068:
Samuel Blitz, Gabriel Herczeg, and David McNutt study the geometry of null hypersurfaces, surfaces swept by light rays. Space-like and time-like surfaces inherit a natural connection from the spacetime around them. Null surfaces, like black hole horizons and the edge of all we can see, do not. That gap makes the physics built on them harder, flat-space holography included.

The authors examine potential Carroll structures on such surfaces. Carrollian geometry, named for the other Carroll limit of relativity, is the natural geometry of null surfaces. They identify special Carrollian manifolds with extra good properties. Clarifying this geometry supports holographic descriptions of gravity in flat space. The work is basic mathematics with physical targets. These are the sheets that light sweeps out. They rim black holes and the far edge of space. Their shape is a deep, hard thing. Few tools fit them well.
arxiv-2601-20268:
Long Van Tran, Truyen Tran, and Phuoc Nguyen study how to estimate the parameters of stochastic differential equations when time information is missing or hidden. These equations model real processes in finance, health, and biology. Standard estimation needs a correctly ordered, accurately stamped sequence of observations.

When the order is corrupted, missing, or withheld for privacy, standard methods often fail. The authors aim for robust estimation that works despite the lost time stamps. Their work matters for fields like medicine, where privacy rules may strip timing from data that researchers still need to model.
arxiv-2601-20468:
Mathis Brossier and four colleagues explore how touch-enabled spherical displays can support climate conversations in museums and science centers. A globe you can touch invites direct, embodied interaction with complex climate data. Groups can gather around it and explore together, which suits public discussion of a shared problem.

Current spherical displays, though, offer limited interaction. The authors run an exploratory study to find chances for richer interaction and the technical means to build it. Better globe interfaces could turn climate data from a lecture into a conversation visitors steer themselves.
arxiv-2601-20568:
Efstratios Zaradoukas, Bardh Prenkaj, and Gjergji Kasneci present a method for making large language models forget chosen training content. During pretraining, models memorize sensitive or copyrighted data. Laws such as the GDPR and the EU AI Act can require that information to be removed from a deployed model, without retraining from scratch.

Their approach uses reinforcement unlearning driven by group relative policy optimization. Unlearning by reinforcement steers the model away from the unwanted content while sparing the rest. A dependable forgetting method would let providers meet legal duties at a fraction of full retraining cost.
arxiv-2601-20668:
Shuhao Liao and nine co-authors study how to train legged robots to walk and move their whole bodies. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents a method they call Growing Policy Optimization, or GPO. The work uses reinforcement learning, where a robot learns by trial and error. The authors frame this as a hard training problem.

The paper explains why such training is so hard in practice. The robot must choose smooth actions across many joints at once. Real hardware also limits what the robot can safely try. And the robot gets few chances to test new moves. GPO is the team's answer to these limits. Readers get a clear view of one current path toward robots that walk well and use their full bodies with skill.
arxiv-2601-20768:
Sergey Meliakov and six co-authors report long-lived electron spins in a perovskite semiconductor. Their 2026 paper measures spin coherence times in the millisecond range. Spin coherence is how long an electron's spin keeps its quantum state. Long coherence is essential for quantum technologies built on semiconductors. The enemy is spin relaxation, which erases that state.

The team used a method called spin mode locking to reveal the long times. They note that spin dynamics hinge on three features of the material. These are the band structure, the crystal symmetry, and quantum confinement. Perovskites are a family of crystals much studied for solar cells. Showing that their spins stay coherent this long opens a path to quantum devices made from them.
arxiv-2601-20868:
Rongzheng Wang and a large team of co-authors rethink how language models design solvers. Their 2026 paper concerns combinatorial optimization, the search for the best arrangement under rules. Large language models have advanced this field through automated heuristic generation. Instead of hand design, an LLM-driven process proposes solvers. It then refines them in rounds to reach high performance.

The authors add dynamics-aware optimization to that loop. The name signals attention to how a solver behaves as it runs. A solver that looks good on paper may waste time in practice. Watching its dynamics can guide the search toward speed as well as quality. The goal is solvers that are both efficient and specialized to their problem. The work speaks to logistics and scheduling, where good heuristics save real money.
arxiv-2601-20968:
Yulie Arad, Stav Ashur, and Nancy Amato speed up how robots refresh their roadmaps when the world changes. Their 2026 paper tackles roadmap graphs in non-static environments. A roadmap is a network of safe paths a robot can follow. When obstacles move, some edges become invalid. Checking each edge with full collision tests is slow. The authors want fast, semi-lazy updates.

They introduce the Red-Green-Gray paradigm. It modifies the earlier SPITE method. Cheap heuristic checks classify each node and edge by validity status. Green edges are safe, red ones are blocked, and gray ones need a closer look. The robot can then repair only what matters. The method suits warehouses and homes where scenes shift often. It keeps planners responsive without full rebuilds.
arxiv-2601-21568:
Antonio Almudévar and Alfonso Ortega unify two ways of judging whether two model representations are alike. One view is functional: can parts be stitched together and still work? The other view is about the information the parts carry.

The authors tie stitching success to conditional mutual information, a classic measure of shared usable content. Their frame covers both views across three dimensions of comparison. A shared yardstick helps researchers decide when two models really compute alike. That judgment matters for merging models, reusing parts, and trusting that a smaller model mirrors a bigger one.
arxiv-2601-21668:
Philipp Krah, Zetao Lin, and five co-authors blend two flow-mapping methods to solve the Vlasov-Poisson equation. That equation governs plasmas and galaxies, where particles move under their own collective field. Semi-Lagrangian methods trace the flow backward to where each parcel began.

One parent method iterates the flow numerically, and the other composes flow maps directly. Each has strengths the other lacks. The hybrid aims for accuracy over long runs without the cost exploding. Long, accurate runs matter for fusion and space plasma work, where small errors compound into wrong predictions about stability.
arxiv-2601-21768:
Alon Rozental argues that large language models are held back by the way they chop text into fixed pieces. Tools such as Byte Pair Encoding split words before learning starts, and that split cannot adapt during training. His 2026 preprint presents Zonkey, a model built to remove that fixed step.

Zonkey is a hierarchical diffusion model with a fully trainable path from raw characters up to representations of whole documents. Its tokenization can be learned along with the rest of the model, and its attention works in terms of probabilities. The aim is a system that adapts better to noisy text and to special fields where standard token splits fit poorly.
arxiv-2601-22068:
Mehmet Ozgur Turkoglu and co-authors make foundation models less cocky. These large pretrained models perform remarkably across tasks, but their predictions are often overconfident and poorly calibrated. The standard cure, training an ensemble of independent models, costs far too much at foundation scale.

The team's 2026 preprint builds ensembles from singular value pieces of a single model, creating varied members without full retraining. Spread among those members gives an estimate of epistemic uncertainty, the model's own ignorance. Calibrated uncertainty matters wherever a model's confidence drives action, from medical triage to financial risk. Because a system that knows when it does not know can hand off to a human in time.
arxiv-2601-22368:
Junyoung Park proves that a class of moving surfaces can glide for all time and settle to a stable shape. The flow is mean curvature flow, which moves a surface by its bend at each point. His 2026 preprint starts from the graph of a rough, merely continuous function over a slab.

He then checks the stability of known translator shapes, which move without changing form. They include the grim reaper curve and flatland and cylinder-like forms. Stability tells us which shapes a real flow would keep. The work is pure math, on how shapes evolve. It firms up a classic theory.
arxiv-2601-23068:
Joao Fonseca and Julia Stoyanovich estimate feature importance without opening the model. Knowing which inputs drive a classifier's decisions is key to explaining it. Shapley values are a popular answer, but they need direct model access and can be too costly to compute exactly.

Their ExplainerPFN approach aims at model-free, zero-shot importance scores for tabular data. Foundation-model style design lets it answer for new datasets at once, without retraining. Cheap, access-free explanations help audit models that vendors keep closed. Zero-shot estimation matters because a fresh dataset should not need a fresh explanation model trained before anyone can use it.
arxiv-2601-23268:
Milton Gomez and a large team release TCBench, a benchmark for tropical cyclone forecasting worldwide. It evaluates short to medium-range forecasts of storm track and intensity, from one to five days ahead. The benchmark builds on the IBTrACS observational record of past storms.

Forecasting is framed as predicting how an existing storm evolves, given its starting position and strength. A model-agnostic setup allows fair comparison across very different systems. Shared global benchmarks help weather centers and AI teams improve warnings together. Conditioning on the storm's initial position and intensity keeps the benchmark focused on evolution, not on storm discovery.
