East Germany was then a new state, built in the Soviet zone of the defeated country. Forecast papers like this one show planners trying to read a satellite's politics month by month. Most such guesses were soon tested by events.
cia-0000049168: An update on progress in the Jesuit murder case is preserved in a CIA item from 1990, kept with the Truth Commission records. Updates like this one were the case's pulse, taken for readers in San Salvador and Washington. Each reported a step, a stall, or a name, in a case that took years to reach a courtroom.
cia-0000049268: The 1990 certification of El Salvador fills a CIA item kept with the Truth Commission records. Certification was the recurring act by which Washington declared the country fit, on human rights grounds, to keep receiving aid. Each round forced the war's record into a yes-or-no shape, and this file holds one round's paper.
cia-0000075168: Briefing of General Maxwell Taylor on redacted material is recorded in declassified CIA document 0000075168, dated June 6, 1961. The general is named while the briefing's substance stays blank in the heading. Readers get a short declassified briefing note whose interest lies in that contrast, a named senior officer and a subject the released record withholds.
cia-0000098268: China's Cultural Revolution in 1968 is the title of declassified CIA document 0000098268, dated November 5, 1968. The heading ties the movement to a single year. Readers find a short declassified paper taking that year as its frame. It is a year-specific companion to narrower China reports. Those reports covered provinces, factions, and daily disruption.
cia-0000100168: Biological Warfare USSR: Additional Rumors of an Accident at the Biological Weapons facility, in cut-short heading form, is declassified CIA document 0000100168, dated September 1, 1979. The word additional shows the rumors were not the first. Readers get the cluster's earliest rumor record, dated within the year of the suspected accident itself.
cia-0000102968:
USSR: Forced Labor on Pipeline is declassified CIA document 0000102968, dated August 6, 1982. Its text weighs recent allegations in the Western press about large-scale Soviet use of forced labor on the Siberian gas export pipeline. The finding, stated early, is that reliable evidence does not support those allegations.

The text notes past use of parolees on compressor station building and at large construction projects, pipelines among them. It also cites nearly two million prisoners confined in about eleven hundred heavily secured camps. Charges of new forced labor camps at seven locations along the route are judged not credible on early analysis.
cia-0000106268: Dated September 4, 1964, declassified CIA document 0000106268 passes on comments pointing to an agreement involving Nguyen Khanh. Its heading misspells present as Presnet and breaks off at the word You. The catalog marks the speaker's name blank in the title. The other party is named only by that broken word in the heading. The brief record preserves the blank, the misspelling, and the ending as released.
cia-0000109068: Possibility of Cuban Arms for the Army of National Liberation is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000109068, dated September 6, 1967. The heading weighs a possibility, not a fact: Cuban arms reaching a named army. Possibility is the first word of the title itself. The brief record shares its date with a companion campus item from Venezuela reporting.
cia-0000119768: With information as of midnight on November 1, 1956, this CIA report covers Hungary three days before the Soviet assault. The capital was enjoying a freedom that would not last the week. The paper preserves that midnight picture from inside the crisis watch. Midnight fell between Nagy's boldest steps and the Soviet reply, which gives this routine hour-stamped paper an almost unbearable tension for later readers.
cia-0000124268: A September 1957 CIA report covers Soviet earth satellite and rocket developments, filed days before Sputnik stunned the world. Its timing gives it a rare quality: a warning written just before the shock it warned about. The paper shows what the agency knew on the edge of the space age. Sputnik rose on October 4, days after this report's date, which makes its survey of Soviet progress read like a forecast fulfilled almost at once.
cia-0000126868: A February 1964 CIA appraisal gives the situation in Zanzibar as it stood in the revolution's first weeks. The sultan had been overthrown in January and the islands were in turmoil. The paper offers Washington's early reading of the new order taking shape there. First appraisals after a revolution set the terms for later reporting, and this one's judgments about the new rulers echoed through the file for years afterward.
cia-0000132568: Two Central American stories share a CIA item dated October 1, 1960. One covers the situation in Guatemala. The other reports rebel incursions into Nicaragua. Six years had passed since the coup that reshaped Guatemala, and new armed challenges were rising in the region. The short item covers both fronts as analysts saw them that autumn.
cia-0000132668:
Latin American reaction to the break between the United States and Cuba fills a CIA paper dated January 5, 1961. Washington had cut its ties with Havana two days before, on January 3. The paper gathers the first shock waves from that cut.

Capitals across the region answered in statements, votes, and private calls. The break was the largest diplomatic shock the hemisphere had felt in years. For readers, the entry catches the response while it was still fresh and unsettled. Later positions hardened, but this paper preserves the first confused days of a new era in the Americas.
cia-0000132768: Action on Cuba at two world bodies fills a CIA paper dated June 4, 1960. One body was the Organization of American States. The other was the United Nations. Havana was taking its case to every forum open to it that year. The short paper covers both tracks and the events inside Cuba that stood behind them.
cia-0000134268: Cuba widening its ties with the Sino-Soviet bloc fills item 4 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated February 3, 1960. Both Moscow and Beijing were courting Havana that winter, and Havana welcomed both sides. Each fresh tie bound the island tighter to the communist world. The short item tracks the growth of those links.
cia-0000135868: The CIA meeting record of 3 October 1952 is about a psychological warfare conference in a place deleted from the heading, and it survives in declassified form. Behind the paper stands PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA campaign against President Arbenz that closed with the 1954 coup in Guatemala. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000135968: On 2 January 1954, the agency filed a cable, now declassified, on a possible penetration operation, a plan to plant the station's own people inside the other camp. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136068: The CIA cable from 2 April 1954 deals with the importance of a mission, name deleted, with a substitute plan judged unsatisfactory, in a file now declassified. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136168: A cable of 6 April 1954 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with tasking ODACID. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136268: Policy guidance for the officers CADICK and BRODFROST fills this June 1954 LINCOLN cable from the PBSUCCESS operation. Among the permissions granted, CADICK may request flak suppression attacks on anti-aircraft positions, choosing targets far from barracks, buildings, and crowds. Other passages insist attacks be carried out in ways that limit the number of combatants exposed. It is headquarters setting rules for air power while the Guatemala fighting was under way.
cia-0000136368: Aircraft disposition needs rethinking, LINCOLN cables in June 1954, because new factors have arisen: an OAS inspection team is returning and STORAX is holding aircraft. In view of these, the station proposes immediate implementation of a plan under which PBSUCCESS must clear out. The fragment is brief and partly garbled, but its direction is plain: the operation's planes had become a liability once foreign inspectors were watching. Cover, not combat, now drove the air plan.
cia-0000138968: Panama's communist party has issued a flysheet, this December 1963 report states. The Partido del Pueblo stands behind it. A national democratic movement ostensibly sponsors it. The flysheet attacks both government and opposition alliances. They failed to fix the country's grave problems, it says. They failed to win full sovereignty over national territory. They care only for political control and material benefit. The flysheet calls on independent groups to act. The report also covers communist talks with Arnulfo Arias. A party plenum will fix strategy for the May 1964 elections.
cia-0000139168: A 1978 excerpt from a daily diary. Diaries record day-to-day events. The typo is in the original catalog. The catalog spells it 'Daily Dairy.' The excerpts cover daily entries. The document is kept here.
cia-0000139368: Terms of reference for NIE 11-8/1-61 are forwarded in this July 1961 memorandum. The estimate covers Soviet capabilities for long range attack. Representatives are asked to meet on 14 August. The meeting sits in the Administration Building. The same representatives will discuss the annexes of a companion estimate. Both discussions will run at one sitting. Willard Matthias signed the memo. The sample preserves the forwarding memo only. The estimate's missile and bomber judgments are not in this excerpt. It is paperwork behind the missile-gap era's central estimate.
cia-06711368: CLOAKS, DAGGERS, AND DICE: HOW THE CIA USES GAMES, a CIA document. The gaming article. This file preserves that declassified paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Writers of history may cite it later in their work.
condon-report-1968:
The United States Air Force paid for a full science study of UFOs, and the study closed the file in 1968. The Condon Report, made at the University of Colorado under Edward Condon, is that study in full. Its word was blunt: more study of UFOs was not worth the cost.

Teams weighed sightings, photos, and physical traces case by case for two years. The report found no proof that the things seen came from past the earth, and much proof of error and hoax. On its word the Air Force shut Project Blue Book in 1969. No paper in the UFO file has weighed more since.
darwin-variation-vol-1-1868:
After the Origin of Species, Darwin set out to print the mass of facts behind his theory. The first volume of The Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication appeared in 1868. It surveys bred animals, from pigeons and dogs to horses and cattle.

Darwin records how breeders pick traits, how traits pass to the young, and how strange forms appear without plan. He moves through poultry, rabbits, fruit trees, and grain in dense, careful detail. Pigeons get special care, since their many breeds showed Darwin how far selection could go. Breeders and biologists mined the volume for years as a storehouse of evidence.
darwin-variation-vol-2-1868:
The second volume of Darwin's Variation, also published in 1868, turns from facts to causes. Having listed how bred animals and plants change, Darwin asks why those changes happen and how they pass on. It is the more daring half of the work.

Here he sets out pangenesis, his guess that tiny particles from every part of the body gather in the seed. Later science dropped that guess, but the questions he framed drove the study of inheritance for decades. The volume closes his case that selection, by man or nature, explains the forms of life.
dilke-greater-britain-1868:
Charles Dilke was a young British writer and member of Parliament who traveled around the English-speaking world in the 1860s. His 1868 book Greater Britain reports that trip through America, Australia, and India. He was only in his twenties when the trip made his name. It was a bestseller in its day.

Dilke described how English speech, law, and habits were spreading across whole continents. He asked what that spread meant for the future power of Britain and the United States. The book gave a name and a shape to the idea of a worldwide English-speaking family of nations.
dryden-essay-dramatic-poesy-1668:
John Dryden published An Essay of Dramatic Poesy in 1668, just after the London theaters reopened following plague and fire. Dryden was already England's leading playwright and critic. The essay takes the form of a conversation among four friends.

The friends drift in a boat on the Thames while a naval battle sounds in the distance. They debate whether ancient or modern writers are better, and whether French order or English variety makes stronger plays. Dryden gives each side its best case before siding, mostly, with the English. The essay is graceful, balanced, and often called the first real work of English literary criticism.
europmc-pmc10117668:
Zhao, Sun, and Liu review bacterial biofilms in a 2023 paper, from their definition to treatment strategies. Biofilms are communities of bacteria wrapped in a self-made slime layer. They form on teeth, implants, wounds, and pipes, and they make infections hard to clear because drugs and immune cells struggle to reach the bacteria inside.

The review explains how biofilms build up step by step. It covers the diseases they cause and the ways doctors fight them, from antibiotics to surface coatings. The paper is a full guide to a stubborn problem in medicine.
europmc-pmc10567568:
Luedtke and a vast team of co-authors gave the second world check on amphibians in 2023. The check scored 8,011 species for the IUCN Red List of threatened species. Frogs, toads, and salamanders face threats from habitat loss, disease, and a warming climate. Set checks over time guide where rescue funds should go.

Amphibians rank as the most threatened backboned group, at 40.7% of species. Luedtke reports that their state has worsened since the first check in 2004. Disease and habitat loss drove 91% of declines from 1980 to 2004. Since 2004, climate change leads, at 39% of declines. Salamanders and the tropics of the Americas fare worst. Some species have bounced back with aid.
europmc-pmc10834368:
Yin and co-authors profiled blood immunity in people with long COVID in this 2024 study. Long COVID is the set of lasting symptoms that follow at least one in ten COVID infections. Its cause is still poorly understood. The team used deep lab assays and antibody tests on blood taken eight months after infection, comparing people with clear long COVID against those who recovered.

People with long COVID showed body-wide swelling and off-track immune patterns, the team found. Their T cells, a type of white blood cell, were shifted toward tissue sites and worn out. Antibody levels against the virus were higher, yet T cell and B cell responses did not line up well. The authors say this poor teamwork between immune arms may drive the lasting illness. They frame the work as a map for future treatment ideas.
europmc-pmc11177268:
Wang and a large team review glow-based probes that detect disease molecules in this 2024 paper. Fluorescent probes are molecules that light up when they meet a chosen target. Finding disease-related biomarkers early is essential for diagnosis and for judging how a disease progresses. Probes offer high sensitivity and selectivity, meaning they react strongly and only to the right target.

The review covers probes for active molecules tied to organ damage, inflammation, cancers, heart disease, and brain disorders. It explains the design strategies that let a probe find and quantify its target inside cells and in living tissue. Some designs pair diagnosis with therapy by also regulating the target molecule. Challenges and the outlook close the paper. The authors aim at accurate detection of disease biomarkers for both research and clinic use.
europmc-pmc11323968:
Wang and colleagues review nanotechnology for finding and treating malignant tumours in this 2024 paper. Cancer is still a major threat to human health. Nanomedicine engineers particles at the scale of billionths of a metre for medical use. Such particles can serve as contrast agents that sharpen scans, enabling high sensitivity and high-resolution tumour detection.

Nanoprobes and nanobiosensors open further routes to label and detect tumours, the authors say. For therapy, engineered carriers ferry drugs or gene fragments into tumour tissue. They reach it by passive leaking through tumour vessels or by active homing to tumour markers. That targeting boosts effect while sparing healthy tissue. Particles also sensitise tumours to radiation and power heat-based therapy. The review summarises designs and results across these uses.
europmc-pmc1141268:
Saito, Ishizuka, Siomi, and Siomi pin down the complex that finishes making microRNAs in fly cells in this 2005 study. MicroRNAs are small RNAs that do not code for protein. They bind target messages and either cut them or block their use. They are cut to size in steps: a complex in the nucleus frees a hairpin-shaped early form, and Dicer cuts it again in the cell body.

Dicer-1 works with Loquacious, a protein that binds double-stranded RNA, they show. Removing either protein made the early forms pile up in cultured S2 cells. Pulling the proteins out of cells brought down a working complex that held both. Loquacious sped the cutting and aimed it at the right early form. The authors say this partner is how the cell controls the making of microRNAs, and so the use of the genes they govern.
europmc-pmc1160568:
Weisz, Moratti, Meinzer, Dohrmann, and Elbert compare resting brain activity in people with and without tinnitus in this 2005 study. Tinnitus is the perception of ringing or noise with no external source. Its neural mechanisms were poorly understood, and no group study had compared spontaneous brain activity. The team recorded five minutes of resting brain signals with a whole-head neuromagnetometer.

The tinnitus group, 17 people, showed markedly reduced alpha power and enhanced delta power versus 16 controls, they found. Alpha means brain waves at 8 to 12 cycles per second, delta at 1.5 to 4. The pattern was strongest in temporal regions, the brain areas above the ears. It also tracked with tinnitus-related distress, especially in right temporal and left frontal areas. Effects were stronger for alpha than delta. The authors link distress to this abnormal activity pattern.
europmc-pmc11607068:
Liu, Zhou, Ali, Lathia, and Chen review immunotherapy for glioblastoma in this 2024 paper. Glioblastoma is an aggressive and lethal brain tumour in adults. Standard care offers minimal benefit, and most patients see the tumour return. Immune-based treatments have advanced in many cancers but benefit this one little, for three named reasons.

The brain's unique immune profile, the tumour's cell heterogeneity, and its immunosuppressive microenvironment all block progress, the authors explain. The review details current strategies: immune checkpoint inhibitors, adoptive T-cell therapies, tumour vaccines, and oncolytic viral therapies, which use viruses that infect tumour cells. It then discusses the molecular mechanisms behind resistance. Strategies to overcome resistance likely require combination therapies, they argue. Future perspectives for each approach are laid out in depth.
europmc-pmc1240368:
Carmichael and a large team investigated deadly poisonings in Brazil in 2001. At a dialysis clinic in Caruaru, patients fell ill after treatment. Most showed vision problems, nausea, and vomiting. One hundred developed acute liver failure, and 76 died.

Water source checks found algae that make potent toxins. Patient blood and liver samples held the same toxin groups. Two toxin types from cyanobacteria were identified. Animal study comparisons pointed to one group as the main killer. Carmichael shows how tainted water reached patients through dialysis lines. Fifty-two deaths were tied to the named syndrome by December 1996.
europmc-pmc1716168:
Filling gaps in survey answers can be done many ways, with unlike results. Shrive and co-authors compared six methods in 2006 on a 20-question depression scale completed by 1,580 patients. They deleted values under three missing-data patterns to test each filler.

With ten percent missing, all methods but random filling scored near-perfect agreement, above 0.80. Multiple imputation gave the most valid values, with a kappa of 0.89. Single regression and each person's own mean also performed well. Random selection from 1 to 4 lagged badly. Shrive gives scale users an evidence-based ranking for patching holes.
europmc-pmc1779568:
Collins and co-authors set out in 2006 to sharpen how genetic interaction data are read at large scale. A genetic interaction occurs when the effect of changing two genes together differs from what each change alone predicts. Such data come from tools named synthetic genetic array and E-MAP, which test many gene pairs.

The paper presents a new scoring method that turns raw growth data into quantitative epistasis scores, with epistasis meaning one gene masking or altering another. The method accounts for the strength of each single mutation before judging the pair. That step yields high-confidence scores rather than rough yes or no calls. Cleaner scores let researchers group genes into shared pathways and map how the cell is organized by function.
europmc-pmc1867968:
Eskenazi and co-authors followed Mexican-American children in 2007 to test whether organophosphate pesticides harm early brain development. These insect killers are widely used on farms and in homes, and animal work flags them as developmental neurotoxicants. The children came from a California birth cohort of mostly Latino farm-worker families.

The team measured pesticide breakdown products in urine from mothers during pregnancy and from the children themselves. Development was scored at 6, 12, and 24 months with the Bayley Scales, plus a behavior checklist near age two. Higher pregnancy levels generally went with lower mental development scores. At 24 months the link was firm: each tenfold rise in prenatal metabolites meant 3.5 points lower on the mental index. The children's own levels pointed the other way, a contrast the authors discuss.
europmc-pmc2000968:
Hatta and co-workers examined in 2007 how one viral protein position affects H5N1 flu growth in mice. H5N1 bird flu had spread across Asia, Europe and Africa, killing many infected people. Yet it rarely passed between humans. The team focused on position 627 of the PB2 protein. They compared viruses carrying lysine there against those carrying glutamate.

Lysine viruses grew well in lungs and in nasal turbinates, the upper airway tissues. They also grew well in cells at 33 degrees, the cooler upper airway temperature. Glutamate viruses grew less well in the nose and at low temperature. The authors argue that strong upper airway growth could help bird viruses adapt to humans and spread between people.
europmc-pmc2124968: Another medical paper on the spleen's relation to blood destruction and hemolysis. The organ again. This article preserves that hematology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2125468: A medical paper with a study of the physiological activity of adenomata of the thyroid gland. The overactive thyroid tumors. This article preserves that endocrinology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2128168: A medical paper on preparation of collodion sacs for bacteriology. The sacs, made. This article preserves that laboratory method. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2128368: A medical paper with further studies on the etiological significance of Vibrio fetus. The cattle germ. This article preserves that veterinary bacteriology. Future scholars will discover it. History keeps its place secure. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2131068: A second installment asked again how fierce the paratyphoid germ is and how well hosts withstand it. Virulence met susceptibility in fresh experiments. The germ-host contest, remeasured. The article preserves that bacteriology research. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2131768: A medical paper on biology of Bacterium lepisepticum, physical and cultural characteristics. The rabbit germ's nature. This article preserves that bacteriology. It awaits future readers. Its place in history is secure. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2140768: A biology paper on the activation of starfish eggs by acids. The wakened eggs. This article preserves that embryology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2140868: A biology paper on curves of growth, especially in relation to temperature. The growth curves. This article preserves that biology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2259168:
Hurt, Kawasaki, Klarmann, Thomas and Farrar isolated a stem-like prostate cancer cell population in 2008. Cancer stem cells are thought to seed tumours and survive treatment, causing relapse. Using flow cytometry, the team separated prostate cells marked CD44 positive and CD24 negative. They tested these cells for colony growth, tumour formation in mice, and gene expression, and compared their expression pattern with patient survival data.

As few as 100 of these cells formed tumours in immunodeficient mice. They also formed colonies in soft agar and grew as floating spheres in special media, keeping their gene pattern. They expressed stem cell maintenance genes including BMI-1 and Oct-3/4. Adding serum made them settle and shift toward the differentiated parent pattern. Their gene signature predicted poor patient prognosis, making them a model matching the worst human disease.
europmc-pmc2394368:
Bradburn, Clark, Love, and Altman continued their survival analysis series in 2003 with multi-factor methods. Single-factor comparisons can mislead, since groups often differ in age or stage as well as in the factor under study. This second part explains how statistical models separate those tangled effects.

The authors introduce models that estimate the effect of one or more predictors on survival at once. Central among them is the Cox proportional hazards model, which expresses each factor's effect as a hazard ratio, a multiplier on the risk of the event at any moment. They show how to read such ratios and their uncertainty ranges. The part builds on the first paper's curves and logrank tests, which compare groups without adjustment. Their stated aim was correct use: adjusting for the right factors, in the right way.
europmc-pmc2474968:
O'Mahony and colleagues showed that a friendly gut bacterium trains immune calming cells in mice in 2008. The bacterium, Bifidobacterium infantis, normally lives in the gut without causing disease. The team fed it to mice, then challenged them with Salmonella, a food-poisoning bacterium, or with a bacterial toxin.

Live imaging showed the bacterium strongly suppressed activation of NF-kappaB, the immune system's master alarm switch, during both challenges. Bacterial counts and sickness scores fell as well. Alarm cytokine release and immune cell activation markers dropped in the fed mice. Meanwhile, regulatory T cells, the immune cells that restrain overreaction, rose in gut lining and spleen. Moving those regulatory cells into unfed mice transferred the calming effect with them. The authors said one commensal species can build the cell population that keeps gut immunity from overshooting.
europmc-pmc2483468:
McCoy described solving protein complex structures with the Phaser program in 2007. Protein complexes are machines built from several protein parts locked together. X-ray crystallography can reveal their shapes, but the raw data give wave phases that must be recovered. Molecular replacement recovers them by fitting a known similar structure into the new data.

The paper walks through four case studies where that approach worked on complexes. Phaser uses maximum likelihood, a statistical method that scores fits by how probable the data are given the model, rather than simple pattern matching. That scoring handles weak and noisy data better, a common problem when the model is only partly right or the complex is large. The case studies show the settings and decisions that got each structure solved. McCoy presented them as practical guidance for crystallographers facing stubborn complex structures.
europmc-pmc2658868:
Excoffier, Laval, and Schneider presented in 2007 version 3.0 of Arlequin, a software package for studying how gene patterns vary across populations. Such data reveal how groups mate, split, and spread over time. Field researchers gather many data types, from DNA sequences to fast-changing markers, and need one tool that handles them all.

Arlequin computes standard diversity measures, estimates gene and haplotype frequencies, and tests whether patterns fit neutral evolution or past population growth. Its centerpiece method, called AMOVA, splits variation into parts within and between groups. Version 3 added a fresh graphic interface and sturdier handling of input files. Two new methods came with it: one guesses the hidden pairing of gene copies from mixed data, the other estimates how a population spread across space from DNA patterns. The Windows version was free to download.
europmc-pmc2660368:
Boyer and co-authors mapped in 2009 a bacterial weapon called the type VI secretion system by comparing more than 500 bacterial genomes. The system was newly found to help bacteria attack hosts, but its parts and spread were unclear. Computer comparison across genomes let the team sort core parts from optional extras.

They found a core of 13 proteins, kept nearly the same in harmful and harmless bacteria alike. Around it sat extra pieces that varied by setting, as if the system had been tuned for many homes. In all, 176 copies turned up in 92 kinds of bacteria, each arranged in the same gene order. Family trees of the core genes showed the system spreads mainly by jumping sideways between bacteria, not by inheritance alone. Some exported proteins carry tails resembling glue or cutting enzymes, hinting at how the weapon harms its targets.
europmc-pmc2672368:
Valavanidis, Vlachogianni, and Fiotakis studied in 2009 how tobacco smoke damages the body through free radicals, unstable molecules that tear at cells. Smoke carries both short-lived radicals and stable ones stored in tar. Using magnetic resonance tools that can hear radicals directly, the team measured what those radicals do.

They found the tar's semiquinone radicals can recycle themselves, keeping their attack going. Watery tar extracts also marked DNA with a damaged building block known as a signpost of cancer risk. Worse, smoke teamed up with other breathable particles to brew extra hydroxyl radicals, the most violent kind. The boost was strongest with asbestos fibers, fine city dust, and diesel soot. Plain and special bio-filters, they add, barely cut the radical load, undercutting claims that filtered smoke is safer on this count.
europmc-pmc2723868:
Roepstorff and co-authors compared in 2009 how six growth-factor ligands, signals that bind the EGF receptor, affect where that receptor goes inside the cell. Pulling the receptor inside and destroying it in lysosomes, the cell recycling bins, is a main way to switch its signal off. One ligand was known to send it for destruction, while another caused recycling and lasting signaling.

All six ligands pulled the receptor inside, but sorting differed sharply. Two sent all receptors for lysosomal destruction, and two caused full recycling to the surface. EGF destroyed most but not all receptors, while amphiregulin recycled them at fast and slow rates. Lasting tagging of the receptor for destruction tracked with lasting activation.
europmc-pmc2734568:
Lugtenberg and co-authors asked in 2009 why Dutch family doctors often do not follow guideline advice in daily practice. Guidelines are widely shared and promoted, yet uptake stays poor. Each advice item within one guideline can face distinct obstacles. So they studied barriers per item rather than per guideline as a whole.

Thirty doctors in six focus groups discussed fifty-six key items from twelve national guidelines. Barriers differed widely, with each item showing its own pattern. Doubt over whether advice fits a patient or rests on solid proof topped the list. Office limits, lack of knowledge, and unclear wording followed. Tailored plans per item are needed, plus clearer proof reporting in guidelines.
europmc-pmc2762768:
Atkinson, Saperstein, and Pleis analyzed in 2009 a national probability sample to map how United States Internet users employ the web for health. Online tools could help people manage health and care, but who uses which tools was unclear. They studied three behaviors in a 2005 national survey. It covered over three thousand Internet users. The behaviors were searching for health information, joining online support groups, and buying medicine or vitamins.

Fifty-eight percent had searched for health information for themselves in the past year, while support group use was rare and online purchases sat in between. Women searched more, as did heavier Internet users. Those with home or work broadband access searched more. Less educated users searched less. Support groups drew users in fair or poor health. They also drew users with lower incomes. Online buying peaked in middle age.
europmc-pmc2792768:
Terwilliger set out a new math method in 2000 for sharpening the electron density maps used to build models of large molecules. Such maps come from X-ray experiments, but the phase data they rest on is often too weak to give a clear picture on its own.

Older fixes altered the map directly, then struggled to weigh old and new data fairly. The new approach builds likelihood functions, which score how probable a map is given what is already known about likely density patterns. Because the scoring can fold in many kinds of prior knowledge, it applies across a wide range of cases in crystallography, the field that reads molecule shapes from crystals.
europmc-pmc2844368:
Arantes and Saddler reviewed in 2010 a hidden bottleneck in turning plant fiber into fuel alcohol: enzymes often cannot reach the cellulose they are meant to digest. Cellulose chains lie buried inside tightly packed, ordered fibers wrapped in other plant polymers. Pretreatment plus heavy enzyme doses work around the problem, but at a cost that blocks commercial use.

Rather than shaving fibers layer by layer, certain helper proteins seem to loosen and disrupt the packed regions first, opening fresh surface for the cutting enzymes. The authors call this opening step amorphogenesis. They survey the agents proposed to perform it, from expanding proteins to oxidative enzymes, and weigh how each might raise the speed and completeness of cellulose breakdown.
europmc-pmc2858668:
Sorting lung cancers by looks alone predicts survival poorly, so Hou and colleagues turned to gene activity patterns in this 2010 study. They profiled tumors from ninety-one patients with non-small cell lung cancer, the most common lung cancer type. Gene expression means which genes are switched on in the tumor cells.

Hou found a five-gene pattern that cleanly split tumor samples from healthy lung tissue in two large groups. A second pattern of seventy-five genes separated the main tumor subtypes seen under the microscope. Best of all, seventeen genes tracked how long patients lived after surgery and split them into high-risk and low-risk groups. The same split held in a separate group of ninety-six patients from another center.
europmc-pmc2872668:
Zeller and a very large team charted in 2010 how gene activity varies in human blood cells and what drives that variation. They studied monocytes, immune cells tied to heart and vessel disease, from nearly fifteen hundred unrelated adults. Gene activity was matched against more than six hundred seventy-five thousand DNA variants and ten common heart risk factors.

Out of nearly thirteen thousand active genes, thousands of activity traits traced to nearby DNA variants, most acting locally. Traits linked to blood pressure, blood fats, or body weight rarely explained how known risk variants work, which warns against simple stories. Hundreds of activity traits did track the risk factors themselves at strict thresholds. The dataset became a reference for separating genetic control of gene activity from lifestyle effects.
europmc-pmc2887168:
Rossaint and the Advanced Bleeding Care in Trauma task force issued in 2010 an updated European guideline for stopping bleeding after major injury. Uncontrolled bleeding is a leading preventable cause of trauma death, and practice had shifted since their 2007 version. A multidisciplinary panel graded the published evidence with the GRADE system, a standard ladder for rating proof quality.

New advice covers how to monitor clotting at the bedside and support it early. It also covers local clot-promoting measures and tourniquets. The roles of calcium and the drug desmopressin are spelled out too. Older recommendations were re-graded against the newer literature. The document walks teams from first assessment through surgery and clotting support in one shared sequence.
europmc-pmc3000368:
Mendenhall and co-authors showed in 2010 that GC-rich DNA stretches recruit a silencing complex called PRC2 in mouse embryonic stem cells. Polycomb proteins shut off development genes in the early embryo, but the mammal signal calling them in was obscure.

Inserting large engineered DNA pieces, they found one region that drew the complex in fresh. They then narrowed the trigger to a CpG island inside it. That island proved both required and enough on its own. Removing activating motifs from a busy island let it recruit the complex too, and even bacterial DNA pieces with matching richness worked. The rule: rich, quiet stretches call the silencers.
europmc-pmc3014868:
Napierska and co-authors reviewed the hazards of nanosilica, tiny silica particles made at industrial scale for products and medicine, in a 2010 article. Unlike the well-studied larger crystalline form, the nano form's safety record was thin and confusing.

Cell studies report uptake, dose and size linked cell death, raised reactive oxygen, and inflammatory stimulation. The few animal studies show mostly reversible lung inflammation, small nodules, and patches of lung damage, without progressive scarring. Because particle traits vary so much between products, the authors call for standardised materials before firm safety verdicts.
europmc-pmc3029168:
Shepard and coauthors estimated in 2011 what dengue illness costs the Americas each year. Dengue is a mosquito spread virus that causes fever and, in severe cases, dangerous bleeding. The team combined national case counts from 2000 to 2007 with cost studies and with estimates of how many cases never get reported.

Their total came to roughly two billion dollars a year on average, though the figure swung widely between years and outbreak sizes. Even so, the count left out spending on mosquito control, so the true burden is likely higher. The authors note the cost tops that of several other viral illnesses. The numbers are meant to help governments weigh prevention programs against the losses dengue already causes.
europmc-pmc3061868:
Nanthakumar and colleagues traced in 2011 the cause of a devastating gut disease of premature babies to an immune system that has not yet grown up. The disease, necrotizing enterocolitis, strikes mainly preterm infants and kills many of them. Diseased gut tissue shows an outsized outpouring of one inflammatory signal. The team compared immune gene activity in gut lining cells from fetuses, children, and patients.

Alarm sensors and their helper molecules were turned up in immature gut cells, while the brakes on those pathways were turned down, and patients showed the pattern pushed further still. The same lopsided profile appeared in immature human gut grown in lab animals, but not in mature gut. A maturing hormone partly corrected it. Silencing either of two brake genes in fetal cells reproduced the runaway response. The authors conclude the disease exploits a normal developmental stage.
europmc-pmc3117868:
Sandra Varum and colleagues compared energy use in flexible human stem cells and their mature offspring in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Such stem cells can become any body cell type, which makes them prized for research and future therapies, though stray undifferentiated cells can form tumours. How they power themselves was the focus here.

Both embryo-derived cells and reprogrammed adult cells leaned mainly on sugar breakdown without oxygen, even when oxygen was plentiful, unlike their mature counterparts. Their power stations sat in a less developed state, and key enzymes favoured the fast sugar route. Reprogrammed cells clustered with embryo cells rather than with the adult cells they came from. The profile may help spot fully reprogrammed cells and understand tumour-like growth.
europmc-pmc3262968:
Ashour Ahmed and colleagues measured how universal TP53 mutations are in the most important form of ovarian cancer, in this 2010 study in the Journal of Pathology. Earlier estimates were muddied by mixed patient groups and inconsistent methods. The team sequenced the gene thoroughly in tumor DNA from a carefully defined set of patients with high-grade serous carcinoma.

Pathogenic mutations appeared in almost every confirmed case, well over nine in ten. Reviewing the few mutation-negative samples changed the picture. They showed either hidden p53 failure, through overactive partner proteins, or samples that were not truly this cancer type. The rate of p53 dysfunction thus approached one hundred percent. Mutation status did not predict survival. The authors conclude that a broken TP53 is a founding driver of this cancer, present too uniformly to serve as a prognostic marker.
europmc-pmc3269368:
Jérôme Galon and a large group of colleagues proposed classifying cancers by their immune score in this 2012 paper in the Journal of Translational Medicine. Standard staging measures tumor size, lymph node spread, and metastasis, but patients at the same stage often fare very differently, and staging cannot predict response to therapy. Mounting evidence shows the host immune system strongly shapes outcomes.

Large patient cohorts indicate that scoring the immune cells infiltrating a tumor can predict prognosis as well as or better than conventional staging. The authors argue immune scoring should join routine diagnosis and classification. The obstacle is harmonization: laboratories differ in assays, cell types counted, regions chosen, and counting methods. The paper announces an international task force to standardize the assay and push the immune score into clinics worldwide.
europmc-pmc3289668:
Kraning-Rush, Califano, and Reinhart-King measured how hard cancer cells pull on their surroundings, in work published in 2012. Cells that spread to new sites must push through dense tissue, yet doctors have no direct test for how likely a tumor is to spread. Using a microscopy method that tracks cell pulling forces, the team compared lines of breast, prostate, and lung cancer cells.

Cells known to spread pulled much harder than lines that stay put, and the same pattern held in a related set of breast cells. Stiffer, collagen rich surfaces raised the pulling forces further. The results suggest that the physical strength of a cell helps drive spread, and that the tissue around a tumor shapes that strength.
europmc-pmc3302668:
Corcoran and co-authors introduced a computer tool for pinpointing where proteins grip RNA, in a 2011 methods paper. New lab methods freeze proteins onto the RNA they hold and then sequence the fragments, revealing binding sites across the whole cell. The variant they studied uses a light activated building block that marks the exact contact point with a telltale letter change in the sequence.

Their tool, named PARalyzer, turns that letter change signal into high confidence binding sites with far less background noise. It also recovers the short sequence patterns that each protein prefers. The authors provide practical guidelines for using the approach, which helps researchers map how proteins control RNA splicing, stability, and decay.
europmc-pmc3302868:
Lou and colleagues found direct living bridges between cells in a rare chest cancer, reporting in 2012. The bridges, called tunneling nanotubes, are thin strands of cell membrane that link cells and pass cargo between them. They had been seen before only in lab grown cell lines, leaving their role in real tumors unknown.

Working with mesothelioma cells, an aggressive cancer of the chest lining, the team watched nanotubes carry small parcels, proteins, and even mitochondria between cells in both directions. The bridges formed between cancer cells, or between healthy lining cells, but not across the two kinds. Two common drugs suppressed their formation. Microscopy of surgical samples then confirmed nanotubes inside human tumors for the first time.
europmc-pmc3316968:
Swerdlow and fellow members of a large consortium used human genetics to test whether blocking an inflammation signal could prevent heart disease, reporting in 2012. High blood levels of the signal, interleukin 6, track with higher heart risk, and a licensed arthritis drug already blocks its receptor. The question was whether that blocking would help hearts or merely treat joints.

Nature provided the experiment. People born with a gene variant that mildly dulls the receptor showed the same blood changes the drug produces, including lower levels of two inflammation markers. Across forty studies with well over a hundred thousand people, carriers also had modestly lower odds of coronary heart disease. The authors conclude the signal likely helps cause heart disease, and that receptor blocking deserves proper trials as prevention.
europmc-pmc3326568:
West, Milne, Truong, Macpherson, Nelson, and Watson asked whether immune cells inside a tumor predict how breast cancer answers chemotherapy, reporting in 2011. Some breast tumors are crowded with lymphocytes, the white blood cells that attack cancer. The team focused on tumors lacking the estrogen receptor, a group that often carries many such cells and has fewer treatment options.

In the first group of patients, treated with anthracycline drugs before surgery, tumors rich in lymphocytes vanished completely far more often than lymphocyte poor ones. Killer T cells were the subtype carrying the signal, and it held for both major aggressive subtypes. In a second group followed for years, the same drugs improved survival only when tumors carried plenty of these cells, while a different drug mix showed no such pattern. The authors call for trials of lymphocyte based tests to guide drug choice.
europmc-pmc3368268:
Schmidt and colleagues compared DNA binding maps from six mammals in 2012 to trace how one key regulator spreads. CTCF is a protein that binds set places on DNA and helps organize how genes are switched on. Its binding sites are usually kept much the same across species.

The team catalogued over five thousand shared binding sites, then found waves where jumping DNA elements had copied CTCF sites into new places. Rodents, dogs, and opossums each gained their own sets this way, and many copies now act as insulators for nearby genes. Fossil repeats near the oldest sites suggest the process began hundreds of millions of years ago.
europmc-pmc3386168:
Li and co-workers showed in 2012 how the plant Arabidopsis controls production of ethylene, a gas hormone plants release under attack. A fungus infection drives ethylene output, which helps immunity. Earlier work had shown two kinase enzymes steady the proteins that start ethylene building, but leftover output hinted at more control.

Gene studies added three more builder enzymes to the infection response. The same kinases also switch the builder genes themselves on, through a partner factor called WRKY33 that binds their control regions directly. So control runs at two levels: gene activity and protein lifetime. Together they set how fast and how strongly the plant answers invasion.
europmc-pmc3405068:
Barber and colleagues profiled blood fats in 2012 and found one family, called lysophosphatidylcholines, falls in obesity and type 2 diabetes. Most attention goes to ordinary fats, which rise in these conditions, while individual fat species stay unmapped. The team ran detailed lipid scans in fat-fed mice and in lean, obese, and diabetic people.

In mice the drop in these fats appeared within the first week of a fatty diet. Human blood showed the same pattern, with lower levels in both obese groups. Telling apart the healthy obese from diabetic patients, though, the fats did not differ. Diet and body fat itself, rather than diabetes as such, seem to drive the change.

frus-1861-d168:
Horace Perry wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 July 1861. The dispatch is document 168 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Perry's July report kept Madrid covered while the legation's work grew. Summer brought heat, slow mails, and steady court routine. His letter is one of the staff papers that gave the Spanish file its unbroken run through 1861. The unbroken run of staff papers is the quiet strength of the Spanish file. An unbroken run of papers is what lets a reader trust a file's whole tale. Trust in a file grows from unbroken runs.
frus-1861-d268:
Guidance for James Shepherd Pike left Washington on 11 November 1861, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 268 in the President's message volume for 1861. It was written in the autumn of the war's first year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d68:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 August 1861. The dispatch is document 68 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams reported a London that had begun to doubt the Union would win. Doubt was dangerous, since it fed calls to step in and end the war. His mid August letter let Seward see that risk plain, from the one post where it could turn real. Doubt in London was the seed of every scheme for mediation that year. Mediation schemes died that year because Adams met each one early and square.
frus-1862-d168:
The second of three Seward letters dated 25 October 1862 appears as Document 168 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, whose talks with Earl Russell shaped British dealings with the Union.

By late October, France was urging Britain to join it in proposing a truce in the American war. London had not yet agreed. Washington's mail in this window, this letter included. Fed Adams the facts and the tone he needed while the two European powers sounded each other out. The State Department printed the London mail in full for Congress, enclosures and all.
frus-1862-d268:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 17 April 1862 in a letter printed as Document 268 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Dayton reported while French troops in Mexico marched toward Puebla, where they would meet a famous defeat on 5 May. His court's Mexican venture shaped its American policy in ways Washington worked to map. A report like this one, written between great events, shows the envoy's daily craft: listening, noting, and judging what an emperor's government might do next. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d368:
F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State. He wrote to Henri Mercier on 12 June 1862, in a letter printed as Document 368 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Frederick William Seward was the Secretary's son and deputy.

When the assistant signed, business moved at the working level while the Secretary's hand stayed in reserve. The French channel saw such letters whenever the matter was routine or the Secretary was pressed. This June note shows the Department's second rank keeping a major channel in motion during a crowded summer. Cases in this channel often mixed the war at home with French designs in Mexico.
frus-1862-d468:
On 13 January 1862 George Perkins Marsh reported from Turin to Secretary of State William H. Seward, a week after his previous dispatch. The report is Document 468 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Weekly reporting was Marsh's habit, and his Turin letters mixed Italian politics with the war's reception in the new kingdom. In January 1862 Italy was settling its place among the powers while watching whether the American republic would split in two. Marsh, a scholar by trade, wrote with unusual care about what he saw. His reports helped Seward count Italy among the Union's sincere well-wishers, a small but cheering fact in a winter of hard news.
frus-1862-d568:
On 2 September 1862 Henry Shelton Sanford wrote from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is Document 568 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's printed record.

Sanford wrote a fortnight before Antietam, while Lee's invasion of Maryland was still news in the making in Europe. His Brussels vantage caught the anxiety of the smaller courts, which feared a long war and French ambition in equal measure. Reports from such posts helped Seward decide that the danger of intervention, though real, was not yet ripe. The dispatch is a small piece of the evidence on which that judgment rested. It was filed from a minor capital. The minister who filed it missed very little.
frus-1862-d668:

From China, an envoy's mail told Washington about trade, the treaty ports, and the acts of the Qing court. frus-1862-d68:

The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

frus-1863p1-d168:
On 24 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 168 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, the middle piece of three he sent that day.

The middle sheet of Adams's sets often held the day's meat. On 24 April there was meat enough: the ships, the law, and the talk of London all in flux. This letter holds the center of his three. With the two Seward sheets of the same date nearby in the volume, the day is one of the fullest in the printed record. It tells the war abroad in a single date.
frus-1863p1-d268:

Seward on 21 August 1863, and it is document 268 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

Read in sequence, these reports show a diplomat testing how far he could push a stronger power without provoking a second war. That balance was the heart of Adams's whole mission. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.

frus-1863p1-d468:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State directed a letter to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington on 17 April 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d568:
Writing on 17 June 1863, Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington addressed William H. Seward, the Secretary of State in an official letter. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d668:
Among the day's business on 19 November 1863 was a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely.
frus-1863p1-d68:
On 30 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is document 68 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It bears the same date as an Adams dispatch printed just before it.

Same dates on both sides of the file are a quirk of the sea mail. Each man wrote from the last news he had, weeks old. Seward's letter set out Washington's line for the points then live in London. It is part of the close weave of the exchange. Orders and reports crossed on the ocean and still, in time, formed one clear talk.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d168: Roosevelt wrote to Secretary Hull in Moscow on October 26, 1943, in a letter placed by the editors in the Moscow section as Document 168 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. It shares its date and its parties with a second such letter, and the pair belongs to the conference's closing week. The record gives no subject for either. Both are printed in the Foreign Relations series with the Moscow papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d268: An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume covers a Cairo meeting of November 1943 for which no official record of the substance has been found. What the editors know of the meeting and its participants comes from the President's Log, with a cross-reference to a later page of the volume. One outside source adds a single detail: in Elliott Roosevelt's account, the principal subject of conversation at the meeting was supply.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d368:
Charles Bohlen's minutes, the third set for 29 November 1943, record the dinner that evening at half past eight. They are less a record of decisions than of mood, and their most notable feature, Bohlen writes, was Stalin's manner toward Churchill.

Stalin kept a sharp edge on nearly every remark to the Prime Minister while staying entirely friendly. He teased him over Overlord. He implied a secret liking for the Germans and a wish for a soft peace. He spoke frankly of the Red Army's poor showing against Finland and its slow climb to a genuinely good army. On Germany he set two conditions: the physical liquidation of at least fifty thousand, perhaps a hundred thousand, of the German commanding staff, and Allied retention of the world's strong points. Roosevelt joked the figure down to forty-nine thousand; Churchill objected fiercely to cold-blooded execution.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d468:
Reginald Leeper, the British ambassador to the Greek government-in-exile in Egypt, wrote to Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden on December 3, 1943. Greece was under German occupation, and its exiled government worked from Cairo. The catalog heading misspells “government,” but the parties are clear. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Leeper spoke for London to a restless exile government whose country was a battleground of resistance groups and rival claims. His reports to Eden fed British decisions about Greece at a moment when Cairo hosted both the exile court and the Allied conference. The message opens a window on the war's tangled Greek question.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d568:
Ambassador Averell Harriman recorded this memorandum on November 13, 1944, in Moscow. Harriman's memoranda often preserved his conversations and judgments about the Soviet leadership for the record in Washington. It appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

By late 1944 Harriman's tone about Moscow was hardening: the cooperation promised at Tehran was meeting the facts of Soviet power in Poland and the Balkans. His written record from this season is a key source for the alliance's turn toward friction. For readers, the memorandum shows the ambassador setting down, carefully and on paper, what a year of dealing with Stalin's government had taught him.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d68: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 29, 1943, and a second Churchill note of the same date follows it in the volume. This one is Document 68 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The last days of October were a summing-up season after Moscow and a planning season before Cairo. The catalog record gives the date and the names only. The text in the Foreign Relations series carries its errand.
frus-1944-quebec-d168:
An editors' note introduces the document printed next in the volume, the President's Log for the Quebec Conference. The Log was a booklet covering September 9 to 21, 1944, prepared by Lieutenant William Rigdon and approved by Rear Admiral Wilson Brown. The note describes its contents in detail, from the list of the president's party to the conference communiqué in an appendix.

The editors also compare the Log's party list with the one in Rigdon's later book, White House Sailor. Three names appear only in the book, and seven only in the Log, including Henry Morgenthau. Morgenthau's inclusion is explained: he accompanied Roosevelt from Washington to Hyde Park before being summoned to Quebec. The note is a small lesson in how the volume checks its own sources.
frus-1944-quebec-d268:
A draft directive to Admiral Mountbatten is proposed in C.C.S. 452/28, the British Chiefs' paper of September 13, 1944. His primary object would be the recapture of all Burma at the earliest date. That object must not prejudice the security of the air supply route to China, including the staging post at Myitkyina, whose protection was essential throughout.

Approved operations were the stages of Operation Capital needed for the air route, and Operation Dracula, the seaborne stroke at Rangoon. The chiefs attached the greatest importance to executing Dracula before the 1945 monsoon, with a target date of March 15. If it slipped past the monsoon, Capital would be exploited while Dracula was prepared for November 1945.
frus-1944-quebec-d68:
Under Secretary of State Edward R. Stettinius recorded this memorandum on September 12, 1944, the opening day of the Second Quebec Conference. Stettinius remained in Washington while the leaders met in Canada. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

An opening-day memorandum from Washington shows the home government keeping pace with a traveling summit: positions restated, information supplied, and the department's interests guarded from a distance. Stettinius was also guarding the newborn United Nations project agreed at Dumbarton Oaks. For readers, the paper marks the State Department's parallel work while the conference ran.
frus-1945-50-intel-d168:
Dated 6 September 1946, this letter runs from the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (Hoover) to the President’s Chief of Staff (Leahy). It survives in print as document 168 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d268:
A memorandum by the Chief of the Special Procedures Group, Central Intelligence Agency (Cassady) bears the date 1 May 1948. The State Department prints it as document 268 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d368:
A memorandum from Daniel DeBardeleben reached the Acting Deputy Assistant Director for Special Operations, Central Intelligence Agency on 17 February 1949. The State Department prints it as document 368 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was a season of stock-taking: the CIA was a year old, and its friends and critics were both writing things down.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d68:
Byrnes, Royall, and Forrestal wrote jointly to President Truman on 7 January 1946. Three cabinet secretaries, State, War, and Navy, signed one letter to the president. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A joint letter from the three secretaries told Truman the departments had settled their fight and were ready for his order. Such unity is rare, and presidents act fast when they see it. Readers have arrived at the climax of the volume's first act: five months of memoranda, committees, and turf wars compressed into one agreed paper. The directive that followed on 22 January bears the shape these three men, with the Budget Bureau's help, had given it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d168:
Who really ran the armistice commissions in the Balkan capitals? This briefing book paper states the American position on the Allied Control Commissions in Rumania, Bulgaria, and Hungary. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The commissions mirror the Allied Commission in Italy, the paper explains, but with the leading role reversed: Russia leads, as Britain and America lead in Italy. Rumania's body works under rules drawn up by the Soviet government. Washington has not objected to Soviet officers running the day-to-day work while Germany still fights. But orders to local governments must not go out in the commission's name without prior word to the other members. Otherwise the United States is tied in public to acts it never saw.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d268:
Stalin surprised Churchill on war criminals at Moscow, and this excerpt of 22 October 1944 tells how. Paragraph five of message number 801 is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The Soviet leader took what Churchill calls an unexpectedly ultra-respectable line.

There must be no executions without trial, Stalin held. Otherwise the world would say the allies were afraid to try the accused. Churchill pointed out the difficulties in international law. Stalin answered that if there were no trials, there must be no death sentences either, only lifelong confinement. Faced with that view from that quarter, Churchill tells Roosevelt, he will not press the memorandum he had given him. He asks that it be treated as withdrawn.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d368:
Matthews caught the money talk in pencil at the foreign ministers' session of February 7, 1945. His rough notes move from dismemberment to reparations. On a study commission, Molotov proposed Eden, Winant, and Gusev. Eden worried about France's absence, since France was Germany's neighbor. The three, he argued, could decide French participation themselves.

Then Ivan Maisky explained the Soviet reparations figures. Half would come at once, half in yearly payments. He set Germany's prewar national wealth at 125 billion, cut by war losses. From the mobile part, ten billion might be removed as a first payment. The shorthand shows how the famous reparations demand was built.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d468:
Victory by cable: Stettinius reported home in this top secret message to Grew of February 11, 1945. The conference had agreed on the American proposal on voting procedure. America would consult China and France on behalf of the other two powers. The United Nations conference was fixed for April 25, 1945, at San Francisco.

The communiqué, out Monday night for Tuesday's papers, would announce the substance. It would not itself say the voting plan was America's. But Washington was free, at the same moment, to state that the adopted proposal was the United States one. The wire shows the deal and the credit arranged together.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d68:
Readers opening the Malta and Yalta volume meet this editorial note before the documents of late 1944. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States explain why the volume reaches back months before the conferences themselves. Many papers printed here date from the mid-autumn of 1944.

The note says the chapter gathers key documents showing where each main subject stood before the talks. Those subjects were the problems later discussed at Malta and Yalta, and each paper shows the position the United States had taken. The editors add that the military talks had a set agenda, while the political talks did not, and that fuller coverage would wait for later volumes.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d168:
Only a fragment of President Truman's June 25, 1945 message to Stalin is printed as document 168 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The extract, sent from Olympia, Washington, concerns the Belgrade agreement on Venezia Giulia, the disputed territory around Trieste that Yugoslav and Allied forces both claimed.

The surviving lines close the message. Truman tells Stalin that if any further aspect of the agreement should be considered, they will have a chance to discuss it at their early meeting. The full text appears elsewhere in the volume. Even this scrap shows the President's habit of steering hard questions toward the summit table, where the three leaders could deal with them face to face rather than by cable.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d268:
A briefing paper weighed Austria's provisional government in a paper dated June 23, 1945. The paper is document 268 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It covers the recognition of an Austrian government acceptable to all the Allied powers, an item on the American agenda.

Moscow set up Karl Renner's provisional government in Vienna in April without consulting its allies, the paper notes, a one-sided act hard to square with joint action. Yet the Renner government is, in its men and its spread of parties, as good a coalition as could be devised, the paper concedes. One worry stands out: the interior ministry, which controls the police, sits in Communist hands, and so does public instruction. The paper balances acceptance of Renner against the precedent of letting one power install governments alone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d368:
Two State Department officials, Collado and Despres, drafted substitute wording on July 7, 1945, for a telegram to Pauley in Moscow. Their paragraph backs the heart of his formula for dividing reparations. The major powers, it says, would settle their own collective share among themselves, without fixing the split with the other allies before consulting them.

The draft also agrees that naming France a major power in the formula raises the sharpest difficulties, since France sat outside the talks. A closing thought notes America's odd position: its direct war damage was relatively small, even though the resources it poured into the war were vast.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d468:
Italy's ambassador calls on Grew in a memorandum of conversation dated July 6, 1945, filed under the subject of a declaration of war against Japan. Ambassador Tarchiani left with Grew a letter addressed to the President. It enclosed a memorandum setting out the present position of Italy, and her vital needs and aspirations.

Knowing how occupied the President must be at this particular moment, Tarchiani had not ventured to ask to see him personally. He sought Grew instead as an intermediary for delivering his letter. Grew replied that he would with pleasure see that the letter gets into the President's hands without delay. The extract shows Italy pleading its case in Washington on the eve of Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d568:
Belgrade charge Harold Shantz offered Washington a piece of advice on June 23, 1945. His short secret wire is document 568 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It responds to Tito's public claim that civil rule in Venezia Giulia was still an open question.

Shantz suggests that the U.S. and British governments act through their Belgrade embassies. They should remind the Yugoslav government that article 3 of the Belgrade agreements settled the question. They should also warn that stirring up trouble in the area under Allied military government is unlikely to help the Yugoslav case. The wire is a small, sharp bid to hold Tito to a deal signed only two weeks before.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d668:
Ambassador Norman Armour reported Spain's anger over the Soviet Tangier demand from Madrid on July 5, 1945. His confidential wire is document 668 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. An under secretary of the Spanish foreign ministry had spoken to him the day before.

The official, del Castillo, strongly denounced Moscow's bid for a seat at the Paris talks. Madrid had wired its London embassy to tell the Foreign Office Spain's line. Spain would welcome talks with the Americans, British, and French on restoring an international regime at Tangier. It would not discuss the matter with any other power, a phrase whose target was plainly Russia. Armour adds that Spain opposed reviving the 1923 statute as amended. It feared Russian entry into the administration and a return to French dominance.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d68:
Acting Secretary of State Joseph Grew sent the President's naval aide a staffing plan for the Berlin trip on June 15, 1945. The letter and its enclosures form document 68 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Grew appends a list of State Department people whose presence, he says, would help Truman at the meeting of heads of government.

The suggested party runs to about forty names, grouped by the issues they would cover. It includes the Secretary of State, Russian interpreters Charles Bohlen and Llewellyn Thompson, and specialists on German politics, reparations, the Balkans, and the Near East. Grew notes that Secretary Stettinius had approved the list at San Francisco. The document shows the expert team Washington thought a new president would need at the table.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1068:
Ambassador Lincoln MacVeagh reported from Athens on July 24, 1945, on the fall of Greece's foreign minister. Ioannis Sofianopoulos came home on July 22 and resigned the next day. Fresh from talks with Molotov, he had urged a cabinet drawn in thirds from left, center, and right. The prime minister found such a government unworkable, and the Regent declared the question did not arise.

MacVeagh reads the timing darkly. The resignation was Russian-inspired, he suggests, and lands during the Potsdam talks beside a threatening Yugoslav note. Moscow may plan, he warns, to refuse election supervision by claiming a nonrepresentative Athens cannot run fair elections amid chaos. Sofianopoulos, he adds, seemed pleased with himself and hungry for the premiership.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1168:
Team to team, the Soviet delegation addressed this note straight to the United States delegation on 31 July 1945. Such messages skipped the foreign ministers and the leaders. They carried business between the staffs who ran the talks day to day.

Two days before the close, that channel still had work to do. Last points needed answers while the final text was being drafted. A direct note of this kind shows Moscow talking to Washington with no one between. It is part of the summit's working machinery, preserved because the files kept everything the channel carried.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1268:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 18 July 1945. Staff papers like this one did the thinking that leaders later turned into choices. The British chiefs wrote for their own team, in parallel with the American series across the hall.

A British paper in an American volume testifies to the allies' shared staff habits. The two machines exchanged paper as a matter of course. This memorandum is the British chiefs' view at the talks' start. Read beside the American notes of the same days, it shows two staffs framing one war and one peace in matching forms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1368:
Artemus Gates, the under secretary of the Navy, wrote to a senior plans officer of the fleet staff on 21 July 1945. The paper stayed inside the Navy's own house, moving between its civil head and its planners.
