Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Summit volumes mostly print papers between governments or departments, so an inside-Navy paper stands out. It shows the service sorting out its own position while the talks ran in Germany. Readers get a glimpse of how one armed service thought through the questions of the hour before its views joined the wider argument in Washington. Small papers like this one keep the record honest about where policy starts.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-68:
Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 23, 1945, record a morning session at Potsdam with two items printed here. The top secret extracts are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. The first item concerns command in Indo-China.

Admiral King read a memo on approaching Chiang Kai-shek about a boundary change. The southern part of Indo-China would be reallocated to the Southeast Asia area. General Marshall proposed amending the statement the British wanted in the final report to the President and Prime Minister. The chiefs approved Marshall's amendment and directed that it go to the Combined Chiefs. The second item printed concerns personnel shipping for allied governments. The chiefs agreed to recommend approval of the transport committee's recommendation, subject to a wording change in its enclosure. Routine in form, the minutes move real forces on paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d768:
A second American working paper bears the date July 24, 1945, as document 768. Two staff papers in one day reflect Potsdam's pace. The conference ran on paper: drafts, checks, and re-drafts. This one joined the delegation's files in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Companion papers let readers divide the work by topic and team. Each drafting group left its own trail. The document shows how a large mission organized its thinking. It also hints at the strain of the schedule. By July 24 the staff had served a week of sessions, and the hardest files were still open.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d868:
American drafters at Potsdam prepared this undated working paper as a proposed directive to the Allied commanders in Germany. It sets out the immediate economic tasks of the occupation. The paper bears no author's name. It was meant to push the commanders toward one shared program in the Control Council.

The tasks cover exports, including coal, to pay for reparations and minimum imports. They also cover fair sharing of supplies, uniform ration scales, and farm and coal output. Further items call for repair of transport, housing, and utilities. Industry would be cut back to peacetime needs. Currency, credit, public finance, and frontier controls would follow uniform rules.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d968:
J. Howard Marshall, general counsel to the reparations delegation, wrote to Edwin Pauley on July 31, 1945. He reports the firm view of two State Department men, Collado and Despres. Three subjects, they hold, must appear in the final Big Three agreement: restitution, property of Allied nationals in Germany, and German external assets.

Those men will cover the subjects through additions to the Economic Principles. Marshall still urges Pauley to push a Big Three declaration on German assets abroad, plus a vesting decree from the Control Council. On the principles themselves, he flags two deletions: the last sentence of 14(d) and all of paragraph 18, on supplies for Greater Berlin.
frus-1977-80v29-d168: Another 1977-1980 FRUS letter from President Carter on Panama. The canal diplomacy. This document preserves that letter. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
gao-gaoreports-b-295968: HMR Tech doubled its May 2005 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-297168: Bernard Cap Company took its November 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297968: Project Resources took its March 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298568: Brian X. Scott took his October 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. He said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Individuals get the same full hearing as the firms.
gao-gaoreports-b-299368: International Filter Manufacturing came back for more in April 2007 — a second protest and a second ruling in the same month. The firm challenged another award; the call tests these claims too. Repeat filers get repeat fairness, handled case by case.
gao-gaoreports-b-305368: An Armstrong Williams contract got a fiscal ruling in this September 2005 GAO call, which tests the Education Department's pundit deal. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the contract was legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-308968: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by No-Cost Contracts for Event Planning Services. The November 27, 2007 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-b-310568: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Done Right Building Services, Inc. Decided December 17, 2007, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-368: The paper money's paper needed a second source in 2005, and GAO's report says more analysis would settle whether a new supplier was required. The currency's supply chain got the once-over. One mill or two was the question. The analysis had to be done.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-768: Short sea shipping got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says the option showed the importance of systematic public investment decisions. The findings take the measure. The report shows the coastal freight was studied. The approach had to be systematic.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-968: Elderly asset transfers for Medicaid got a GAO review in 2005, and the report examines the shelter-and-qualify practice. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the long-term care dollars deserved honesty. The transfers had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1068: Reserve mobilization data needed fixing in 2006, and GAO's report says the Pentagon and services had to improve the records. The findings demand the data. The report warns that the call-up lists had to be accurate. The numbers had to be right.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-268: School grant awards needed tighter rules in 2006, and GAO's report says firmer steps could open the process to light. The findings demand the rigor. The report warns that the education dollars deserved daylight. The grant dollars deserved daylight. The education dollars deserved daylight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-368: Major weapons kept busting budgets in 2006, and GAO's report says cost and schedule problems persisted under the revised policy. The findings document the overruns. The report warns that the arsenal's price tags needed taming. The problems had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-468: National park air tour fees needed enforcing in 2006, and GAO's report says better verification and enforcement were required for compliance. The findings demand the follow-through. The report warns that the scenic flights' fees deserved collecting. The compliance had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-568: Title insurance got a GAO first look in 2006, and the report shares preliminary views and issues for further study. The findings open the inquiry. The report warns that the closing-table fees deserved scrutiny. The study had to continue. The closing fees deserved scrutiny.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-668: Oil trouble in South America threatened U.S. fuel in 2006, and GAO's report looks at what falling output there could mean. The findings map the risks. The report warns that the foreign barrels mattered to home pumps. The risk had to be weighed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1168: This 2007 Government Accountability Office report argues that better information and a systematic process could improve how agencies allocate fuel-reduction funds and select wildfire-prevention projects. Billions were being spent thinning forests and clearing brush, but GAO found the choices were not always guided by the best risk data. The report pushes for a more strategic fight against catastrophic wildfires.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1268: This 2007 Government Accountability Office report exposes government-wide abuse of premium-class travel: internal-control weaknesses let federal employees fly business and first class improperly at taxpayer expense. GAO documents the patterns of misuse across agencies. The findings fed public outrage over bureaucrats living large on the public dime — and pressure for the tighter rules that followed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-268: The telecom switchover was funded but fuzzy in 2007, and GAO's report says the GSA had the money for new contracts but needed real cost estimates. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the dial tone of government should not go silent mid-switch.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-368: The FBI's critical networks had holes in 2007 — GAO's report says the bureau had to fix weaknesses in its most sensitive systems. The findings target the digital doors. The report's irony bites: the nation's top cops could not lock their own computers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-68: First-responder grants had a cash-flow quirk in 2007, and GAO's report examines the exemption and the advance-funding rules. The findings parse the plumbing. The report asks whether the firefighters' money arrived when the fires did. The cash had to flow like the need.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-868: Homeland Security's science shop filed its spending plan in 2007 — GAO's report reviews the technology directorate's budget line by line. The findings check the dollars behind the gadgets and lab work. The report asks whether the research arm was buying real breakthroughs or just burning cash.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-168: A 2007 Government Accountability Office financial audit of the Bureau of the Public Debt's schedules of federal debt for fiscal years 2007 and 2006. The audit tested the accounting behind the national debt figures the bureau reports — the official ledger of what the United States owes. GAO's opinion affirms whether those numbers fairly represent the debt, a judgment that underpins confidence in Treasury reporting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-68: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report pressing the Defense Department to tighten its handling of Global War on Terrorism spending. GAO argues DOD needed to encourage fiscal discipline and make better use of tools meant to improve cost reporting for the wars. The report documents how foggy accounting made it hard for Congress to know what the conflicts were really costing taxpayers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-768: The Government Accountability Office dug into national Response Framework: FEMA Needs Policies and Procedures to Better Integrate Non-Federal Stakeholders in the Revision Process in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
grosh-oddfellows-manual-1868:
Aaron B. Grosh was a clergyman and a leading Odd Fellow in the United States. His Odd-Fellow's Improved Manual came out in 1868. It set out the past, the rules, and the aims of the Independent Order of Odd Fellows. The order was then one of the largest friendly groups in the land.

Grosh defends the order against its critics and explains its signs, degrees, and lodge work. He also gives the laws that govern local lodges and grand lodges. For the years when such groups cared for the sick and buried the dead, few books show their inner life so well.
how-to-read-character-a-new-illustrated-: How to Read Character, 1868. Another handbook. This book preserves that manual. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lublin-meir-ben:
Meïr ben Gedaliah Lublin (1558–1616), known as the Maharam, was a Polish rabbi born at Lublin. A Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Solomon Schechter and M. Seligsohn profiles him. From a family of rabbis, he learned chiefly from his father-in-law, the rabbi of Cracow. Before age thirty he was called to Cracow’s rabbinate.

Lublin later served at Lemberg until 1613, arguing sharply with Joshua Falk, then returned home as rabbi until his death. Wherever he settled he ran a yeshivah, drawing pupils such as Isaiah Horowitz. The article describes his printed notes on the Talmud, still included in major Talmud editions, and his 140 published legal replies. It also describes his bold method: he corrected texts, attacked famous rivals, and rejected parts of the Shulhan Aruk. Readers get a full picture of a forceful scholar whose opinions carried across Poland.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o: This volume of the memoirs spans the Regency's middle years. Philippe d'Orleans rules France with charm and worldly cynicism. Saint-Simon watches, judges, and advises in turn. France caught between two great reigns, watching and waiting.
nilsson-primitive-inhabitants-scandinavi:
Sven Nilsson, a Swedish sage of beasts and old times, wrote this classic on the first folk of Scandinavia. John Lubbock turned it into English in 1868. Nilsson had long taught that the north had its own stone age, rich with finds.

He sets out the stone tools, shell heaps, and graves of the first north men. He matches them with the ways of wild folk of his own day to guess their life. The book is the north's match to the French case for deep age man, and a classic of its kind.
npt-1968:
The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty opened for signing in 1968, after years of fear that atomic weapons would spread to many nations. It rests on a bargain between the states that already had nuclear arms and those that did not. Nearly every country in the world has since joined, making it the widest arms control agreement in force.

States without nuclear weapons promise never to build or receive them, and they accept inspections of their atomic programs. The nuclear powers promise to work toward disarmament and to share peaceful nuclear technology. The bargain has kept the circle of nuclear-armed states small for over fifty years, even as disputes over disarmament and enforcement continue to test it.
nsa-ufo-hypothesis-1968:
Analysts at the National Security Agency weighed what UFOs might mean for human survival in 1968. UFO Hypothesis and Survival Questions sets out five hypotheses for the things seen in the sky. The paper is laid to Lambros Callimahos, a famed code man of the agency.

Each hypothesis is tried for what it would ask of mankind if it proved true. The close is a fable, the Tale of the Rattler, on how pride can blind a mind to a new fact. The monograph is philosophy from inside the most sealed of agencies. It shows cleared men wondering aloud at their own desks.
nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-1868:
Henry Callaway published Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus in 1868. Callaway, an English missionary and later bishop in Natal, took the tales down in the Zulus' own words. He prints the Zulu text with English translation and notes, so readers meet the storytellers' phrasing, not a summary.

Tricksters, ogres, and clever children fill the nursery tales, while the traditions recount chiefs and migrations. The histories preserve how Zulu elders of that generation told their own past. Callaway's method was new: record first, interpret with care, and credit the speakers. His volume became the founding English collection of Zulu oral literature. Folklorists still build on the texts he saved from vanishing.
openalex-w1979540468: Mosquitoes bite at dawn too — not just at night. This work studies human exposure to early morning Anopheles funestus, a malaria vector. The thin catalog record hides the details, but the study measured when people meet the mosquito.
openalex-w2059124668: A decade of ocean census — what did we learn? Costello and colleagues' 2010 paper integrated the Census of Marine Life's findings into a global perspective on marine biodiversity knowledge. The synthesis mapped what we know, what we lack, and what's next.
openalex-w2118672468: Brazil's heartland forests have deep roots. A 2010 study traced the origin of central Brazilian forests through 106 plant checklists and dot-maps. The analysis linked them to eastern tropical South America's forest formations — ancient connections, mapped.
openalex-w2134712068: First-time and older mothers face higher small-baby risk. A 2013 study explored links between parity, maternal age, and small births. The work moved beyond snapshots toward causes — better proof for clinicians now — mothers' risk, clarified.
openalex-w2229420368: Most microbes on Earth have never been grown in a lab — metagenomics studies them by reading DNA straight from the environment. This 2015 review traces the road from classical microbiology through DNA sequencing technologies to the bioinformatics that make sense of it all. It is a field guide to how scientists now explore the invisible majority of life, one genome at a time.
openalex-w2788640168: Cells can die in a dozen different ways — apoptosis, necroptosis, ferroptosis — and the terminology was chaos. This 2018 Cell Death & Differentiation paper delivers the Nomenclature Committee on Cell Death's recommendations: precise molecular definitions for each subroutine. By Galluzzi, Vitale, Aaronson and dozens of colleagues, it's the field's official dictionary.
openalex-w2797697368: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis — when pancreatic tissue dies — demands careful, stepwise care. This 2018 Endoscopy paper delivers the European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy's evidence-based guidelines: contrast-enhanced CT as first-line imaging on admission, MRI as an alternative, and the endoscopic strategies that follow. The consensus standardizes a high-stakes intervention.
openalex-w3034125968: Hospitals look clean but teem with microbes — including drug-resistant pathogens. This 2020 Nature Medicine paper maps opportunistic pathogens and antibiotic resistance genes across a tertiary hospital environment, the first extensive genomic characterization of its kind. The cartography reveals where disinfection fails.
openalex-w4378349368: Free radicals — reactive oxygen species from everyday metabolism — are normally cleared by antioxidants. This 2023 Frontiers in Chemistry paper reviews oxidative stress, free radicals, and antioxidants: potential crosstalk in human disease pathophysiology. The review maps where the balance breaks down.
openalex-w4391649568: Extracellular vesicles carry molecular cargo reflecting their cell of origin — promising biomarkers and therapies. This 2024 Journal of Extracellular Vesicles paper sets MISEV2023: minimal information standards for vesicle studies, from basic to advanced approaches. The guidelines tame a booming field.
openalex-w4410594468: Some random patterns are more orderly than they look. This paper studies hyperuniform point arrangements, where large-scale density fluctuations vanish, with an ecological example and new models. The authors connected the math to real-world scatterings. A statistical-physics study of hidden order in randomness.
openalex-w4412156568: Growing microbes side by side can wake up silent chemistry. This paper reports griseolutein T, a new compound from a Streptomyces germ found by co-growing it with a rival. The team screened island soil germs for the find. A study of germ rivalry yielding new molecules.
openalex-w7204195968: Dental implant surgery in the upper jaw risks piercing the sinus membrane, a complication striking up to one in four procedures. This review studies the risk factors and prevention strategies for Schneiderian membrane perforation during sinus lifts. The authors gather what implantology knows about avoiding the tear. A technical review where millimeters matter.
openalex-w7204266568: Active learning asks teachers to teach differently, and this study asks what they need to pull it off. The authors analyze how teachers' craft knowledge supports hands-on methods in basic education. The research is qualitative, built on published and documentary sources. A thoughtful study of the teacher behind the method.
openalex-w7204789668: In complex crystals, each metal site plays its own role. This case study asked how post-heat treatment shifts the jobs of metals sitting on different crystal sites. The authors traced function to position. A materials study of heat rewriting a crystal's division of labor.
openalex-w7214947768: Dental crowns face acid and wear daily. This study tested how acidic storage aged milled and 3D-printed temporary crowns: wear, roughness, strength, hardness. The authors compared materials head to head. A dental-materials study of teeth under chemical attack.
philosophia-maturata-an-exact-piece-of-p: Philosophia Maturata, 1668. The ripened philosophy. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes.
plos-pbio-0000068:
Philippe Boutin, Christian Dina, Francis Vasseur, and co-workers named a candidate gene for human obesity in PLOS Biology in 2003. The gene is GAD2, found on chromosome 10 at a spot already linked to severe obesity in several groups. GAD2 makes an enzyme tied to a brain signal that affects hunger.

Obesity has strong genetic roots, yet few clear genes had been pinned down at the time. A gene that helps control appetite signals is a strong lead worth testing. The paper lays out the link between GAD2 variants and body weight. It gives later studies a clear target: check the gene, check the pathway, and see how much of the risk it explains.
plos-pbio-0020268:
William G. Fairbrother, Dirk Holste, Christopher B. Burge, and their team tested RNA splicing signals in PLOS Biology in 2004. Genes are copied into RNA, then cut and rejoined to remove gaps. Short RNA stretches called splicing enhancers help the cutting land in the right places.

Some DNA changes thought to be harmless may in fact break these enhancers. The team used such changes, called SNPs, to test whether predicted enhancers are real. The predictions held up well. That result has a medical edge: a change that looks silent in a gene may still cause disease by wrecking splicing. Doctors reading genomes need that warning.
plos-pbio-0020368:
David L. Smith, Jonathan Dushoff, and F. Ellis McKenzie modeled mosquito-borne infection risk in PLOS Biology in 2004. Diseases like malaria spread where mosquitoes bite people. Risk is not spread evenly: some homes and villages sit in hot spots while others nearby stay safer.

The model shows how that patchiness changes the math of spread. Average bite rates can mislead, since a few heavily bitten people drive much of the transmission. Control efforts aimed at hot spots can thus beat blanket efforts. The paper gave malaria programs a clear reason to map risk finely. Scarce tools, like bed nets and spraying, work best where risk bites hardest.
plos-pone-0000068:
Philip C. Hill, Roger H. Brookes, Annette Fox, and a large team tested a tuberculosis skin test in The Gambia in PLOS ONE in 2006. The PPD skin test is the classic check for TB infection, but it often cannot tell TB from related germs or from the BCG vaccine. The team focused on people with recent exposure.

In that group, the test proved surprisingly specific: positive results truly pointed to M. tuberculosis infection. Timing, it seems, is part of the test's meaning. Close contacts of TB cases are the very people health workers most need to sort. A cheap skin test that can be trusted in that setting is valuable for clinics with few resources.
plos-pone-0000168:
Mark B. Bain, Nancy Haley, Douglas L. Peterson, and colleagues published this fisheries paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It reports the recovery of an endangered fish in the United States. Once in steep decline, the species had rebounded enough to stand as a conservation success.

Recovery stories are rare enough to be worth documenting in detail. The authors lay out the evidence for the rebound and the conditions behind it. Their account gives managers a worked example of what a fish recovery looks like, useful when other endangered species need a path back.
plos-pone-0000268:
Honglin Song, Susan J. Ramus, Susanne Krüger Kjaer, and colleagues published this cancer genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tests whether tagging single nucleotide polymorphisms, common one-letter DNA variants, in the BRIP1 gene relate to susceptibility to breast and ovarian cancer. BRIP1 works in DNA repair and partners with the famous BRCA1 gene.

Faulty DNA repair is a known route to these cancers, so repair genes are natural suspects. The authors genotype the variants in patients and controls to test the link. Association studies of this kind sort which inherited variants genuinely shift cancer risk and which are innocent bystanders.
plos-pone-0000368:
Beth Burgwyn Fuchs, Robin J. Tang, and Eleftherios Mylonakis studied a disease-causing fungus, Cryptococcus neoformans, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The fungus can cause serious illness in people with weak immune systems. Their work focuses on a gene called ROM2 and on how it shapes the fungus's cells, with special attention to the role of temperature.

Cell shape in fungi is tied to growth, survival, and the ability to cause disease. A gene whose effect changes with temperature is of special interest because the fungus must adapt to the warmth of the human body. Understanding how ROM2 guides cell building helps explain how this fungus copes with its host.
plos-pone-0000468:
Yonatan Savir and Tsvi Tlusty proposed a way that molecules double-check their partners, in a 2007 PLOS ONE theory paper. Molecular recognition must be specific: a protein should bind its true partner and reject near-matches. The authors describe conformational proofreading, in which a molecule's change of shape on binding adds a check that improves specificity.

The idea extends the classic proofreading concept from DNA copying to shape-shifting molecules generally. A flexible molecule pays an energy cost when it molds to a partner, and the wrong partner makes that cost higher. Theory of this kind gives experimentalists a sharper question: how much of a molecule's selectivity comes from its willingness to change shape?
plos-pone-0000568:
Andrey O. Kiselev and colleagues followed one chlamydia protein through the germ's life cycle, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Chlamydia trachomatis causes a common infection passed by sex, and can blind in its trachoma form. The team tracked the protein PmpD: when it is made, how it is trimmed, and where it sits in the cell.

This germ swaps between a hardy spread form and a growing form inside cells. Each stage wears a different set of proteins. A protein's timing and place hint at its job, be it entry, growth, or exit. Proteins tracked this closely become vaccine leads for an infection that often does harm before it is noticed.
plos-pone-0000668:
Supriya Srinivasan, Pamela Santiago, Cecile Lubrano and co-authors retooled a cell receptor so its signals could be turned up or down in live animals. Their 2007 PLOS ONE target was the melanocortin-4 receptor. It belongs to a large family of receptors that sit in cell membranes and pass signals inward. That family runs many body processes, from hunger to hormone release.

The hard part is proof: with so many receptors at work, which signal causes which body response? By building a receptor they could control, the team could switch its signals on at will. That covered both its steady activity and the activity sparked by a binding molecule. The melanocortin-4 receptor is known for its role in appetite and weight, so a controllable version is a sharp tool for that field.
plos-pone-0000768:
Lars Palmqvist, Nicolas Pineault, Carina Wasslavik and colleagues hunted for genes that let fusion proteins expand blood stem cells. Hox genes help regulate hematopoietic stem cells and are also implicated in leukemia, through fusions with the nucleoporin gene NUP98. An engineered NUP98-HOXA10 fusion can expand these stem cells several hundred-fold in vitro, a striking and useful effect.

The team sought candidate genes behind that expansion and the transformation toward leukemia. Knowing which downstream genes do the work could separate the welcome expansion from the dangerous transformation. Stem cell expansion is a prize for transplantation medicine, where too few cells limit treatment. Leukemia risk is the shadow that comes with it.
plos-pone-0000868:
Amro Zayed, Serban Constantin and Laurence Packer studied an invading species that thrived despite a heavy genetic load, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Invasions can do real harm to local wildlife and to farming. Oddly, invading groups often show little loss of genetic variety, even when they start from few founders.

The authors take up a case where the genetic burden was severe, yet the invasion still worked. That puzzle tests simple ideas about why some introductions fail and others spread. Their work speaks to anyone trying to predict which new arrivals will take hold. It also shows that genes alone do not settle the outcome.
plos-pone-0000968:
Niyaz Ahmed, Vikram Saini, Saurabh Raghuvanshi and colleagues analyzed a bacillus used in leprosy immune therapy, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mycobacteria include both germs that cause disease and harmless soil dwellers. How they split into those paths is a question of evolution, driven by how they colonize hosts and spread.

The team read the bacillus at the molecular level to place it among its relatives. A therapy strain needs a clear identity before its effects can be judged. Their analysis also feeds the wider story of mycobacterium evolution. Knowing which traits came with host living helps explain why some relatives cause leprosy or tuberculosis.
plos-pone-0001068:
Tali Sharot, Mieke Verfaellie and Andrew Yonelinas examined how emotion makes memories feel vividly recollected, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Emotion strengthens the subjective sense of remembering, even when the memory is no more accurate than a plain one. That gap between feeling and fact is a known trap in eyewitness settings.

The authors test whether the effect runs through hippocampal memory consolidation over time. They lay out two critical predictions of that idea and test them. A time dependent hippocampal process would mean the vividness grows as the memory settles. The work helps separate the feeling of certainty from the evidence behind it.
plos-pone-0001168:
In 2005 and 2006, the island of La Réunion in the Indian Ocean suffered a large outbreak of chikungunya, a fever spread by mosquitoes. Marie Vazeille and colleagues studied the outbreak's virus in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The mosquito blamed was Aedes albopictus, the Asian tiger mosquito.

The authors present the first study of how local mosquito populations responded to virus isolates taken from the same outbreak. Two isolates showed different patterns of infection in the mosquito. Differences like these can help explain why an outbreak explodes in one place and fizzles in another.
plos-pone-0001268:
Violence fills much media fare, and claims that it breeds aggression are old. Christopher Kelly, Jack Grinband, and Joy Hirsch looked for effects in the brain networks that control behavior, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging, they studied repeated exposure to media violence.

The authors report a diminished response in an inhibitory frontolimbic network after repeated exposure to violent media. Just as thrilling nonviolent media did not produce it. That network usually helps restrain impulses. Their finding gives the media violence debate a measurable brain correlate to argue over.
plos-pone-0001368:
Kui Yang and colleagues reported work in PLOS ONE in 2007 on a fast way to read fats in cell walls. These fats, called ether lipids, are common in the heart and brain. They help cells work well. Shifts in their mix have been tied to a number of gene based ills.

By blasting samples and reading the mass of each fat, the team found a paired rule. The rule links which forms of these fats show up side by side. A clear rule like this can speed up lab work. It can also help track how fat levels shift in health and in disease.
plos-pone-0001468:
Gilles Charvin, Frederick Cross, and Eric Siggia published a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on watching yeast cells grow over many cycles. Films of single cells with glow markers are a strong tool for cell cycle work. Tiny fluid devices now let labs control the cell's world with care. The team built one such device for yeast.

Their device lets them switch genes on at set times and film cells for days. The cells divide in a calm, unstressed way in the device. That calm is key, since stress can fake or hide gene effects. The tool should serve any lab that tracks slow cell change live.
plos-pone-0001568:
Bob Uttl wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE review on memory for future acts and aging. This kind of memory is the knack of recalling a plan at the right time and place. After two decades of work, reviews had reached clashing verdicts on whether age harms it. Uttl pooled the past studies in an open, checkable way.

His pooled read sorts lab tests from real world tests, which give unlike answers. That split may explain much of the clash in the field. A clear verdict guides how older adults can be aided with cues and tools. It also sets the bar for future aging and memory work.
plos-pone-0001668:
Jane F. Fearnside, Marc-Emmanuel Dumas, Alice R. Rothwell, and their co-authors compared mouse strains on a high-fat diet in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Insulin resistance, in which tissues stop responding well to insulin, sits at the center of type 2 diabetes and obesity. Both genes and environment shape it. Inbred mice fed a high-fat diet develop insulin resistance, making them a useful test system.

The team used phylometabonomics, a method that combines family history of strains with chemical profiles of their bodies. The full text gives the strain comparisons, the chemical patterns, and which strains adapted well or badly to the diet. Matching chemical profiles to strain ancestry helps predict which animals, and by extension which people, are most at risk from a fatty diet.
plos-pone-0001768:
Gesa Feenders, Miriam Liedvogel, Miriam Rivas, and their co-authors mapped movement areas in bird brains in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Vocal learning, the ability to imitate sounds, underlies human spoken language. It is rare, found in three distant bird groups: songbirds, hummingbirds, and parrots. Those groups share strikingly similar systems of cerebral vocal nuclei for learning and producing sounds.

The team mapped movement-associated areas in the avian brain to test a motor theory. The theory holds that vocal learning circuits evolved from motor circuits. The full text gives the brain maps across species. If language's roots are motor, bird brains offer the clearest living evidence of how the system was assembled.
plos-pone-0001868:
Simona Wagner, Chris J. Storbeck, Kristin Roovers, and their co-authors studied a kinase required for cell movement in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Cell migration involves a host of signals that meet on the cell's internal frame, and it is needed for growth, immune defense, and tissue repair. Cells move by building and removing focal adhesions, the anchors that grip their surface.

Using knockdown and blocking tricks, the team shows the microtubule-associated Ste20-like kinase SLK is required for focal adhesion turnover. It acts under control of FAK and src family kinases. The full text gives the migration assays. Adhesion turnover is also the step wandering cancer cells exploit to spread.
plos-pone-0001968:
Caroline Esnault and co-authors measured how far two forms of the malaria mosquito have split, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The mosquito Anopheles gambiae, a main carrier of malaria in Africa, comes in two molecular forms, called M and S. Plans to release lab-made mosquitoes that cannot carry the parasite hinge on how freely the forms mix in the wild.

The team compared genes across the forms in Africa and found high genetic differentiation between them. A deep split means a released strain may stay in one form and not spread to the other. That fact shapes any plan to fight malaria by changing wild mosquitoes.
plos-pone-0002068:
Jules Beekwilder and co-authors asked what happens to pests when a plant loses its chemical shields, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Aliphatic glucosinolates are sulfur compounds found at high levels in Arabidopsis and kin plants of the cabbage family. When tissue is chewed, they break into biting products that resist pest insects.

The team used plants that lack these compounds and measured insect herbivory, the feeding damage done by insects. Past work showed the making of the compounds is governed by gene switches. Removing the shield tests how much protection it truly gives in practice, not just in the lab.
plos-pone-0002168:
Dongna Li, Hui Li, Caiying Ou, and co-authors traced the paternal lines of the native people of Hainan Island, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hainan sits at the southern entrance to East Asia, a crossroads where early migrations shaped the Y chromosome patterns of the whole region. The island's aboriginal groups have lived apart for a long time, which can preserve old genetic patterns.

By studying Y chromosome variation in these groups, the team assessed how isolated their gene pool is. They also used the data to infer what the region's early population structure looked like. Island peoples like these act as living records of how humans first spread through East Asia.
plos-pone-0002268:
Li-Qun Fang and co-authors mapped the environmental factors behind bird flu spread in mainland China, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Since late 2003, the highly pathogenic H5N1 virus had killed millions of poultry and tens of thousands of wild birds. By March 2008 it had also caused at least 373 confirmed human infections, of which 236 were fatal.

The team analyzed where outbreaks occurred and which features of the landscape went with them. Factors like water bodies, poultry density, and climate can flag high-risk areas in advance. Maps of risk help authorities aim surveillance and culling before the virus flares again.
plos-pone-0002368:
Caterina Hatzifoti, Andrew Bacon, Helen Marriott, and co-authors packaged a vaccine booster and its target together in fat bubbles, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Antibody against CD40 can strongly enhance vaccine responses when chemists link it to the vaccine antigen. That chemical linking step, though, creates production and quality control headaches, worse still when several antigens are combined.

The team instead packed the CD40 antibody inside liposomes along with bacterial sugar and protein antigens. The shared package induced enhanced IgG responses without chemical linking. A simpler way to get the boost could make combined vaccines easier to make and check.
plos-pone-0002468:
Research by Stahl and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from James E. Stahl, Jennifer E. Kreke, Fawaz Ali Abdul Malek, and others. Its subject is consequences of Cold-Ischemia Time on Primary Nonfunction and Patient and Graft Survival in Liver Transplantation: A Meta-Analysis. The ability to preserve organs prior to transplant is key to the organ allocation process.

The purpose of this study is to describe the functional relationship between cold-ischemia time (CIT) and primary nonfunction (PNF). What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002568:
Traka and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Maria Traka, Amy V. Gasper, Antonietta Melchini, and others. Its subject is broccoli Consumption Interacts with GSTM1 to Perturb Oncogenic Signalling Pathways in the Prostate. Past studies suggest that people who eat more than one portion of cruciferous vegetables per week face a lower risk of prostate cancer.

Yet the processes behind that link are still poorly understood, a gap the authors note at the start. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002668:
Work by Maya Shakèd and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with histone deacetylases control neurogenesis in embryonic brain by inhibition of BMP2/4 signaling. The catalog record names Maya Shakèd first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Histone-modifying enzymes are essential for a wide variety of cellular processes dependent upon changes in gene expression. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002768:
Research from Julian W. Tang and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers seasonality of influenza A(H3N2) virus: a hong kong perspective (1997–2006). Authorship is credited in the record to Julian W. Tang and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The underlying basis for the seasonality of influenza A viruses is still uncertain. The authors add a further point. Phylogenetic studies investigated this phenomenon but have lacked sequences from more subtropical and tropical regions, particularly from Southeast Asia. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002868:
Work by Pascal Vrtička and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with individual attachment style modulates human amygdala and striatum activation during social appraisal. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Pascal Vrtička, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Adult attachment style refers to individual personality traits that strongly influence emotional bonds and reactions to social partners. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002968:
Charles Chapple and Roderic Guigó tracked the loss of selenoproteins in insect genomes in 2008. Selenoproteins are a varied family built around selenocysteine, the twenty-first amino acid. Until recently, every animal genome checked had them, so they were thought essential for animal life.

Challenging that view, some insects had lost them. The authors argue that relaxed selective constraints let the losses happen independently in different insect lines. Published in PLOS ONE, the study shows even a once-universal protein family can be dropped when its benefits no longer outweigh its costs. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003068:
Takanari Inoue and Tobias Meyer used synthetic activation to find a logic switch for cell movement in 2008. The enzyme PI3K is widely studied as a principal regulator of cell polarization, migration, and chemotaxis. Surprisingly, neutrophils and Dictyostelium cells could still polarize and migrate in some studies without the usual inputs.

By switching on endogenous PI3K and Rac synthetically, the team identifies an AND-gate switch: both signals are needed together for polarization and migration. Published in PLOS ONE, a clear logic rule helps explain conflicting results in the cell movement field. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003168:
Ranjan K. Dash, Yanjun Li, Jaeyeon Kim and colleagues model energy use in muscle under low blood flow in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Control of cell metabolism and energy in skeletal muscle under stress, such as reduced blood flow and oxygen supply to mitochondria, can be understood in numbers with a multi-scale computer model. The team use such an integrated top-down model in in-silico studies.

Readers see how whole muscle behaviour and cell level processes can be linked in one framework. Models like this let researchers test stress responses that are hard to measure directly. They can also guide lab work by showing which measures matter most.
plos-pone-0003268:
Yasser EL-Manzalawy, Drena Dobbs and Vasant Honavar evaluate peptide prediction methods in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Choice of one method over another for MHC-II binding peptide prediction is typically based on published reports of estimated performance on standard benchmark datasets. The team show that several standard benchmark datasets of unique peptides used in such studies contain substantial overlap problems.

Readers learn that benchmark flaws can inflate how good prediction tools look. MHC-II binding prediction guides vaccine and immunology work, so honest benchmarks matter. The paper is a useful warning for any field that ranks algorithms on shared test sets.
plos-pone-0003368:
Xi-Song Ke, Yi Qu, Naomi Goldfinger and colleagues induce a cell transition in prostate cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Epithelial to mesenchymal transition, or EMT, has been connected with cancer progression in vivo and generation of more aggressive cancer cell lines in vitro. EMT has been induced in prostate cancer cell lines, but had previously not been shown in primary prostate cells.

The authors report EMT of a primary prostate cell line with switches of cell adhesion modules but without malignant transformation, as the title states. Readers learn the transition alone does not make cells cancerous. Separating shape change from malignancy refines how EMT is used as a cancer warning sign.
plos-pone-0003468:
Tristan H. Coady and co-authors built a gene therapy tool for a muscle disease in this 2008 paper. Spinal muscular atrophy comes from losing a gene called SMN1. A near-twin gene, SMN2, remains but its RNA is spliced wrongly. RNA tools that redirect splicing offer a possible fix.

Their single vector system boosted a method called trans-splicing of SMN2 messages. Better efficiency matters as such tools move toward patient use. One vector is simpler to deliver than several parts. The work moves RNA repair for this disease a step forward. The disease strikes infants, which makes each step toward treatment urgent.
plos-pone-0003568:
Alexander Karnowski and co-authors studied gene silencing in young B cells in this 2008 paper. B cells mature in stages toward making antibodies. At the pre-B stage, one gene locus, λ5, must be switched off. Switching off also involves moving the locus within the nucleus.

Two factors, Aiolos and OBF-1, were each implicated in B cell growth. Mice lacking either one developed early B cells largely normally. Together, the two proved required for silencing and repositioning λ5. Developing B cells thus lock away genes they have outgrown. B cells that fail these steps can leave the body short of antibodies.
plos-pone-0003668:
Tohshin Go and Yukuo Konishi published this newborn study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Healthy babies copy an adult's mouth movements within hours of birth. This oral imitation fades by about two to three months, as higher brain control grows.

The authors tested newborns with severe brain damage to see if the copying still appears. Whether it does can hint at which brain parts the reflex needs. The study uses a simple behavior to probe the workings of the injured newborn brain, where direct tests are hard to run. Few studies can test such questions in newborns at all.
plos-pone-0003768:
Armando Bartolazzi, Calogero D'Alessandria, Maria Gemma Parisella, and colleagues published this imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Thyroid nodules are common, and about ninety percent of them are benign. Telling harmless lumps from cancer before surgery is a standing problem. The team targeted galectin-3, a protein that helps cells avoid death.

They used that target to image thyroid cancer in living patients. Because galectin-3 marks malignant tissue, scans could flag the dangerous nodules. The approach could spare many patients needless surgery on growths that would never harm them. Better triage before surgery is the prize the authors aim at.
plos-pone-0003868:
Janet Mann, Brooke L. Sargeant, Jana J. Watson-Capps, and colleagues published this animal behavior study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Some bottlenose dolphins carry sea sponges on their beaks while foraging. Tool use is rare in wild animals and prized as a window on cognition, social learning, and culture. Its costs and benefits are hard to measure.

The authors quantified what sponge carrying gains dolphins and what it costs them. Because nearly a whole population can be compared, spongers and non-spongers offer a rare natural test. The analysis weighs tool use the way evolution would: payoff against effort.
plos-pone-0003968:
Warunee Dansithong, Cordula M. Wolf, Partha Sarkar, and co-authors tested a proposed cause of myotonic dystrophy in 2008. Type 1 myotonic dystrophy comes from an expanded CTG tract in one gene. The mutant RNA forms clumps, called foci, in cell cytoplasm. Those clumps were thought to drive much of the disease.

Their PLOS ONE article reports the foci alone are not enough. Key features of the disease failed to appear from foci by themselves. Heart involvement in the disease also centers on the mutant RNA. The result pushes the field to find what else the expansion does.
plos-pone-0004068:
Saori Morino, Tatsuya Kondo, Kazunari Sasaki, and co-authors tested mild electric stimulation in diabetes models in 2008. Mild electrical stimulation can activate the PI3K and Akt signal path. Insulin resistance involves marked failure of that same path. Heat shock proteins also help cells handle stress.

Their PLOS ONE article combined mild stimulation with heat shock treatment. The pairing improved insulin resistance through stronger insulin signaling. A physical treatment that restores signaling would differ from drug therapy. The result invites tests of device-based help for type 2 diabetes. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004168:
Nathan Georgette published this modelling study in PLOS ONE in 2009. During an outbreak, officials need to know how much vaccination is enough to stop spread. The target is the coverage level that brings the average number of new infections per case below one.

Georgette built a new algorithm, a step-by-step computing method, that predicts this threshold from field survey data gathered while an outbreak unfolds. He calls the target the Outbreak Response Immunization Threshold. A tool that updates the target as real data arrive could help teams vaccinate enough people without wasting scarce doses.
plos-pone-0004268:
Marcela Guzman-Ayala and colleagues published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The TGF-beta signalling family includes morphogens such as Nodal and Activin, signals that guide vertebrate development. The concentration of a morphogen is critical: cells read the dose to decide their fate. Smad2 and Smad3 carry those signals inside the cell.

Using embryonic stem cells, the team asked how graded activation of Smad2 and Smad3 translates into gene activity. They report that the graded signal is converted directly into levels of target gene expression. Dose in, dose out: the study shows a simple arithmetic at the heart of development.
plos-pone-0004368:
Katherine Hammond and colleagues published this zebrafish ear study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The bone morphogenetic protein genes bmp2 and bmp4 are expressed in highly conserved patterns in the developing vertebrate inner ear. Elucidating BMP function during ear development has proved difficult, because mutations in these genes cause early embryonic defects that mask later roles.

The team focused on a late role for bmp2b in the morphogenesis of semicircular canal ducts in the zebrafish inner ear. Those canals sense head rotation and balance. Finding what builds them, stage by stage, informs the biology of balance disorders.
plos-pone-0004468:
The prion protein may help cells take in iron, a new role proposed by Ajay Singh, Maradumane Mohan, Alfred Isaac, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Prion disease begins when the normal prion protein folds into a harmful, sheet-rich shape. That shape change is the main event behind the brain damage of prion disease, yet how it kills cells is still debated.

The team reports that the normal protein modulates how cells absorb iron. If the protein's day job involves iron, then its warping could disturb iron balance in the brain. Too much or too little iron can harm nerve cells, so the link offers a fresh route to explain the damage. It also suggests iron handling as a place to look for treatments.
plos-pone-0004568:
Family trees of species can be tripped up by duplicated genes, warns Scott William Roy in PLOS ONE in 2009. Comparative genomics has shown that gene and genome duplication, followed by gene loss, happen everywhere. When a gene duplicates and one copy is later lost, the family tree of the gene no longer matches the tree of the species.

Roy works in phylogenomics, the use of whole genomes to rebuild evolutionary trees. He examines how unrecognized paralogy, mistaking duplicate copies for the same gene, distorts those trees. He also examines outgroup choice, which distant relative is used to root the tree. Both choices can quietly wreck a reconstruction. The paper is a caution and a guide for anyone building trees from genome data.
plos-pone-0004668:
James Kijas and colleagues surveyed sheep DNA across many breeds for a study published in PLOS ONE in 2009. They looked at small changes in the code that differ from one animal to the next. Their aim was to map how breeds relate after taming and years of careful breeding by farmers.

The survey shows that taming and breed making left clear marks in sheep genes. Knowing that pattern helps breeders pick traits with more care. It also gives gene hunts for growth, wool, and health a firmer base. Work on linked traits in farm animals can build on the breed map the team provides.
plos-pone-0004768:
Nobuo Masataka and colleagues found that free ranging macaque mothers exaggerate tool use when offspring watch, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tool use at group level occurs in various animals. How such skills spread through a group, though, is still an open question for scientists who study animal culture and learning.

The team watched mothers use material to clean their teeth in the wild. Mothers slowed and repeated the acts when their young were watching. That display looks like a form of teaching. It suggests tool traditions may pass by guided showing, not just copying. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing.
plos-pone-0004868:
Arti Santhanam and colleagues performed computational inference on roles of 3 prime UTRs in mRNAs regulated by oncogenic eIF4E, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Eukaryotic cap dependent translation is mediated by initiation factor eIF4E, which binds mRNAs and stimulates efficient initiation. eIF4E is often overexpressed in human cancers. Sequence review of untranslated regions sought the molecular signature distinguishing target mRNAs sensitive to excess eIF4E in tumor cells.

Untranslated regions carry regulatory codes for translation control. Signatures predict which messages cancer exploits. Targeting those messages may spare normal cells. Computation narrows experimental searches. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0004968:
Adiponectin is a hormone made by fat tissue. It protects against several obesity-related complications. Low adiponectin levels are linked to breast cancer development. Janice Lam and colleagues tested that link in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used mice prone to mammary tumors. The mice carried only half the normal amount of adiponectin.

The shortage promoted mammary tumor development in the mice. The effect ran through changed activity of PTEN. PTEN is a well-known brake on cell growth. The result connects a fat hormone to a cancer brake. It helps explain why obesity and breast cancer so often travel together.
plos-pone-0005068:
Ethiopia has one of the world's largest cattle populations. Its economy depends heavily on livestock. Bovine tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium bovis, burdens those herds. Stefan Berg and colleagues surveyed the burden in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ethiopia also has one of the highest human TB rates. The two diseases are close cousins.

The study measured mycobacterial disease across Ethiopian cattle. The burden is a major animal-health problem. It also carries spillover risk to people who live with cattle. Milk and close contact provide routes. The findings argue for stronger control measures. Protecting herds protects human health too. The work gives policymakers numbers to act on.
plos-pone-0005168:
Kidney damage is a feared result of type 2 diabetes, and genes that drive swelling in the body may help decide who gets it. Ahluwalia and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Asian Indian patients with the disease. They asked whether common forms of genes for swelling signals, acting together, track with kidney risk.

The team looked at the combined effect of several gene forms rather than at one gene at a time. Their title states the main result: common variants in these genes are linked with nephropathy risk in this group. For readers, the work shows how small gene differences may help flag patients who need closer kidney checks.
plos-pone-0005268:
Spinal muscular atrophy weakens muscles by starving them of a protein called SMN. Early lab and patient work suggested the drug valproic acid could raise SMN levels. Swoboda and colleagues ran an open-label phase II trial of the drug in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Forty-two subjects with the disease took valproic acid in the trial. Open-label means everyone knew what was being given, so the study mainly tests safety and early signs of benefit. Repurposing a cheap, known drug would be a major gain for this devastating disease.
plos-pone-0005368:
Brucella melitensis is a bacterium that lives inside macrophages, the very cells meant to kill it. Its type IV secretion system, encoded by the virB operon, helps it survive inside cells. Wang and colleagues used proteomics to see how virB shapes that survival in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Comparing protein profiles with and without a working virB system revealed which intracellular survival proteins it affects. The secretion system acts like a remote control over the bacterium's own protein set. Knowing its reach points to steps where the hiding strategy could be broken.
plos-pone-0005468:
Steven Pino and co-authors studied T cell death in rats prone to diabetes, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A gene called Gimap5 helps T cells stay alive, and changes in the human form of the gene are linked to autoimmune disease. Rats with a faulty form lose T cells and develop diabetes.

The team found that stress inside the cell, acting through a protein called CHOP, drives the death of these T cells. Naming that pathway matters because blocking it might one day protect T cells in diseases where the immune system attacks the body itself.
plos-pone-0005568:
Kevin Tetteh and co-authors searched malaria parasite genes for signs of balancing selection in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Parasites that live with people face strong pressure from our immune systems. Genes under a certain kind of selection keep several forms in the population, which leaves a telltale pattern in their DNA.

The team scanned parasite genomes for that pattern to flag genes worth attention. Several known target genes of immunity showed the pattern already. New flagged genes are strong candidates for vaccine work, since immunity clearly acts on them. A flagged gene must still be tested in the lab, but the scan gives vaccine teams a far shorter list.
plos-pone-0005668:
Gabriel Morrhaye and colleagues published a 2009 PLOS ONE study on growth hormone and the thymus, the gland where T cells mature. They looked at adults who lack growth hormone and at what changes when the hormone is replaced. The work sits where hormone science meets immune science.

The authors note that T cell output from the thymus continues past puberty, even as the gland shrinks with age. In rodents, growth hormone and related signals can undo some of that age-linked decline. Their study asks whether the same link holds in adult patients. The results matter for doctors who weigh hormone treatment in people whose immune defenses may also be weak.
plos-pone-0005768:
Ali Khoshnan and co-authors studied in 2009 how DNA damage triggers the cutting of huntingtin, the protein behind Huntington's disease. Cutting huntingtin into pieces is a key step in the disease. What tells the cell to cut it was poorly known.

The team linked two enzymes, IKK alpha and IKK beta, to that cutting after DNA damage. Damaged DNA builds up in neurons over a lifetime, which may be one trigger. Blocking the cutting step is a long-standing hope for treatment. Naming the enzymes that license it gives drug work a concrete pair of targets to test.
plos-pone-0005868:
Naoki Hida and co-authors built a sensitive imaging system in 2009 to watch two protein partnerships at once inside living subjects. Proteins rarely act alone; their interactions run most cell processes. Fragment complementation assays light up when two proteins meet, but watching pairs inside whole animals was hard.

Using multicolor luciferases, enzymes that glow in different colors, the team imaged dual interactions in real time. Separate colors let two partnerships be tracked side by side. That opens studies of how drug treatment reshuffles protein networks in a living body, not just a dish. Sensitivity gains make faint interactions visible too.
plos-pone-0005968:
Doppel is a close cousin of the prion protein, but it is not found in the healthy adult brain. Stefano Benvegnù, Diego Franciotta, Josh Sussman and colleagues probed what Doppel does in 2009. When Doppel shows up in the brain it can harm nerve cells, and their PLOS ONE paper hunts for the partner that helps it do so.

The team found that Doppel binds alpha-2-macroglobulin, a large protein that traps other proteins in the blood and tissues. That binding offers a plausible route for the harm Doppel causes. A named partner turns a vague threat into a testable chain of events, and it gives later work a clear place to check the idea.
plos-pone-0006068:
A cell's cleanup crew can also protect it from harm. Andrew Arsham and Thomas Neufeld screened fruit fly genes for such protection in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper searches for new jobs of the autophagy-lysosome pathway, the system that breaks down and recycles worn cell parts, already tied to defense against cancer, brain decline and infection.

The genetic screen found fresh protective roles for the pathway, beyond its known recycling work. Each new role widens the list of diseases where boosting cleanup might help. Screens of this kind are how biology finds unsuspected jobs for old systems, and the fly makes the search fast enough to cover the whole genome.
plos-pone-0006168:
Potassium channels are among the first electrical parts a young brain cell installs. Grit Schaarschmidt, Florian Wegner, Sigrid Schwarz and colleagues cataloged them in human neural progenitor cells in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper characterizes voltage-gated potassium channels in these stem-like cells, testing the idea that the channels are required for the cells to multiply or mature.

An early channel set may steer whether a progenitor keeps dividing or becomes a neuron. That steering matters for any hope of growing replacement brain cells in a dish. The catalog gives that work a parts list, drawn from human cells rather than animal stand-ins, which makes it directly useful to medicine.
plos-pone-0006268:
Keeping time in the head may not work like a single stopwatch. Catalin Buhusi and Warren Meck test that assumption in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper framed around relativity theory. Standard theories assume one absolute internal clock that can start, stop, and reset on command.

The authors evaluate the rival view: many clocks run at once, each tied to its own context. Relativity in physics replaced absolute time with local times, and psychology may need a similar shift. The paper weighs evidence for the multiple-clock account. Its argument shapes how timing experiments should be designed.
plos-pone-0006368:
Ravens and keas are clever birds from two different lineages, corvids and parrots. Christian Schloegl and colleagues tested both on exclusion tasks in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Exclusion means choosing correctly by ruling out the wrong option, a sign of advanced reasoning.

Comparing the birds reveals similarities and differences in their cognitive tools. Hardly anything was known about how the two groups' minds compare. Convergent intelligence in separate lineages shows evolution finding similar solutions. The tests help map which reasoning skills birds share with mammals. Work like this helps show how two far apart bird lines came to think alike.
plos-pone-0006468:
Dongxin Zhao, Song Chen, Jun Cai, and colleagues grew early liver cells from stem cells for PLOS ONE in 2009. Making hepatic progenitor cells, cells that can become liver cells, from human embryonic stem cells has two uses. It helps scientists study how the human liver first forms. It could also create an unlimited source of donor cells for liver transplant therapy.

The authors report, for the first time in their account, a route to derive and characterize these cells. They describe what the cells are and how they behave. A reliable supply of liver progenitors would ease a chronic shortage of donor tissue. The work is an early step toward that goal.
plos-pone-0006568:
Jill Rosenfeld and co-authors tied small deletions of one gene to a growth syndrome in PLOS ONE in 2009. A new syndrome had been linked to missing chunks of chromosome 2, in a region called 2q32q33. Its signs include severe learning problems and slow growth. The team studied people with very small deletions of the SATB2 gene in that region.

Their title says SATB2 deletions cause some of the signs of the 2q33.1 syndrome. Finding one gene behind part of the signs aids diagnosis and advice for families. It also shows how a single protein that binds DNA shapes early growth. Small deletions make the gene's role far more clear than large ones.
plos-pone-0006668:
William Mason and Eric Skaar assessed how Staphylococcus aureus steals iron during pneumonia in PLOS ONE in 2009. S. aureus acquires heme-iron using the iron regulated surface determinant system and the heme transport system. Both systems show critical importance in several infection models. The team assessed the contribution of heme-iron acquisition to S. aureus pneumonia using computed tomography.

Iron is scarce inside hosts, and bacteria must steal it to grow. Imaging lung infection in progress shows how acquisition mutants fare. If iron systems prove essential in pneumonia too, they become drug targets. Blocking iron uptake is a strategy that avoids classic antibiotics.
plos-pone-0006768:
Gagan D. Gupta and colleagues traced routes cells use to swallow material in fruit fly cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. In mammal cells, one route forms compartments called GEECs. That route takes in fluid and certain anchored proteins. It works without dynamin, using other proteins instead. The authors asked whether fly cells use the same route.

Using four fluorescent tracers, they followed uptake pathways in Drosophila cells. A protein called GBF1 proved necessary for the GEEC route. Its role is conserved between flies and mammals. Conservation suggests the pathway is ancient and basic. The fly system now offers a genetic model for studying this form of endocytosis.
plos-pone-0006868:
Min Ni and colleagues found a new form of a stress protein that helps leukemia cells survive in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells answer endoplasmic reticulum stress with the unfolded protein response. A chaperone called GRP78, or BiP, is its major survival arm. It raises the cell's protein-folding capacity. The team identified a novel cytosolic isoform of GRP78.

The new isoform regulates PERK signaling, one branch of the stress response. Through that branch it supports leukemic cell survival. A survival helper specific to stressed cancer cells is a drug target candidate. Blocking it might sensitize leukemia to other treatments. The discovery adds a hidden player to stress biology.
plos-pone-0006968:
David Aanensen, Derek Huntley, Edward Feil, and colleagues built a data collection system in PLOS ONE in 2009. Field researchers often collect data far from any laboratory. They then re-enter it into a database by hand back home. New Android phones offered GPS, cameras, and internet in one device.

Their system, EpiCollect, links those phones to web applications. Users design forms, gather records in the field, and view data on maps. It was aimed at epidemiology, ecology, and community data collection. The approach cut transcription errors and sped up field science for small teams.
plos-pone-0007068:
Maria Katsogiannou, Charbel El Boustany, Florian Gackiere, and colleagues studied stubborn prostate cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. After hormone treatment fails, prostate cancer grows without normal controls. These androgen-independent cells adapt to signals around them, including neurotransmitters. One receiver, the alpha 1A adrenoceptor, helps them resist death.

The team found that caveolae, tiny pockets in the cell membrane, support that resistance. The receptor's protection against apoptosis depended on these structures. Targeting membrane pockets is an unusual therapy angle. It might strip advanced prostate cells of one survival trick.
plos-pone-0007168:
Martin Gulliford, Judith Charlton, Mark Ashworth, and colleagues studied medical coding in PLOS ONE in 2009. Primary care databases hold electronic records for millions of patients. Researchers use them for public health studies. Yet the methods for picking which diagnostic codes define a disease are poorly described. Different code lists can yield different case counts.

Using stroke as their test case, the team evaluated which codes are relevant. Their aim was a defensible standard for finding cases. Consistent coding choices make studies comparable. Without them, two teams can study the same database and report different disease rates.
plos-pone-0007268:
Sónia Pascoal, Simon Creer, Martin I. Taylor, and colleagues developed genetic markers for an invasive crab in 2009. The shore crab Carcinus maenas is common on European coasts. It has recently become a global invader, causing drastic ecological and economic effects where it spreads into new coastal waters.

The authors develop and apply microsatellite markers for the species. Microsatellites are short repeated DNA stretches useful for population genetics. They compare northern and central Portuguese populations for genetic differentiation. Their markers give invasion biologists a tool to trace where new crab populations came from.
plos-pone-0007368:
Thomas A. McWalter and Alex Welte compared methods for estimating new HIV infections from surveys in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Cross-sectional surveys with biomarkers of recent infection offer a convenient way to estimate HIV incidence. The BED assay was developed for that purpose, classifying infections as recent or long-standing from a blood sample.

Controversy surrounded false positive results from such assays. False recents can inflate incidence estimates badly. The authors compare biomarker based incidence estimators. Their comparison helps epidemiologists choose methods and corrections. Accurate incidence figures guide where HIV prevention money should go.
plos-pone-0007468:
Nicole Plaskon, Zach Adelman, and Kevin Myles published a methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on measuring RNA viruses. When an RNA virus copies itself inside a cell, it produces both its genome strand and a full-length mirror strand. Detecting those strands separately is a hallmark test of true replication. Existing assays often confuse one strand with the other. The authors set out to fix that.

They present a method that quantifies each viral RNA strand accurately and specifically. Reliable strand counts let researchers follow the virus's life cycle step by step. That precision helps in testing antiviral drugs and in basic studies of infection. The paper is a tool-building contribution. It gives virologists a cleaner way to answer a basic question: is the virus really replicating?
plos-pone-0007568:
Guillaume Chapron and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on saving a declining brown bear population. The usual rule says never add animals to a shrinking population until the cause of decline is reversed. That sounds prudent, but the authors question it. When decline stems from behavior or demography, waiting may doom the group. Their case was an endangered population of brown bears in Europe.

They diagnosed the mechanisms behind the decline and planned recovery around them. In a small population, problems like skewed sex ratios or poor breeding structure can drive losses. Adding the right animals can fix exactly those problems. The study offers a sharper framework for when translocation helps rather than harms. It replaces a blanket rule with diagnosis first, then action matched to the cause.
plos-pone-0007668:
Nataly Perez and colleagues published a genome-wide survey in PLOS ONE in 2009 on small regulatory RNAs in group A Streptococcus. This bacterium causes strep throat and far worse diseases. Coordinated gene regulation is essential for it to infect and cause harm. Small RNAs, a recently appreciated class of regulators, help run that coordination. The team set out to assess how many such RNAs the pathogen carries.

The analysis built a genome-wide list of the bacterium's small regulatory RNAs. Each entry is a candidate control point in the infection program. Lists like this redirect attention from protein genes alone to the RNA managers between them. Managers are attractive drug targets because they steer many genes at once. The study supplies strep research with a new regulatory map. It is a census of the germ's middle management.
plos-pone-0007768:
Mona Meyer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It reports a surprise effect of a cancer gene in leukemia cells. Acute myeloid leukemia starts in blood-forming progenitor cells with varied genetics. Mutations in the RAS gene are frequent in this disease.

Standard chemotherapy uses high-dose cytarabine. The team found that oncogenic RAS lets leukemia cells respond to chemotherapy in an unusual way. With DNA damage and the protein p53 present, the cells differentiate instead of just dying. Forcing cancer cells to mature is a known treatment idea. This work shows one path by which it can happen.
plos-pone-0007868:
Ming-Jen Lee and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It follows a new mouse model of a human brain disorder over time. Normal pressure hydrocephalus usually appears late in adult life. Its classic signs are gait trouble, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline.

The mice were created with a chemical, ENU, that mutates genes at random. The team evaluated the model longitudinally, checking the animals as they aged. A faithful animal model lets researchers test treatments before human trials. It also reveals how fluid buildup in the brain produces the classic trio of symptoms.
plos-pone-0007968:
Etienne Couturier and colleagues proposed a broad rule behind leaf shape in PLOS ONE in 2009. Leaves start folded and then open into their final form. Biologists often seek the rule in molecules, while physicists seek it in growth and stress across the whole leaf.

The team argued that one global pattern of growth can set the shape as the folded leaf unfurls. Local cell rules alone need not carry the whole plan. Their model joins a long effort to read plant form through physics, and it can be tested against real leaves of many kinds.
plos-pone-0008068:
Hariklia Eleftherohorinou and colleagues read the genetics of three inflammatory diseases by pathway in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genome-wide scans had found many risk genes, yet together they explained only a small share of why these diseases run in families. Single-gene thinking was missing something.

Adding up small effects across whole pathways showed where the hidden risk mass sits. Several pathways carried more risk variants than chance allows, across more than one disease. The pathway view steers drug hunters toward processes to calm, rather than lone genes to fix. Shared paths are prime leads for the next round of work.
plos-pone-0008168:
Harmony Salzler and colleagues removed a histone-message helper in fruit flies and watched genomes wobble in PLOS ONE in 2009. Histone messages end in a stem-loop rather than the usual tail, and a protein called SLBP is needed to finish them rightly. Histones pack DNA, so their supply guards genome order.

Without the helper, flies showed unstable genomes and cells that multiplied poorly. The chain from a small message fault to genome-wide disorder is now plain. It also hints why cancers, which often strain histone supply, can slide into the chaos that marks them.
plos-pone-0008268:
Carlos Enrique Orozco-Barrios and colleagues modelled vitamin B12 problems in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. Vitamin B12 is essential for proper brain function. It also supports production of a key molecule called S-adenosylmethionine. Whether B12 deficiency kills neurons was unknown. The question matters especially for Parkinson's disease research.

The rats expressed a special chimera protein in the substantia nigra, a brain area lost in Parkinson's. Impaired B12 metabolism there produced cell death and a Parkinson-like condition. The model links a vitamin pathway to a disease phenotype. It may help test protective strategies.
plos-pone-0008368:
Stefan Nierkens and colleagues tested cancer immunotherapy routes in mice in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. CpG is an agonist of TLR9, a sensor that sparks immune defenses.
