It is increasingly applied to enhance tumor immunity in studies and trials. Clinical success, however, has lagged behind animal results. One reason might be differing routes of administration.

The route of giving CpG critically determined therapy efficacy in mice. How a drug enters the body can change which immune cells it reaches. Matching the mouse route to human use may improve trial outcomes. The study is a practical lesson for immunotherapy design.
plos-pone-0008468:
Mark Field and co-authors study protein folding help in a parasite in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The parasite Trypanosoma brucei causes sleeping sickness. Its surface is coated with a protein called VSG. That coat shields it from the host immune system. Unlike most cells, the parasite does not respond to some folding stress in the usual way. That hints at odd quality control in its cells.

The team find which chaperones the coat protein needs. Chaperones are helper proteins that guide folding. Knowing the needed set shows how the coat is built. Weak points in that path could be drug targets against the parasite.
plos-pone-0008568:
Andreas Kern and co-authors study chaperone capacity in worms in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Protein stability under changing conditions is vital for the cell. A fine-tuned network of molecular chaperones controls that stability. Aging and neurodegenerative diseases are directly associated with enhanced protein instability. The team use Caenorhabditis elegans, a small worm used in aging research. They focus on HSF1, a master switch for chaperone genes, in neurons and muscle.

They measure how chaperone capacity changes with age in those tissues. Capacity controlled by HSF1 declines or shifts as worms grow old. That decline may leave neurons exposed to misfolded proteins. The work links a single switch to tissue aging in a model animal.
plos-pone-0008668:
Marc Daigneault and co-authors identify macrophage markers in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Differentiated macrophages are resident tissue phagocytes and sentinel cells of innate immunity. Their phenotype reflects environmental and differentiation-dependent imprinting. Labs often model them with THP-1 cells stimulated by a compound called PMA. The team compare markers in PMA-stimulated THP-1 cells and monocyte-derived macrophages. Monocyte-derived cells come from human blood donors.

They identify markers that reliably show macrophage differentiation in both systems. Some popular markers prove inconsistent between models. A validated marker set improves how labs judge macrophage experiments. It helps align cell line results with primary human cells.
plos-pone-0008768:
Andrew Beck, Ziming Weng, Daniela Witten, and colleagues built a gene-reading method for old tumor blocks. Their methods paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hospitals store tumors in wax after formalin treatment. Those archives hold years of patient history. Standard gene chips, though, work poorly on such fixed tissue. A sequencing method tuned to damaged samples was needed.

Their approach, called 3SEQ, reads the tail ends of gene messages. It counts messages even from degraded archival material. Reliable counts unlock huge stored collections for cancer research. Past patients' samples can now answer questions no one asked when they were stored.
plos-pone-0008868:
Syed-Wajahat Hassan, Karen Doody, Serge Hardy, and colleagues tested mice missing half of an immune brake against gut inflammation. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. TC-PTP is an enzyme that keeps immune signaling in check. Mice lacking it fully develop broad immune problems. Half-dose mice look fairly normal at rest. A chemical called DSS can trigger colitis, inflaming the colon.

Half-dose mice developed clearly worse colitis after DSS exposure. Even partial loss of the brake weakened gut protection. The gene is also linked to human inflammatory bowel disease. The result strengthens that link with living evidence.
plos-pone-0008968:
Dominik Lermen and co-authors coaxed pig skin stem cells toward nerve and muscle fates, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pigs are close to humans in body plan, so their stem cells model our own. Stem-like cells had recently been taken from pig skin. The question was how many cell types those skin cells could still become.

In lab dishes the team guided the cells down nerve and muscle paths. The cells took on the shapes and markers of those tissues. Crossing from skin into nerve and muscle shows the cells kept wide potential. Such pig cells can test cell therapies before anyone tries them in people.
plos-pone-0009168:
Hongyu Ying and co-authors charted the working life of a glaucoma-linked protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glaucoma is a major cause of blindness worldwide. Its commonest form, primary open angle glaucoma, has many genetic roots. Optineurin is one culprit gene, tied mainly to normal tension glaucoma.

The team mapped the protein's chemical modifications after it is made. They also tracked where optineurin sits in cells and what it binds. Those details show how the protein does its normal job. Knowing the routine exposes what goes wrong in the disease.
plos-pone-0009268:
Leepakshi Sahini, Anna Tempczyk-Russell, and Ritu Agarwal published this flu study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hemagglutinin, the spike protein on influenza A virus, is the main target of vaccines. The problem is that the spike changes shape fast as the virus evolves. Vaccines must be remade again and again to keep up.

The team analyzed huge numbers of hemagglutinin sequences, looking for parts that stay the same. Conserved regions cannot change without hurting the virus, so they make stable targets. An antiviral aimed at such a region could work across many flu strains. Their large-scale search narrows the hunt to the most promising stretches.
plos-pone-0009368:
Yuji Takano and co-authors published this gambling psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Common sense says big losses should make gamblers cautious. The team found the opposite pattern in their tests. They used a computerized card task modeled on the Iowa Gambling Task, with some decks hiding very large losses.

Healthy volunteers who suffered repeated big losses made riskier choices afterward. The authors connect that shift to the balance between deliberation and impulsivity. A paradox like this helps explain how losing streaks deepen instead of ending. It gives gambling researchers a measurable link between recent losses and reckless play.
plos-pone-0009468:
Arianna Tocchetti and co-authors studied mice that lack a protein called Eps8 in PLOS ONE in 2010. Eps8 helps reshape actin, a key part of a cell's inner frame. Eating fewer calories is known to improve health and slow aging in many animals. The team asked whether loss of one protein could mimic some of those gains.

The mice without Eps8 had flaws in the gut. At the same time, their metabolism looked better than normal. That mix links a frame building protein to whole body energy use. It hints that paths tied to diet and aging may run through the cell's skeleton.
plos-pone-0009568:
Lun Yang and colleagues mapped drug and protein interactions by computer in PLOS ONE in 2010. Every drug acts on more proteins than its intended target. Those extra actions cause side effects, but they might also cure other diseases. The team built a network linking chemicals to the proteins they touch. They asked whether drugs with like effects share hidden target patterns.

Patterns in the network pointed to unexpected targets for known drugs. Each such target suggests a new use worth testing in the lab. The study turns a drug's untidiness into a source of leads. It offers a faster route to finding fresh jobs for old medicines.
plos-pone-0009668:
Zhang Guohong and co-authors compared esophageal cancer genetics in two parts of China in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some regions of China suffer very high rates of this cancer. The north and south high incidence areas may not share the same causes. The team studied the genetic character of tumors from both regions. They looked for how the tumors differ at the genetic level.

Tumors from the two regions showed real genetic heterogeneity. One cancer name thus covers distinct genetic faces in different places. Regional maps like this can guide screening tuned to local risk. They also warn against assuming one treatment logic fits every high incidence area.
plos-pone-0009868:
Schistosoma japonicum is a parasitic flatworm that lives in blood vessels and causes schistosomiasis. Hong You and colleagues cloned and described the worm's insulin receptors. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The worm infects people and animals across parts of Asia.

Insulin receptors let cells respond to insulin, the hormone that manages sugar. A parasite with its own receptors may tap into the host's signals to grow. Cloning the receptors is the first step to studying how they work. That knowledge could expose weak points for new drugs. That makes the receptors a window on how the worm grows.
plos-pone-0009968:
Brucellosis passes from livestock to people and causes long, feverish illness. Kunda John and colleagues measured which factors put rural Tanzanians at risk. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study area was rural northern Tanzania.

Quantifying risk factors means putting numbers on habits and exposures. Brucellosis is caused by Brucella bacteria in farm animals. Likely routes include handling animals and drinking unboiled milk. Numbers let health teams target the riskiest practices first. The disease is often missed, so clear risk data matter. Fever from brucellosis can come and go for months.
plos-pone-0010168:
Christopher Potter and Liqun Luo presented a mapping method in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Fruit fly researchers use movable DNA elements to insert thousands of constructs into the fly genome. Those inserts help test gene and cell function and rearrange chromosome arms. Knowing exactly where each insert landed is essential for interpreting the experiments that follow.

Their method, called splinkerette PCR, maps those transposable element insertions. A reliable map turns a random insert into a known, reusable research tool. The technique supports the large mutant collections that fly genetics depends on.
plos-pone-0010268:
The authors were Yuji Zhang, Jianhua Xuan, Benildo de los Reyes, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study rebuilt cell cycle control modules in cancer. Precise cell cycle regulation is crucial to growth in all organisms. Its breakdown sits behind many complex diseases, most notably cancer, where cells divide without proper checks on timing or number.

The team integrated several kinds of biological data to reconstruct regulatory modules. Combining sources can correct errors that any single dataset carries alone. The resulting modules show which controls fail as cancer cells cycle, suggesting points for intervention.
plos-pone-0010368:
Elena Govorunova and colleagues used a tiny worm to study a migraine-linked gene in PLOS ONE in 2010. The worm gene eat-6 makes part of a sodium-potassium pump in cells. Its human counterpart is a candidate gene for a rare inherited migraine type. Migraine is common and often tied to faulty serotonin signaling. The team asked how this pump gene affects nerve signaling in the worm.

They found the gene shapes how serotonin adjusts excitatory nerve transmission. A worm may seem far from a migraine patient, yet its simple nerves expose basic mechanisms. Shared genes let such findings cross species lines. The study gives migraine research a cheap, fast test system. It also ties an ion pump to a brain chemical long tied to attacks.
plos-pone-0010468:
Peng Wu and colleagues studied how tuberculosis spreads in a newly developed Chinese city for PLOS ONE in 2010. They drew lessons from Hong Kong, a rich subtropical city with strong health services but a stubborn TB burden. Case rates there fell for decades, then the decline slowed. The team's Hong Kong experience framed their look at transmission in the developing city.

Fast-growing cities crowd people together and mix migrants with locals. Those conditions can keep TB circulating despite good clinics. Transmission models help officials see where control efforts bite. They also forecast how rates may move as the city grows. TB control in new cities is a growing global problem. This study offers a template drawn from a comparable city.
plos-pone-0010568:
Grant Mackenzie and colleagues tracked two falling infections in Gambian children for PLOS ONE in 2010. Severe Salmonella blood infections dropped alongside malaria. Malaria raises the risk of invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella, a dangerous blood infection in children. Over ten years, malaria measures in The Gambia fell steeply. The team compared trends for both infections at two sites. They asked whether Salmonella disease fell as malaria retreated.

The Salmonella decline unfolded in step with the malaria decline. That parallel supports a real causal link between the infections. It also means malaria control quietly prevents other deadly diseases. Counting such side benefits changes the value of malaria programs. This study provides rare long-term data tying the two together.
plos-pone-0010668:
Peter Etnoyer, Herman Wirshing, and Juan Sánchez surveyed soft corals on Saba Bank, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Saba Bank is a vast submerged platform near Saba Island in the Caribbean. Ships heading to nearby oil terminals anchor on the bank and crush bottom life.

Divers rapidly assessed octocorals, the soft corals and sea fans, across many sites. They recorded which species lived where and the habitat each preferred. The survey gives managers a first solid baseline for this group. With a baseline in hand, later damage from anchoring or storms can be measured instead of guessed.
plos-pone-0010768:
Anja Weinreich Olsen and colleagues compared a chlamydia vaccine with natural infection in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chlamydia is a common sexually spread infection that can scar the fallopian tubes. A first infection gives only partial protection, so a vaccine must do better than nature. Their candidate, CTH1, joins two chlamydial proteins into one.

Mice were vaccinated or first infected through the nose, then challenged in the genital tract. The subunit vaccine protected at least as well as the prior infection. It did so through a cleaner, defined immune response. A two-protein shot that matches nature's best effort is a strong starting point for human trials.
plos-pone-0010868:
Ravichandran Panchanathan, Hui Shen, Xiang Zhang and co-authors published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lupus, an autoimmune disease where the body attacks itself, strikes women far more often than men, and high levels of interferons are a hallmark. The authors hunted for a molecular link between interferons and estrogen, the female hormone.

In mouse immune cells, both major interferon types raised levels of estrogen receptor alpha, the protein that lets cells respond to estrogen. The rise depended on a signal factor called STAT1 and came from increased gene activity. The group also traced effects running the other way, forming a self-reinforcing loop. Panchanathan and colleagues offer a concrete mechanism that could help explain the strong female bias in lupus and point to new treatment angles.
plos-pone-0010968:
Sonja Ständer, Dorothee Siepmann, Ilka Herrgott and co-authors published this itch treatment study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chronic itching can wreck quality of life, arises from kidney, liver, and skin diseases that often cannot be cured, and frequently ignores antihistamines. Substance P, a nerve messenger, is a major driver of itch and acts through a receptor called NKR1, so the team tried blocking that receptor.

Twenty patients whose itch had resisted all standard treatment took the blocker aprepitant, an existing anti-nausea drug, for one week. Four out of five patients reported a considerable drop in itch intensity on a standard rating scale. Ständer and colleagues present the first clinical hint that this pathway can be drugged in people. A repurposed drug offering relief where nothing worked would be significant for a neglected symptom.
plos-pone-0011068:
Moupali Das, Priscilla Lee Chu, Glenn-Milo Santos and co-authors published this HIV public health study in PLOS ONE in 2010. At the individual level, the amount of virus in a person's blood predicts transmission risk. The authors asked whether the same holds for a whole city, using San Francisco's unusually complete HIV surveillance records from a period when testing and treatment were expanding.

They computed community viral load, the average and total virus carried by all diagnosed residents, year by year, and modeled its relation to new infections. As community viral load fell between the mid-2000s and the end of the decade, new HIV infections fell with it. Das and colleagues validate a population-level gauge of epidemic momentum. Cities can now track one number to judge whether treatment-as-prevention is working.
plos-pone-0011168:
Jaramillo-Gutierrez, Molina-Cruz, Kumar and colleagues studied malaria mosquitoes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mosquitoes must survive harmful oxygen based molecules made during blood feeding and infection. A gene called OXR1 helps resist that damage in the mosquito that spreads malaria in Africa.

The team found this gene controls enzymes that detoxify those harmful molecules. Weakening that defense could make mosquitoes less hardy and worse at carrying malaria. That makes the pathway of interest for new vector control ideas. It adds a genetic angle to the long fight against a disease that kills many children.
plos-pone-0011268:
Guo, Scott and Ren studied binge alcohol in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. A sudden high dose of alcohol can weaken the heart's pumping. Mice engineered to make extra alcohol breaking enzyme in the heart suffered worse dysfunction after such a challenge, and the team tested a fuel sensing protein's role in that harm.

The sensing protein, AMPK, was involved in the added heart damage. That identifies a cardiac mechanism by which alcohol hurts some hearts more than others. It informs care for alcohol related heart disease. Blocking the harmful arm of this pathway could one day protect heavy drinkers' hearts.
plos-pone-0011368:
Tobias Riede, John Fisher, and Franz Goller compared the voice boxes of male and female zebra finches in 2010. Male zebra finches sing learned songs with notably high notes, while females do not sing the same way. The team measured the syrinx, the organ birds use to produce sound, looking for built-in sex differences that fit that vocal gap.

The male syrinx differed in structure in ways suited to producing high fundamental frequencies, the base pitch of a note. Those differences point to an adaptation shaped by song itself, not a random side effect of body size. The work helps explain how anatomy and behavior evolve together in songbirds. It also gives voice researchers a clean case where one sex's sound organ is plainly tuned for the sounds that sex must make.
plos-pone-0011468:
Asimina Hiona and co-authors traced in 2010 how DNA errors in mitochondria waste away mouse muscle. Mitochondrial DNA mutator mice accumulate errors in their energy factories at a fast rate and age early. The team examined their skeletal muscle, the tissue that weakens in sarcopenia, the loss of muscle that comes with age and frailty.

Muscle in the mutator mice showed failing mitochondria, increased death of muscle cells, and clear sarcopenia. That chain, from DNA error to energy failure to cell death to wasted muscle, makes the mouse a vivid working model of one route to human aging. It supports the idea that protecting mitochondrial DNA could protect strength in old age. For researchers, the model offers a place to test such protection with the whole chain visible at once.
plos-pone-0011568:
Craig Thalhauser and Natalia Komarova measured in 2010 how crisply a yeast signaling relay passes its message. Yeast cells relay mating and stress signals through the MAP kinase cascade, a chain of proteins that activate one another in sequence. A relay can amplify, muffle, or distort its input, and systems biology needs the numbers: how sensitively does the final output track the signal that entered?

Their measurement of signal response sensitivity across the cascade reveals design principles of a cellular telephone game that usually, and usefully, resists distortion. Knowing a cascade's sensitivity predicts how a cell will answer drugs that block one link, a question at the heart of cancer therapy, since human cells use the same cascade design. Yeast, cheap and fast, here serves as the wind tunnel for a signaling architecture humans share.
plos-pone-0011668:
Sreelatha Gopinath and co-authors combined two targets against glioma brain tumours, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Two proteins, cathepsin B and uPAR, are produced in excess in gliomas and are tied to the tumours' invasive spread. Earlier work from several groups suggested the pair work together to give glioma its infiltrative character.

Removing both proteins at once stalled tumour cells in the resting phase of the cell cycle. The arrest ran through a regulator called FOXO3a, which raised levels of a brake protein, p27. A double hit that parks cancer cells in neutral offers a promising combined strategy.
plos-pone-0011768:
Brian Cherrington and co-authors studied a chemical modification in dog mammary cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Enzymes called PADs convert the amino acid arginine on proteins into citrulline, a change called citrullination. PAD2 levels were known to vary with the reproductive cycle in rodent tissues, but its role in mammary cells was unexplored.

The team examined whether PAD2 citrullinates histones, the proteins that package DNA, in canine mammary epithelial cells. Their evidence supports such a role. Testing this mechanism in dogs also matters because canine mammary tumours share features with human breast cancer.
plos-pone-0011868:
Na Chen and colleagues recorded nerve signals in 2010 to solve a puzzle about how the brain keeps its messages consistent. Spikes fired from a neuron's cell body in the mouse cortex can vary in size, especially in quick trains. Yet synapses at the far end of the axon need dependable signals to pass messages on.

The team found that the axon itself evens things out, boosting weaker, incomplete spikes until they reach a uniform size. The axon is therefore not a plain cable but an active shaper of the code it carries. That reshaping helps explain how cortical circuits stay readable even when the starting signals are uneven.
plos-pone-0011968:
Christine Ward-Paige and colleagues documented in 2010 how thoroughly sharks have vanished from greater Caribbean reefs. Shark numbers offshore had fallen sharply under fishing pressure, but reef populations had never been assessed at this scale. Exploitation of reef sharks has a long history in the region.

Drawing together contemporary records, the team found a large-scale absence of sharks across reefs where they once were common. They read that absence as a footprint of human pressures. The finding matters because reef sharks are top predators whose loss can ripple through reef food webs, and because a documented baseline stops each generation from accepting emptier reefs as normal.
plos-pone-0012068:
Jejoong Kim, Natasha Matthews, and Sohee Park used brain scanning in 2010 to study a specific weakness in schizophrenia: holding spoken information in mind. The prefrontal cortex's role in working memory deficits in schizophrenia is well established, but how the components of working memory map onto brain activity patterns was unclear. Their focus was phonological verbal working memory, the rehearsal of sounds and words.

An event-related fMRI design ties brain responses to single task moments, separating storage from rehearsal steps. Pinpointing which step's circuitry falters helps explain why everyday tasks like following spoken instructions break down. It also gives treatment studies a sharper target than global memory scores.
plos-pone-0012168:
Elena Paskaleva, Jing Xue, David Lee, and co-authors designed compounds aimed at HIV's doorway into cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV enters immune cells by first gripping a surface protein called CD4, then fusing with the cell. The team had earlier found that a common fatty acid can sit in a pocket on CD4 and block that fusion step surprisingly well.

Guided by computer models of the pocket, they built look-alike compounds that bind far more tightly, at very low doses. A blocker that works at such low amounts is a stronger drug candidate. The work shows a new pocket on a well-known protein can still yield fresh strategies against a heavily studied virus.
plos-pone-0012268:
Michael Koch, Joachim Denzler, and Christoph Redies analyzed the hidden geometry of pictures, from fine art to manga, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Photographs of nature share a statistical signature: their pattern strength falls off with detail size in a smooth power law, the same at every scale. The team checked whether drawings, cartoons, comics, and photos of different subjects follow the same rule, and whether the pattern stays even in all directions.

Art made by hand turned out to share much of nature's signature. That hints artists absorb the statistics of the visual world and reproduce them without knowing it. Vision science uses such regularities to explain why some images look natural and others feel wrong.
plos-pone-0012368:
David Nickens, Nirmala Bardiya and James Patterson worked on a lab method for hunting RNA enzymes, described in PLOS ONE in 2010. They want to select kinase ribozymes, strands of RNA that can add phosphate groups to small target molecules. To pick winners from billions of strands, they first need a way to tag the active ones so those can be kept and copied.

Their method uses the enzyme T4 DNA ligase to join a short DNA-tagged building block onto RNA strands that do the kinase job. Only strands that grab the block get tagged and survive selection. The trick opens a path to evolving RNA enzymes that sense or process cell metabolites, useful tools for research and medicine.
plos-pone-0012468:
Sebastian Königsberger, Doris Peckl-Schmid, Nadja Zaborsky and colleagues studied a brake on white blood cell sticking, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The kinase HPK1 is switched on by stress, growth factors, and immune signals. B lymphocytes must stick firmly to act, and a partner protein named Rap1 drives that sticking, so controls on Rap1 decide how strongly B cells respond.

The team found HPK1 joins with an adaptor, SKAP-HOM, to damp Rap1-driven adhesion in B cells. A defined brake helps explain how immune responses stay proportionate. Faulty brakes could contribute to autoimmunity, making this pathway worth watching in immune disease research.
plos-pone-0012568:
Daniel Frynta, Silvie Lišková, Sebastian Bültmann and colleagues asked whether good looks pay off for parrots in captivity, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Parrots are among the most kept and bred birds, and captive stocks could rescue wild species from poaching pressure. If keepers favor attractive species, breeding effort and zoo space will tilt toward the pretty, not the neediest.

The team tested whether parrot attractiveness to humans predicts advantages such as larger captive populations and more breeding success. A beauty bias would quietly distort conservation priorities. Knowing the bias exists is the first step to correcting it, so rare but plain species get a fair share of help.
plos-pone-0012668:
Mueller, Scott, Ishak and co-authors checked whether leafcutter ant gardens really hold just one fungus strain. The ants farm Attamyces fungi for food, cutting leaves to feed their gardens. The gardens were long thought to be pure single-strain plantings, kept clean by the ants over whole colonies.

Their 2010 genetic tests examined that monoculture claim across ant gardens. Whether a garden holds one strain or several changes how we see the ants' farming skill. It also bears on how this ancient partnership stays stable against disease and cheating strains.
plos-pone-0012768:
Matsuda, Shao, Boulanger and co-authors pictured packed chromosomes at a scale of a few nanometres. When a cell divides, its DNA condenses into tight chromosomes whose inner layout was long disputed. Their 2010 study used PALM, a light method that locates single glowing molecules, with tagged histone proteins marking the DNA spools.

The images resolved chromosome structure far finer than normal microscopes reach. That detail tests old models of how DNA folds for division. Folding faults underlie some cancers and birth defects, so the basic map has medical weight.  Histone tags let the team see DNA packing directly.
plos-pone-0333868:
Drajad Seto, Lee Karp-Boss, and Mark Wells grew three bloom-forming diatom species in the laboratory to see how past hunger shapes future growth, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Diatoms are glass-shelled algae that feed ocean food webs. As warming seas stratify, surface nutrients run out for longer stretches, so the team starved cultures for two weeks or four, then fed them again at five temperatures.

The two Pseudo-nitzschia species bounced back faster after long starvation than Skeletonema costatum did, with shorter delays and quicker growth. Warmth favoured the fast recoverers further. Which species wins the rebound helps decide what a plankton community looks like after a nutrient pulse, with knock-on effects for fisheries.
plos-pone-0334868:
Juan Martín and Alessandro Indelicato explore in 2026 why Americans differ in what they expect environmental rules to cost. They used a national survey panel and grouped answers about fuel prices, personal freedom, and jobs in fossil fuel areas. Fuzzy methods let people fall partly into more than one group rather than forcing a sharp split.

People who expected heavy costs were more often religious, conservative, older, and male. Views reflected religious identity and how strongly faith was held, not only politics or income. Because the items record expectations rather than measured effects, the authors treat the results as a map of belief, not proof of impact.
plos-pone-0338168:
Xinfang Zhang and colleagues profiled the chemistry of Chinese chestnut leaves while a tiny mite, the chestnut red mite, fed on them. The mite sucks sap from leaf cells, yellows the foliage, and cuts nut yields, yet breeders knew little about how resistant trees fight back. The team compared four chestnut varieties with different resistance levels, measuring hundreds of leaf chemicals before and after attack.

Resistant varieties rewired their chemistry far more strongly than vulnerable ones. The standout defenders were flavonoids and phenolic acids, a family of bitter plant compounds, and twenty-seven of them piled up in resistant leaves while barely changing in susceptible trees. The authors map the pathways involved and offer the results as a shopping list for breeding chestnut varieties that can shrug off the mite.
plos-pone-0340568:
Heejin Yun and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One study building a blood test for past Lassa virus infection. Lassa fever is a deadly illness across West Africa. No commercial test can measure antibodies against the virus's main target protein. The team built an enzyme-based lab test in Ghana. They tuned its detection limits and precision. They also made a reference standard matched to the World Health Organization standard.

The test was built on one virus lineage's protein. It still detected antibodies from patients exposed to all four major lineages in the region. It coped with damaged blood samples and repeated freezing. It agreed fully with a discontinued commercial kit on comparison samples. The authors say running the test inside West Africa strengthens outbreak research and vaccine work where the disease occurs.
plos-pone-0345368:
HIV treatment only works when pills are taken faithfully, and Cosmas Zyambo and colleagues surveyed more than five thousand people on treatment across one hundred ninety-three Zambian clinics. Their 2026 PLOS One analysis used a 2023 national survey to find what travels with missed doses.

About seven percent reported poor adherence, more men than women. Among those struggling, six in ten drank alcohol and about a fifth smoked. Older age and more schooling each lowered the odds of missing doses. The authors argue clinics should ask about drinking and smoking openly and build support around them, since both habits are changeable risks.
plos-pone-0345868:
Kristina Kokorelias and colleagues present a plan for reviewing what is known about heart disease among older adults who experience homelessness. Heart failure and blocked coronary arteries strike this group earlier and harder than housed peers, yet no one has gathered the scattered studies into one prevalence picture. The protocol also builds in a consultative exercise, asking people with relevant experience to shape the review.

As a protocol, it fixes the search, screening, and pooling methods in advance and reports no results. The finished review aims to give clinics and shelters defensible numbers on how common these conditions are among older homeless adults, a group often invisible in heart statistics. Such numbers matter because services for aging homeless patients are planned today on guesswork more than evidence.
plos-pone-0346268:
Gina Marie Pizzo and colleagues argue that surveys of scientists routinely mismeasure what field a scientist truly belongs to. So they built a better yardstick. Their 2026 paper introduces a five-part measure of disciplinarity. It captures how a researcher's identity, training, methods, and reading stretch. The stretch runs between a home discipline's core and its frontiers. The measure is designed to sit alongside the usual degree label.

They tested it in a survey of more than four thousand tenure-system science faculty. The survey covered eighty-three American research universities. The team presents narrative and statistical evidence that the instrument behaves as intended. The payoff is finer research on cross-disciplinary work. Instead of forcing scientists into single boxes, studies can now measure how loosely each box actually holds.
plos-pone-0346568:
Yufei Li and colleagues measured what happened to vaccine hostility on X, the platform once called Twitter, after it ended its misinformation policy in late November 2022. Their 2026 PLOS ONE study used a large language model to sort posts from the week before and the week after the change by stance and theme.

Anti-vaccine posts rose sharply once the policy ended, driven heavily by retweets that spread existing content, though new posts grew too. Health worries about vaccines became a larger share of the talk, while conspiracy and anti-mandate themes shrank in relative terms. Quote posts also lined up more tightly with one stance. The findings suggest moderation rules had been holding down both volume and spread.
plos-pone-0346668:
Neha Shanker and five colleagues hunt for blind spots in North Carolina's disease surveillance in this 2026 analysis. The state tracks illness both through emergency department visits and through wastewater testing, but some communities sit far from any emergency department and carry high social vulnerability. The team compared the two streams where they overlap, mapped drive times to every hospital, and scored sewer districts by population, distance from care, and a standard vulnerability index.

Where both systems operated, their signals mostly rose and fell together, confirming they complement each other. Twenty-six sewer districts stood out as priority additions: large enough to matter, poorly served by emergency care, and home to highly vulnerable residents, half of them in the highest vulnerability band. The authors present the geospatial method as a way to aim early-warning infrastructure at the places that need it most.
plos-pone-0346868:
Shilpa S. Iyer and colleagues checked whether a rapid test that tells if an HIV infection is recent can be trusted in the hands of clinic staff in Lusaka, Zambia. Knowing how many infections are new helps target prevention. People newly diagnosed at two health facilities received the test on site, with samples rechecked at a central laboratory alongside viral load testing.

On-site and laboratory results agreed more than ninety-six percent of the time. The clinic version produced three false recent results, slightly lowering its sensitivity, but staff in discussion groups called the test feasible and acceptable with proper training and counselling. The authors support wider rollout with those supports in place.
plos-pone-0347468:
Yongjiang Yu and four colleagues study how heat damages coal in this 2026 engineering paper. The work matters for coalbed methane extraction. Pumping heat into a coal seam can free trapped gas, but it may also weaken the seam. The team squeezed coal samples while they were hot, using a high-temperature testing machine. Computer simulations tracked cracks forming inside the rock.

As temperature rose, the coal strained further before failing. Its strength and stiffness both fell. Cracks caused by heat itself were mostly tensile, pulling the rock apart. The failure style also shifted with heat. Cool samples split straight down, while hot samples failed in a mixed tearing pattern. The authors built a staged damage model from these results, giving engineers a tool to predict when heated seams might collapse.
plos-pone-0347668:
Taylor L Davis, Bruce E Rittmann, and co-authors built a mathematical model of digestion that, for the first time, accounts for the energy gut microbes harvest and hand back to the body. The standard calorie factors used on food labels ignore this microbial economy. Their 2026 model tracks a meal through five steps, from splitting food into nutrients to microbes fermenting leftovers into absorbable compounds and gas.

Tested against a clinical feeding study with two very different diets, the model matched measured energy absorption more accurately than the standard factors and nearly erased a systematic bias on one diet. It also predicted how much fermentable material reached the colon and how fast useful byproducts were made. The authors plan to link it to whole-body models of weight and metabolism.
plos-pone-0347768:
Francesca Ferragut-Perello and colleagues assess the skates living around Spain's Balearic Islands in this 2026 PLOS ONE conservation study. Skates grow and reproduce slowly, which makes them easy to overfish, yet the islands are a Mediterranean stronghold for these flat relatives of sharks.

The team sequenced DNA from seven species, including two found only in the Mediterranean, and compared diversity across the region; most species sat on the low side. For three species they also estimated stock health with methods designed for data-poor fisheries, some of which raised concern. The combined genetic and stock picture tells managers which skates need protection first in an island hotspot.
plos-pone-0347868:
Tamiru Kibebew and co-workers measure how much of young sheep growth is written in their genes under smallholder farming in Ethiopia's Oromia region. The Horro breed is raised by community breeding groups that want faster-growing lambs. Their 2026 study analyzes thousands of weight records at birth, three months, and six months from program flocks.

Growth traits showed modest to fair heritability, rising by six months of age. That means choosing parents by their lambs' growth should bring real gains over generations. Links between weights at different ages were weak to modest, so each stage adds its own information. The numbers give community breeders a firmer basis for picking rams and ewes on real farm conditions.
plos-pone-0348068:
Mehdi Borjkhani, Hadi Borjkhani, and Morteza A Sharif used a computer model to ask when magnesium could protect the eye's signal-carrying cells from overstimulation damage. These retinal ganglion cells can be harmed when a receptor lets too much calcium flood in, a process linked to vision loss. Magnesium naturally blocks that receptor, but the helpful dose and timing were unclear.

Simulations varied magnesium levels and signal rates across a wide range. At normal firing rates, extra magnesium cut calcium buildup by half or more without silencing the cells. At harmful rates, only a narrow dose band kept calcium safe while preserving signals. Timing mattered greatly: protection was full when magnesium arrived before or right at the insult, then fell fast with delay. The model offers guidance for designing real protective treatments.
plos-pone-0348268:
Jianchun Wei and colleagues tested whether two ratios computed from a routine blood count can predict which sepsis patients will die within a month. Both ratios pit neutrophils, the infection-fighting first responders, against lymphocytes or platelets. Records from three hundred and ninety-five adults treated for sepsis at one emergency department over five years were analysed, with the ratios compared against procalcitonin, a standard infection marker.

Neither ratio beat the standard marker, and after adjusting for other differences between patients, none of the three markers independently predicted death at all. Flexible curve checks found no hidden threshold where the ratios suddenly matter. With overall mortality near two in five, the authors deliver a useful negative: these cheap ratios, however attractive, should not guide sepsis prognosis on their own.
plos-pone-0348368:
Selda Coşkuner Aktaş surveyed two hundred eleven working parents in dual-earner couples who worked from home during the COVID-19 pandemic. With offices and nurseries collapsed into the same rooms, clashes between job demands and family demands sharpened. Her 2026 study tested what protected parents: confidence in their own coping, a partner who reliably took on time-consuming family tasks, or simply having fewer demands.

Conflict running from work into family life ran higher than the reverse. Heavy demands alone did not predict conflict, but a supportive partner blunted the strain of long work hours. Personal confidence lowered both kinds of conflict directly. The findings highlight backup at home as a real resource in crisis remote work.
plos-pone-0348668:
Mohammad A. ALMohiza and Ravi Shankar Reddy examined how sensing and balance problems show up in the walking of people with early Parkinson's disease. Their 2026 study tested forty-six patients who could still walk well. Each person had their ankle position sense checked, stood through balance tests, and walked while naming words, a dual task that exposes hidden strain.

Patients with poorer position sense walked more slowly under the dual task and lost more speed compared with plain walking. Those who failed a quick stepping test also showed worse sensing and weaker word scores. The authors argue that simple clinic tests of sensing and balance can flag patients at risk of mobility decline early.
plos-pone-0348768:
Xiaohui Zhu and colleagues reviewed more than thirty-one thousand intensive care admissions at a large Chinese hospital from twenty fourteen to twenty twenty-one. They compared patients aged eighty and over with two younger groups. They tracked how often the oldest patients were admitted, how much care they used, and how their outcomes changed across the eight years.

The oldest group's share of admissions fell by nearly a third over the period, especially for non-surgical cases. These patients arrived sicker and with more other illnesses, needed more circulation support and feeding help, yet were put on breathing machines less often. Their death rate stayed highest, but it fell faster year by year than in younger groups. The authors see intensive care for the very old becoming more selective and more effective.
plos-pone-0348868:
Jing Guan, Zhen chao Yang, and Congcong Wang studied how artificial intelligence can raise the competence of safety directors on large engineering-procurement-construction projects, where one contractor designs, buys, and builds. Such sites change daily, and experience-based inspection is hitting its limits. The authors built a framework around sensing risks, seizing responses, and reconfiguring routines, drawing on management theory.

A comparative evaluation scored safety directors working the traditional way against those backed by AI tools, using structured expert weighting. The AI-supported mode's composite competence index rose by roughly forty-six percent, reflecting a shift from experience-driven to data-driven safety work. The framework gives firms a concrete syllabus for what an AI-era safety director must be able to do.
plos-pone-0348968:
Sofia Segura-Pérez and a community team evaluate a program that gave pregnant Latina women in Hartford, Connecticut, a monthly produce allowance. Poor access to fresh food burdens low-income mothers, and produce prescriptions aim to fix that through clinics and community groups. Enrolled women received a card worth a set monthly amount for fresh produce. The card ran for ten months. They also got nutrition sessions and text tips, and answered surveys at start and end.

By the end, women reported readier habits for healthy eating. The authors tracked this as movement through stages of change. They also measured produce intake and household food security. Segura-Pérez and colleagues present the single-group results as encouraging evidence that pairing money for produce with light coaching can shift daily eating during pregnancy.
plos-pone-0349168:
Zhixiang Sun, Meifang Yang, and co-authors published a 2026 protocol for a trial testing whether virtual clinical simulation teaches nursing students end-of-life care better than classroom lessons alone. Palliative care is hard to practice on real patients, so students often graduate with little direct experience. The planned trial will enroll ninety-six students taking an elective course on death and end-of-life topics at a medical university in southwestern China.

Half the students will be randomly assigned to add simulation sessions to normal teaching, and half will receive teaching only. As a protocol, the document describes the design, the comparison, and the authors' expectation that simulation will improve knowledge, skills, and attitudes toward palliative care. Results will follow once the trial runs, and the authors note how few rigorous trials exist in this field.
plos-pone-0349568:
David Wenzel and colleagues ran online focus groups in the United Kingdom on using bacteriophages, viruses that kill bacteria, to treat urinary tract infections that keep coming back. Forty-four people took part: patients worn down by repeated infections, doctors who manage them, and nurses, pharmacists, and other specialists. Views were mapped onto a standard framework for judging whether a treatment is acceptable.

Enthusiasm was high everywhere, and patients rated the idea as effective and welcome. The researchers flag a worry inside that enthusiasm: desperation after repeated antibiotic failure can make patients vulnerable to poor-quality offerings and unfair access. Costs and availability were the main practical barriers named. Acceptability evidence gathered before rollout helps trials and clinics design phage services people will actually trust.
plos-pone-0349768:
Ali Reza Yusefi and Jamshid Bahmaei interviewed thirty-one people in Iran about informal payments in hospitals, money patients hand over outside official billing. Their group included health ministry policymakers, hospital managers, doctors, nurses, and patients who had made such payments. Interviews ran from late 2024 into early 2025 and were sorted into themes.

Six main themes and many subcategories captured why these payments happen and what might curb them. Off-the-books payments damage fairness and trust, because patients who pay may jump ahead of those who cannot. Hearing from both sides of the transaction gives reformers a fuller map of the problem than billing data alone could show.
plos-pone-0349868:
Hadi Khoshnamvand and colleagues sorted out how barbels, a group of river fish, are related across Iran. Looks alone blur the lines between kinds, so the team joined gene data from two markers with body counts and measures, plus climate and place data from major river basins.

Family trees split the fish into three clear groups. Body measures backed the same split, which strengthens the case for revising some names. A few named kinds may in fact be the same fish. Timing checks tie major splits to mountain building and to cold, dry swings in recent earth history. Place and climate together, the authors argue, drove the spread seen today.
plos-pone-0350168:
Ahmed Abdullah Alshehri and Asaad Abdulrahman Abduljawad propose widening a classic health policy analysis frame for reforms run through digital systems. The classic triangle weighs policy content, context, actors, and process. Saudi Arabias Health Sector Transformation Program under Vision 2030, a vast digital reform, supplied the test case, drawn from policy papers and interviews in an earlier doctoral evaluation.

Technology and culture, the authors argue, cut across every corner of the triangle. Digital tools and social norms shaped coordination, accountability, participation, and patient centred aims throughout the reform. Adding those lenses does not replace the classic frame; it makes the frame fit reforms where software and custom steer daily practice.
plos-pone-0350268:
Chen Ying and Yong Jin Kim addressed a costly gap in farm logistics: fresh produce often spoils before it ever gets chilled. In China, weak pre-cooling near farms undermines the whole cold chain. Their 2026 study built a planning model that decides where to place pre-cooling centers and how to route trucks, balancing total cost against freshness while also counting carbon emissions.

A genetic search algorithm explored the trade-offs across three Shandong Province scenarios. Centralized pre-cooling at regional centers won overall, cutting daily cost slightly and losing the least freshness. Cooling at each farm preserved freshness too but cost more, thanks to duplicated equipment and weaker routes. The authors argue pre-cooling placement and truck routing should be planned together, not as separate decisions.
plos-pone-0350568:
Linda Mercy Akello and co-authors surveyed pregnant women at Gulu hospital in northern Uganda in 2026 about hepatitis B vaccination. The virus is common in Uganda and passes to babies at birth, so vaccinating mothers matters, yet uptake was unmeasured locally.

Four hundred thirty women answered an electronic questionnaire. Just over half had received at least one vaccine dose. Older age within the group, better knowledge of the virus, and clear communication from health workers each raised uptake. The findings point to talks at antenatal visits as the cheapest lever: women who understood the risk and heard it from staff acted on it.
plos-pone-0350668:
Liushan Tao and Anhua Zhong built a fully digital route for designing sports bras without sewing trial after trial. Guessing fabric stretch on screen often distorts the cloth, and still checks miss what happens while running. Their route scans a cotton blend knit in three dimensions, maps its look and stretch into design software, and dresses a standard body model.

A bra with a front zip, crossed straps, and an elastic band was drafted on screen, then tested in a running pose. Fit scores in key zones passed ninety eight percent after fixes. Motion tests caught strap slip and poor cup fit before any cloth was cut. Faster, cleaner design with fewer wasted samples is the payoff.
plos-pone-0350768:
Haruki Naruse and colleagues in Japan checked a fast test for infections of the blood in 2026. Finding the germ and its drug resistance quickly matters, because the right antibiotic given early can save a life.

The team compared a rapid panel test with the usual lab route of growing the germ and testing it by mass measurement. They used just over two hundred positive blood samples that held germs the panel can name. Agreement was high for samples with a single germ and lower for mixed infections. Resistance gene results were also checked. A fast, mostly matching test can start better treatment sooner while full lab work proceeds.
plos-pone-0351068:
Dua Nguyen and seven colleagues let pharmacists police surgical antibiotics in a Vietnamese hospital. Their 2026 study ran at Saint Paul General Hospital in Hanoi. Preventive antibiotics around surgery are often chosen badly or run too long in Vietnam. That misuse breeds resistance and infections. A pharmacist-led team audited prescriptions and fed the results back to surgeons. Two audit rounds ran across five months, covering over three hundred patients before and after.

Compliance with the hospital's guidelines climbed from about sixty percent to seventy-seven. Antibiotic choice improved most, alongside correct duration of use. Both rose to nearly ninety percent. Timing and dosing were tracked as separate components too. Audit and feedback is unglamorous medicine: check, report, repeat. Yet this study shows it shifting entrenched prescribing habits within months. Stewardship programmes across the region can copy the model without new drugs or machines.
plos-pone-0351168:
Ryo Tomemori and colleagues reviewed patients whose diabetic eye swelling had resisted standard injections and who switched to a newer drug, faricimab. Swelling at the centre of vision blurs sight in diabetes, and about four in ten cases resist first line care. Records covered twenty eight eyes from nineteen patients, tracked a year before and a year after the switch.

Centre thickness fell by close to one third, and over half of eyes reached a dry centre mark at one year. Injections grew more frequent after the switch, while measured vision barely changed. Deeper layer thickness stayed steady. Switching can dry the retina, the data suggest, even when vision gains lag behind anatomy.
plos-pone-0351468:
Qian Ye and five colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study building a machine learning tool to predict how independently stroke patients will manage daily life by discharge. Records from nearly six hundred inpatients treated between 2019 and 2024 were used to train ten algorithms, after statistical screening narrowed forty-one candidate measures down to six.

A random forest model performed best, separating patients headed for good versus poor daily-living independence with high accuracy. An explanation technique ranked the strongest drivers: how independent the patient already was at admission, standing balance, recovery stages of the arm and leg, and the ability to dress and groom. The authors say the transparent model can help rehabilitation teams set realistic goals and plan support earlier.
plos-pone-0351568:
Alba Macho-Callejo and colleagues buried deer ribs under three Mediterranean plants to study root marks on bone. Roots etch buried bone all the time. Yet no one had tied the marks to the plant that made them. Ribs sat at varied depths and for varied times. The plants were holm oak, olive, and grapevine. The work took place in central Spain. Microscopes later read the bone surfaces.

Each plant signed the bone in its own way. Oak drew wandering grooves that branch like roots themselves. Olive left shallow, straight marks. Grapevine cut lines and circles, sometimes with small cracks. Marks also deepened with depth and time. A root-etched bone may now hint at the plants above a burial. That is a new clue for archaeology and forensic work alike.
plos-pone-0351768:
Tina Saitone, Kenneth Tate, and Benjamin Sacks present this 2026 PLOS One study of what gray wolves eat in California. The animals have just returned after a long absence. Diet shapes how wolves affect livestock and wild game. Yet this new population had never been studied this way. The team collected wolf scat. They used DNA testing to identify both the wolf that left it and the species it had eaten.

Cattle dominated the diet. Beef appeared in nearly three in four samples. It supplied over half the food energy the team estimated. Mule deer and small mammals each contributed much smaller shares. The authors say the results underline a hard practical problem. Wolves in this working landscape meet most of their needs from livestock. That sharpens the need for prevention and compensation steps.
plos-pone-0351868:
David Sánchez-Carracedo and colleagues gave nine hundred twenty-two Spanish health professionals two standard scales of anti-fat attitudes, the first such audit in the country. Weight stigma inside clinics can quietly degrade care, delay diagnoses, and drive patients away. The sample, mostly women and mostly clinicians who treat people with obesity, also answered questions about common misconceptions regarding the condition's causes and controllability.

Negative attitudes were the norm overall. The consistent pattern was personal: professionals with lower body weight scored higher on stigma on both scales. Younger clinicians scored higher on one scale, private-sector workers on the other, and specialties differed, with obesity specialists least stigmatizing. Training rarely touches weight bias; this baseline says it should, since the professionals patients meet first may carry the strongest prejudice.
plos-pone-0351968:
When offices emptied during COVID-19, many feared output would collapse. Sultan Alenazi and colleagues surveyed about six hundred fifty remote workers to test that fear, in a 2026 PLOS One paper on productivity and the future of working from home.

Their statistical model weighed teamwork ties, time habits, stress, and skill growth. The sudden move home showed no meaningful negative effect on how much people got done. Workers valued arranging their own tasks and a healthier balance between job and home life. The authors suggest personnel managers treat remote work as a lasting option that can help attract and keep good staff.
plos-pone-0352168:
Aiwu Yang, Tianli Liu, and Shaopeng Yang model how soft ground slowly settles under foundations. Their 2026 study concerns vacuum-assisted drainage plates, a trick for squeezing water from ultra-soft soil. Earlier models treated the soil as if it barely deformed. They also ignored what happens at the plate's bottom tip. The authors build large-deformation models on an elliptical cylinder equivalence. Soil stiffness and permeability change as it compresses. Vacuum pressure fades with depth.

The decisive test came against laboratory experiments. The model including the plate's bottom influence zone matched the measured settlement closely. A version with vacuum loss alone drifted away from the data. Skipping the bottom zone underestimates total settlement, the authors warn. Under-prediction is the dangerous direction in foundation work. Engineers sizing drainage treatment for reclaimed land and port ground gain a model that respects how these soils actually finish settling.
plos-pone-0352268:
Hugo Ordoñez and two colleagues build an artificial intelligence model to predict disease among Bogotá's homeless residents. Their 2026 study uses the city's 2024 homeless census. Over ten thousand records carried forty-six demographic, clinical, and social variables. This population suffers heavy burdens of hypertension, diabetes, tuberculosis, and HIV. It is also the population surveillance systems see worst. A gradient boosting model was trained to flag disease occurrence, with explanation tools exposing its reasoning.

The model reached about ninety-one percent overall accuracy. Its sensitivity was more modest, catching a little over half of true cases. The balance struck a workable F1 score for screening purposes. Explanation values showed officials which factors drive each risk profile. Prediction is not the end goal here. Targeted outreach is: sending scarce clinics, testing, and treatment to the street locations where risk concentrates. For invisible populations, a defensible model beats no map at all.
plos-pone-0352468:
Yang and colleagues, in a 2026 study, redesign the small DNA rings used to deliver genes into cancer cells without a virus. The carrier here is a soft polymer particle, safer than viruses but often weaker. The cargo ring's own design, its switch, backbone, size, and selection marker, can raise or lower how much gene gets expressed. Fourteen ring variants were built and tested in liver and brain cancer cells.

One switch design beat its rivals in head-to-head tests within the same backbone. Among rings built to resist being silenced, the winner was a minimal ring carrying almost nothing extra, and notably no antibiotic resistance gene, a safety plus. It lit up the most cells in nearly every liver line and gave the strongest signal in most brain lines too. The authors argue cargo design is a lever gene therapy has underused: strip the ring down, and delivery improves.
plos-pone-0352768:
Asano and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask how losing ovarian hormones changes asthma and blood vessel health in mice. Doctors have long suspected female hormones link asthma with heart and vessel disease in women. Female mice were split into four groups: with or without ovary removal, and with or without allergic asthma triggered by egg protein.

Asthma mice whose ovaries were removed had more of the allergy-linked white cells in their lungs, higher antibody levels, and more inflammatory signals in lung fluid. Their lung disease was plainly worse. In the aorta, asthma itself blunted the vessel's ability to relax, by about a quarter, in both hormone groups equally; ovary removal added nothing there. The authors conclude that hormone loss fans lung allergy, and that lung inflammation alone can reach out and stiffen a distant artery.
plos-pone-0352968:
Pierre Galipot and colleagues mapped checkerboard patterns across living things and asked how such squared designs can grow. Checkerboards are common in human art but rare in nature, despite being easy for eyes to spot. Their 2026 survey confirmed the rarity while finding examples scattered across very different branches of life.

Two cases received deep analysis: checkered lily flowers and flesh flies with squared markings. The flower pattern seems to arise when a stripe-forming process is squeezed by the flower's parallel veins. The fly pattern instead seems to reuse body boundaries and left-right symmetry, stacking stripes two ways. Same geometry, different machinery: the authors call it convergence of shape without convergence of process.
plos-pone-0353068:
Pengsheng Fang and co-authors work in 2026 on turning soft dredged sludge into a stronger, lower carbon solid using several industrial wastes together. Cement, slag, and fly ash served as binders, with water glass as a starter. Strength tests plus X-ray and heat based checks on cured samples revealed how the mix hardened over time.

One blend of the three binders, with a modest share of water glass, performed best in their tests. Water glass created the alkaline setting that let the binders react and form products that packed the sludge tightly. The study gives mix guidance for treating waste sludge with waste materials.
plos-pone-0353168:
Jun Xie and three colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One interview study of cardiac care nurses learning to read heart monitor tracings through a fast-cycle practice method. In this training style, nurses practice in short bursts, get coached the moment they stall, and immediately retry, all in a setting designed to feel safe. The researchers interviewed participants and observed sessions, framing the questions around a well-known model of clinical judgment.

Nurses described four shifts: seeing whole patterns instead of scattered data, blending intuition with evidence instead of matching mechanically, acting confidently instead of hesitantly, and rethinking their professional role and responsibilities. The pause-coach-resume rhythm and its emotional safety seemed central to the change. The authors suggest such training builds judgment and identity together, not just technical skill.
plos-pone-0353268:
Yoon Ji Kim and seven colleagues published this 2026 PLOS ONE study on forecasting how wet orchard soil will be hours ahead. Working in an Asian pear orchard, they recorded rainfall and soil moisture over two growing seasons. Sensors buried at three depths tracked how water moved down through the ground after each rain.

Their forecasting tool was a type of neural network built to learn patterns over time. Grouping rainfall into separate storm events, rather than feeding in hourly totals, gave clearly smaller errors. Short-range forecasts tracked the soil closely, while deeper soil stayed steadier than the surface layer. The authors argue such forecasts could help growers water only when the trees actually need it.
plos-pone-0353368:
Morteza Mellati and Sanaz Nademi tested a teaching approach that lets Iranian English learners draw on Persian in class. Strict English-only rules remain common in such classrooms, even though students think in two languages. Their 2026 experiment compared a university group taught with planned two-language use against an English-only group.

The two-language group reported clear gains in agency, class participation, and pride in their identity. They also viewed multilingualism more positively than the control group did. The teaching approach strongly predicted learner agency after the course, even accounting for starting scores. Mellati and Nademi argue that using learners' full language resources can challenge one-language ideologies and support autonomy in exam-driven settings.
plos-pone-0353468:
Mavunga and colleagues mapped structural DNA differences in South Asian work cattle in a 2026 study. Eight native breeds, long used for ploughing and carting, carry stretches of DNA that are copied extra times or missing. Two detection methods scanned each breed's genome, and their overlap defined the final set of regions.

More than six thousand varied regions covered a noticeable share of the genome. Most regions appeared in all breeds, while a small set was unique to single breeds. Such differences can shape traits for work, breeding, and coping with local conditions. The map gives conservation programs a fuller picture of what makes these hardy breeds distinct.
plos-pone-0353668:
Brian Kasagga and seven colleagues measure how long colorectal cancer patients in Uganda wait between diagnosis and treatment, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Sixty-seven patients at the national referral hospital and the national cancer institute were interviewed and their records reviewed over six months. A wait longer than about a month counted as delay.

The typical wait was nearly two months, and seven in ten patients were delayed. Waits were longest for radiotherapy and shortest for surgery. Only one factor predicted delay on its own: being economically vulnerable. Distance, disease stage, and personal traits did not. The authors call the pattern a structural problem — cancer care that the poor reach last — needing targeted fixes.
plos-pone-0353868:
Grace Knowles led a team of eight authors on this 2026 interview study of parents who learned before birth that their baby had a severe heart defect. Ten parents who chose either ending the pregnancy or a hospice-style birth after counseling at a specialist center described what the counseling felt like and how they decided.

Parents valued information that reached beyond medical outcomes to family life and finances. They also prized their own freedom to decide and wanted honest, even-handed guidance. Knowles recommends training clinicians to counsel all options with empathy and without steering.
plos-pone-0353968:
Meng-Jen Wu and seven colleagues use genetically altered mice to work out how a key immune signaling protein keeps eczema-prone skin calm, in this 2026 study. Loss of filaggrin, a structural skin protein, is the strongest known genetic risk for atopic dermatitis and leaves the barrier leaky. The team bred mice lacking both filaggrin and the signaling adaptor MyD88, then profiled their skin's gene activity, immune cells, and microbes.

Without MyD88, the filaggrin-deficient mice developed spontaneous inflammation around the eyes. A particular class of skin T cells flooded in, producing an inflammatory signal, while fat-producing glands in the skin shrank and lipid-related genes switched down. The skin's microbial community also fell out of balance, and that imbalance itself drove inflammation. The authors conclude that MyD88 quietly polices both glands and microbes, a peacekeeping role that suggests new angles for treating filaggrin-linked eczema.
plos-pone-0354168:
Cunha and colleagues, in a 2026 study, work with teenage girls who live along rivers in the Brazilian Amazon to build a teaching tool about menstruation. Girls in these riverside communities often face silence, shame, and folk rules around periods, with little frank talk at home or school. The study followed a participatory method drawn from the educator Paulo Freire.

Ten adolescents at a public school on Caratateua Island joined discussion circles in three stages: surfacing themes, naming them together, and then looking at them critically. Three themes stood out: periods disrupt feelings and daily life; talk about them is rare and hushed; and local beliefs shape how girls care for themselves. The girls then helped create a comic book that speaks to their own lives, teaching body knowledge, self-care, and dignity. The authors argue health teaching works best when learners build it themselves.
plos-pone-0354368:
Aleny Couto led a team of eight authors on this 2026 report of a nationwide data cleaning effort in Mozambique's HIV treatment program. Reported patient numbers had drifted away from pharmacy and clinic records. In early 2024 every facility offering HIV treatment compared its national figures against local clinical and medicine pickup records.

After the review, the national count of people on treatment fell by about a tenth, exposing whole provinces with deep and longstanding record problems. Couto argues the leaner, truer numbers sharpen planning for new infections, deaths, and mother-to-child transmission.
plos-pone-0354468:
Li and Peng, in a 2026 study, ask how smaller Chinese cities win attention on Douyin, the short-video platform. Big cities dominate place branding, while small and mid-sized cities must fight an algorithm for eyes. The team studied Shaoguan in Guangdong, examining thirty high-engagement videos about the city posted over two years.

Using a method that finds which combinations of traits go with success, they found city hashtags were a near-must for wide spread in their sample. Without being indexed by the platform, a video barely travels. Emotional pull and a clear story strengthened the winning combinations. Two routes to impact appeared. Outsiders made splashy, feeling-rich clips that spread fast. Local storytellers built slower, deeper attachment to place, which the authors call cultural resilience. The study frames a small city's image as something co-made by creators, audiences, and the platform's machinery.
plos-pone-0354668:
Kripa Josten and Vennila Jaganathan compared old-fashioned statistical regression against ten machine learning models for predicting depression, using survey data from the World Health Organization's aging study in India. Their 2026 analysis weighed social, health, and psychological factors, asking both which factors matter and which method predicts best for screening programs.

Depression was more common among younger adults, women, and people reporting poor health, stress, and broken sleep. The machine learning models were only modestly accurate, barely beating chance-adjusted expectations, and a regularized regression actually topped the list. Across all methods, age, self-rated health, quality of life, and low mood itself carried the signal. The authors recommend pairing interpretable regression with machine learning rather than trusting either alone.
plos-pone-0354968:
Tesfahun Alemu Setotaw and seven colleagues show how accounting for field layout sharpens crop trial results across two very different crops, in this 2026 study. Neighboring plots share soil and moisture, so raw comparisons between varieties can mislead breeders. The team re-analyzed more than one hundred wheat trials and dozens of cassava trials from public breeding databases, testing models with and without a spatial correction method.

Correction improved the precision of variety evaluation for wheat grain yield, test weight, plant height, and several diseases, and for cassava dry matter, dry yield, and height. Two cassava diseases showed no gain. Results held whether or not genetic marker effects were included. The authors argue that pairing sound trial design with spatial analysis is essential if breeding programs want trustworthy rankings of new varieties.
plos-pone-0355168:
Amparo Sánchez-Hernández and colleagues tested whether stripping telomere protection from blood vessel cells could slow a deadly brain tumour. Earlier work showed attacking the telomere guard protein in the whole tumour delayed glioblastoma growth. Their 2026 mouse study deleted the guard only in endothelial cells, which line vessels feeding the tumour.

Vessel cells showed the expected damage signals, and vessel density tended to dip. Yet tumours started and grew at the same pace as controls. Protecting telomeres in vessel cells, the authors conclude, is not a main brake on this tumour type. The result redirects anti-telomere strategies toward the cancer cells themselves rather than their blood supply.
plos-pone-0355368: Chickenpox virus — varicella-zoster — circulates in strains worth genotyping. This Shanxi Province study analyzed circulating strains and glycoprotein E characteristics. The molecular epidemiology informs vaccine strategy against a virus that also causes shingles.
plos-pone-0355468:
Yoshihiko Ohzawa and Yukio-Pegio Gunji asked whether termites remember where a scent trail used to be. Textbook accounts treat trail following as a simple reflex to the chemical present right now. Their 2026 experiments removed the pheromone-marked surface after exposure and watched where termites wandered next.

Termites did not return to the exact marked spot right away. Over a longer test window, though, previously exposed termites entered and probed the former trail zone more than controls did. The bias grew clearer when broader zones were counted. Ohzawa and Gunji conclude termites keep some spatial trace of past chemical contact, which complicates the pure reflex picture of insect navigation.
plos-pone-0355968:
Shinobu Sugihara and Ichiro Hisatome studied uric acid and muscle health in underweight young women in Japan. Uric acid is a natural antioxidant in blood, and earlier work linked it to muscle strength in older adults. Their 2026 study examined female university students whose body weight fell below the healthy range.

Higher uric acid went together with stronger hand grip, even after accounting for age, diet, activity, and kidney function. Uric acid showed no link with the amount of muscle itself. Students with both low muscle mass and weak grip had notably lower uric acid than those with low mass alone. The authors suggest uric acid tracks muscle function more than muscle size in this group, while calling for more research.
plos-pone-0356068:
Alhassan Hassan and seven others ask dialysis patients in Northern Ghana what good nursing care means to them, in this 2026 study. Fifteen adults who had been on haemodialysis for at least six months at Tamale Teaching Hospital, the region's only public referral dialysis center, described their experiences in interviews. Their care unfolds under strain: too few machines, breakdowns, unreliable water, and staff shortages.

Two themes organized their answers. Respect for preferences covered being involved in decisions, keeping dignity and autonomy, and culturally sensitive treatment. Physical comfort depended on pain being managed well, prompt help with daily activities, and a clean ward. Patients asked for education in simple local language, routine checks for pain and cramps, privacy during procedures, and shorter waits. The authors recommend investing equally in nurses' relational skills and in the dialysis center's battered infrastructure.
plos-pone-0356268:
Daniel Opinile Mark Igga, Nzomo Mwita, and Kennedy Muni ask why babies in Maridi County, South Sudan, start vaccine courses but fail to finish them. South Sudan's fragile health system loses many infants between first and later doses.
