Excoffier, Laval, and Schneider present version three of Arlequin, a software package for the genetics of groups. The package joins basic and advanced methods for analysing genetic data from populations in one place. It computes standard measures of genetic diversity and estimates how common each gene variant and combination is.

The package also tests whether variants depart from expected patterns of independence. Such tests reveal migration, selection, and population history. By putting many analyses together in one shared design, the package became a workhorse for studies of human ancestry and species care.  Field teams use it to judge how cut off an at-risk group is.
pmc-3930868:
Abraham, Pedregosa, Eickenberg, and co-authors show how machine learning with scikit-learn can serve neuroimaging analysis. Brain imaging analysts increasingly turn to statistical machine learning methods. Their main virtue is handling high-dimensional datasets, such as brain activation images or time series recorded at rest.

Supervised learning is typically used to decode brain states or predict clinical traits from scans. The authors connect the general-purpose scikit-learn library to neuroimaging workflows. That bridge let neuroscientists use well-tested machine learning tools without building their own from scratch.  Decoding contests adopted the pipeline as a baseline for comparing new algorithms fairly.
pmc-4823868:
Zheng, Bao, Guo, and their team profiled circular RNAs in 2016. Circular RNAs are a widespread class of RNAs that form closed loops instead of straight chains. They may regulate gene expression in eukaryotes, but human circular RNAs were still largely unknown.

The team generated sequencing data from six normal tissues to build a profile of these molecules. They found one abundant circular RNA, circHIPK3, that regulates cell growth. It acts by sponging multiple microRNAs, soaking them up so they cannot silence their targets. The work showed circular RNAs are not rare oddities but active players in gene control.
pmc-5788068:
Yuxin Chen and colleagues introduced SOAPnuke, software for cleaning high-throughput sequencing data, in 2017. Raw reads from sequencers contain adapters and low-quality bases that must be removed first. Older tools often lacked key functions or ran too slowly on huge files.

SOAPnuke combines quality checks and filtering in one program and speeds the work with a map-reduce design. It can spread a job across machines when files get very large. Clean input data protect every later step from garbage results. Labs that sequence at scale use tools like this as their first gate.
pmc-5847168:
Jan Bottcher and colleagues reported in 2018 how natural killer cells help fight tumors. A dendritic cell type called cDC1 is vital for anti-tumor immunity. Tumors rich in these cells are more often rejected and respond better to therapy.

Working in mice, the team shows that natural killer cells release signals that draw cDC1 cells into tumors. Without those signals, the dendritic cells stay scarce and immunity weakens. The finding links two immune cell types in one chain of defense. It suggests that boosting killer cell signals could make cancer immunotherapy work for more patients.
pmc-5891568:
Cecilia Prinsen and colleagues wrote the COSMIN guideline for reviews of patient-reported outcome measures in 2018. Such reviews differ from reviews of treatments and can be very complex. Reviewing one questionnaire can mean separate reviews for each measurement trait.

The guideline walks authors through each stage, from searching for studies to rating the body of evidence. It pairs with the COSMIN checklists for bias and content validity. Clear steps help readers see how final grades were reached. Teams planning a measurement review can use it as a full roadmap, which raises the standard of published reviews.
pmc-5994068:
Thomas Einarson, Annabel Acs, Craig Ludwig, and coauthors reviewed heart disease in type 2 diabetes in 2018. Heart and vessel disease is a frequent companion of diabetes. Its share among patients had been growing over time.

Searching a decade of studies, the team estimates how common cardiovascular disease is in adults with type 2 diabetes. Roughly a third of patients in the pooled studies had such disease. Heart attacks and stroke dominate the totals. The figures remind clinicians that managing diabetes means managing heart risk at the same time, not after it in everyday practice.
pmc-6421268:
Daniela Parada Venegas, Marjorie De la Fuente, Glauben Landskron, and coauthors reviewed short-chain fatty acids and gut immunity in 2019. Inflammatory bowel diseases arise from tangled genetic, immune, microbial, and environmental causes. A disturbed gut community is now seen as a likely driver.

Gut microbes make short-chain fatty acids when they ferment fiber. These products feed gut lining cells and help keep immune responses calm. Too little of them may weaken the barrier and stir inflammation. The review links diet, microbes, and bowel disease through this chemistry, and weighs therapies that aim to restore it.

poems-pg1568: Poems by William Ernest Henley, the one-legged Victorian who wrote "Invictus" from a hospital bed: "I am the master of my fate." redi-generation-of-insects-1668:
Francesco Redi, doctor to the dukes of Tuscany, ran these famed trials on the birth of insects in 1668. The text here is the 1909 English version by Mab Bigelow. In Redi's day most men held that maggots were born from rot itself.

Redi set meat in jars, some open, some sealed, and some veiled with fine gauze. Flies laid eggs on the gauze, and no maggots grew in the sealed jars at all. The clean result struck the first strict blow at the claim that life springs from rot. His method of matched jars is still taught to young students.
skene-four-ancient-books-wales-vol-2-186:
William F. Skene was a Scots sage of the Celts and their past. His Four Ancient Books of Wales came out in two books in 1868. Book Two holds the texts and their English dress. The four books are old Welsh tomes with poems from the dark age of Britain.

Poems tied to Taliesin, Aneirin, and the bards of the old north fill the text. Gods, kings, and wars of the Britons crowd the wild verse. Skene prints the Welsh text with his dress at hand for the reader. The set is a chief source for the first verse of Wales.
skene-four-ancient-books-wales-vol1-1868:
William F. Skene published the first volume of The Four Ancient Books of Wales in 1868. The book gathers the oldest Welsh poems, the verse that stands behind much of British legend. Skene printed the Welsh texts with English renderings for scholars and general readers.

Taliesin sings praise songs for the princes who paid him. The Gododdin mourns a war band that rode south to its doom. Llywarch Hen, an old man, laments his lost sons and his own cold age. Together these poems open a window on heroic Wales, the bardic world from which the Arthur stories grew.
smyth-antiquity-intellectual-man-1868:
C. Piazzi Smyth argued that man is far more old than most held in On the Antiquity of Intellectual Man, out in 1868. Smyth was a star chief who read dates in stone and sky. He draws on ice ages, star shifts, and the dates writ in the Great Pyramid to push man's dawn far back in time.

His case lands in the midst of the row sparked by Darwin. Church and lab men both felt its force. Smyth holds faith and deep time can stand as one. The book shows his stone school at its most bold.
solomon-in-all-his-glory-1768:
Solomon in All His Glory, printed in London in 1768, carries the subtitle The Master-Mason. Its author claims to be Thomas Wilson, master of a lodge. The exposé centers on the third degree, the Master Mason's own, and it preserves key evidence for the Hiramic legend's ritual form in the 1760s.

The death and raising of Hiram, the master builder of Solomon's temple, form the degree's drama. Wilson's text tells that story in its full ritual shape. Exposés remain the chief printed witnesses to how the legend was worked before official rituals stabilized. For students of the master myth, this pamphlet is a prime source. Solomon's glory here belongs to the builders, and to their slain master.
sterne-sentimental-journey-1768:
Laurence Sterne published A Sentimental Journey, his tour of France and Italy, in 1768, his last work in print. The unfinished travel narrative named sensibility and founded sentimental travel literature in the English tradition of prose. Sterne died weeks after its first volumes charmed London readers with Yorick's gentle, wandering heart abroad.

Parson Yorick drifts from Calais to Paris, collecting small scenes of feeling over sights and facts. A monk refused alms, a caged starling, and a peasant's dead ass become tests of his heart. He flirts, weeps, and moralizes by turns, and the journey breaks off mid-sentence at his death. The book taught Europe to value the traveler's inner weather over maps, miles, and monuments en route. Its influence runs through travel writing and the novel of feeling for a hundred years.
stowe-men-of-our-times-1868:
Stowe gathered short lives of leading men in Men of Our Times, printed at Hartford in 1868. The title page lists Lincoln, Grant, Garrison, Sumner, Chase, and Greeley among its subjects. Eighteen steel portraits illustrate the book, which was sold by subscription only.

Generals, statesmen, and orators of the Civil War years fill the pages, from Farragut and Sherman to Douglass and Beecher. Stowe wrote for young readers and aimed to teach character as much as history. Each sketch asks what made its man great and what boys might learn from him. The volume shows Stowe the moral teacher at work.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume eighteen of Casanova's memoirs: the story deepens. Love, loss, and adventure. The memoirs' rich middle age. Eighteenth volume: love and loss, the memoirs' rich maturity, love, loss, and adventure, the story deepens with age.

Snorri Sturluson, an Icelandic chieftain of the thirteenth century, wrote the Prose Edda to keep Norse myth alive for poets. Christian Iceland was forgetting the old stories, and skaldic verse needed them. Arthur Gilchrist Brodeur's translation is the classic English version.

A deluded king hears the gods' tales from three mysterious hosts: the making of the world from a giant's body, Thor's adventures, and the fires of Ragnarok. Later parts teach the kennings, the riddling phrases of Norse poetry. Verified from a pre-1930 edition, Brodeur's Snorri remains the handbook through which most readers meet the Norse gods.
tob-10468:
Part One of Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologica, the Prima Pars, asks the biggest questions first. Aquinas proceeds by questions: each topic opens with objections, states a contrary authority, gives a reasoned answer, and replies to the objections. The method is as famous as the conclusions.

Does God exist, and what is God like? How did creation unfold, including angels, the six days of Genesis, and the nature of human beings, body and soul? Aquinas argues each step from Scripture, earlier thinkers, and reason. Readers watch the most orderly mind in medieval thought at full stretch, building a system meant to hold together.
tob-4068:
Robert Ernest Hume, a Harvard Sanskritist, gathered the Thirteen Principal Upanishads into one English volume. Isa, Kena, Katha, and their companions appear with his notes and introductions. Generations of students learned Hindu philosophy from Hume's pages, and many still start there.

The Katha sends a boy to argue with Death about what survives the grave. The Chandogya teaches that the self and the world's ground are one: thou art that. Hume renders the Sanskrit with care for both sense and music. Verified from the 1919 public-domain edition, the volume remains the classic school text of the Upanishads in English.
tob-4168:
Ernest Renan published Vie de Jésus in French in 1863, after traveling in the Holy Land, and scandalized Europe. His life treats Jesus as a historical figure, an incomparable Galilean moral teacher, rather than through the creed's claims. Written beautifully, in the landscapes where the story happened, the book sold hundreds of thousands of copies.

Renan's Jesus is a genius of religious feeling whose legend grew after his death, a portrait built from critical history and nineteenth-century sentiment alike. Churches condemned it; the reading public devoured it. By making the historical Jesus a public question for ordinary readers, Renan changed religious debate permanently, and the French original preserves his celebrated style unfiltered.
ufo-symposium-house-1968:
Scientists took the UFO question to a House panel in the summer of 1968. The Symposium on Unidentified Flying Objects, held July 29 by the Committee on Science and Astronautics, prints their talks in full. Allen Hynek, Carl Sagan, and James McDonald stood among the speakers.

The men split: some held the reports hid a true wonder worth a hunt, others saw error and noise. Leo Sprinkle and James Harder added their own cases and claims. The talks form the science counterpoint to the Condon study of the same year. The file shows the UFO fight argued at its highest level.
un-ga-res-a-69-68: Kathmandu hosts the UN office praised in Resolution A/69/68, from the Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Asia and the Pacific was set up in 1987 and renamed a year later. From its Nepal base it gives staff support, on request, to peace and disarmament work agreed by states of the region. The text notes the centre's move into full work on the ground and the Secretary-General's report on it.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/68 comes from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session in 2014. It concerns the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Asia and the Pacific, based in Kathmandu. It thanks Nepal for hosting and funding support. It lists the Centre's recent regional workshops and conferences. It appeals for voluntary contributions. Those are the Centre's only resources for carrying out its disarmament work across the region.

un-sc-res-1568:
Cyprus's force was reshaped as it was renewed in October 2004. The Secretary-General had reviewed UNFICYP after the failed referendum. On 22 October 2004 the Council backed his plan to change its size and working methods. It then extended the mandate until 15 June 2005. Work on missing persons had just resumed after years of pause. The Council welcomed that step. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay.

Turkish Cypriot leaders and Turkish forces had to lift all limits on the force. They also had to restore the military position at Strovilia as it stood before June 2000. The Council restated its Cyprus resolutions, led by 1251 of 1999. The leaner force that resulted still patrols the buffer zone.
un-sc-res-1668: Resolution 1668, a 2006 act of the Security Council, is kept in this collection in its official-record form. The transcription source is English Wikisource. Inside, the members speak first in the language of concern and recollection, then in the language of decision. That shift in register, preserved intact, is the signature of the genre.
un-sc-res-168: Filling the office of Secretary-General is the sole business of Resolution 168, adopted without dissent on 3 November 1961. The General Assembly had fixed a term for the office ending on 10 April 1963, and the post had fallen vacant partway through it. un-sc-res-1768:
Congo sanctions were extended for only ten days by the Security Council on 31 July 2007. The Group of Experts had filed its final report under resolution 1698 (2006). A Council mission had visited Kinshasa on 20 June 2007. Armed groups and militias still plagued North and South Kivu and Ituri. Illegal weapons kept flowing into and within the country.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the arms measures of resolution 1493 (2003), as widened by resolution 1596 (2005), to 10 August 2007. The transport controls ran for the same short span. So did the money and travel measures against embargo breakers. The Group of Experts' mandate was extended over the same period. The ten-day bridge kept the regime in force without a gap while the Council finished work on the longer renewal that followed in resolution 1771 (2007).
un-sc-res-1868: Kept as Resolution 1868, a Security Council act survives in this collection through a transcription of the UN's official record. The document carries the standard signs of its kind: the Council acting under the Charter, prior texts recalled, steps decided in numbered order. The whole is preserved, so nothing depends on a secondhand account of it.
un-sc-res-2068:
Children in war zones are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2068, adopted on 19 September 2012. Some armed groups kept harming children year after year. They recruited child soldiers, killed and maimed children, and attacked schools and hospitals. Naming and shaming alone had not stopped them. Four Council members abstained, the first such split on this theme.

The Council says it stands ready to impose targeted sanctions on groups that keep abusing children. States should prosecute offenders in their own courts. The Council's working group on children and armed conflict must weigh, within one year, fresh ways to press repeat offenders. The text shows the Council shifting from warnings toward punishment for the worst abusers.
un-sc-res-268: The Security Council's numbered decisions include Resolution 268, entered in this catalog under the year 1969. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-368:
The United Nations Emergency Force in Sinai came up for a short renewal in 1975. On 17 April 1975 the Security Council kept the force for three more months. Its mandate now ran until 24 July 1975. The Secretary-General had reported on the force's work. The Council noted events in the Middle East with concern. Tension in the area, it said, remained high.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 without delay. That text demanded a ceasefire and a negotiated peace. The Secretary-General owed a report by the end of the term. It would cover events and the steps taken toward 338. The force stood between Egypt and Israel while diplomacy moved slowly.
un-sc-res-668:
Cambodia's long war moved toward a settlement in September 1990. The five permanent Council members had drafted a framework for peace. All Cambodian parties accepted it at Jakarta on 10 September. On 20 September 1990 the Security Council endorsed that framework. It praised the five powers for their work. The Paris Conference on Cambodia would turn the outline into a full settlement.

The Cambodian parties had agreed to form a Supreme National Council. That body would stand for Cambodia abroad during the transition. The Council welcomed its creation. The parties also pledged free and fair elections under United Nations supervision. The framework became the base of the 1991 Paris agreements. Those deals ended the war and set up a huge peace operation.
un-sc-res-68: Arms control led to a Council vote: Resolution 68, adopted on 10 February 1949 by nine votes to none, with two abstentions. The General Assembly had passed a text on conventional arms that November. It now needed study by the expert body built for that work. The Council sends Assembly Resolution 192 (III) to the Commission for Conventional Armaments. The commission is to act on it as its terms direct. The whole resolution is that single act of referral, a routine step in the early arms-control machinery.
un-sc-res-968:
Tajikistan gained a United Nations observer mission on 16 December 1994. The government and the opposition had stretched their Tehran ceasefire to 6 February 1995 at the Islamabad round of talks. A protocol set up a joint commission to watch the truce. The Secretary-General's report of 30 November set out a mission plan.

The Council established the United Nations Mission of Observers in Tajikistan, UNMOT, on the Secretary-General's plan. It would serve for up to six months. Its life past 6 February 1995 depended on the ceasefire holding and both sides staying pledged to a settlement. The Secretary-General had to report on the mission's work and on the talks. His special envoy would keep pushing for national reconciliation. The parties had to work fully with the mission and guard its staff's safety and movement. Tajikistan had to conclude a status agreement with the United Nations quickly.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Within a day of the 11 September 2001 attacks, the Council answered. Terrorists had struck New York, Washington, D.C., and Pennsylvania, and the scale of the deaths was still becoming clear when members met on 12 September. The text is short and carries the shock of that moment.

The attacks are condemned in the strongest terms and named a threat to world peace and security. Sympathy goes to the victims, their families, and the people and government of the United States. All states are called on to work together to bring the planners, attackers, and sponsors to justice, and anyone who aided or sheltered them is warned they will be held to account.

Peace steps in Congo are welcomed on 20 March 2003, while atrocities in the east are condemned in the same text. Congolese parties had reached agreement in Pretoria on transitional arrangements. At the same time, a report on the Ituri region described grave abuses against civilians there.

Massacres and other systematic violations of human rights and aid law are condemned, including sexual violence used as a weapon of war. Abuses by the MLC, RCD-National, and UPC forces in Ituri are named, with a warning that there would be no impunity for those responsible. In filling key posts in the transitional government, the parties are also told to weigh each person's record and commitment to the peace deal.

Cyprus peacekeeping gets a careful review in Resolution 1568, adopted unanimously on 22 October 2004. The Council welcomed the resumption of work by the Committee on Missing Persons, which had restarted in August after years of inactivity. It also noted the Secretary-General's broader review of UNFICYP, the force present on the island since 1964.

Because conditions on the island still required it, and Cyprus agreed, the Council kept UNFICYP in place past December 2004, extending its mandate to June 2005. It took note of a calmer security picture and a judgment that fighting was increasingly unlikely to resume. Even so, the resolution treats the force as still necessary while a political settlement remains out of reach.

One judge of the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal is allowed to finish a case he is already hearing, in this text of 10 April 2006. Responding to the Secretary-General's request, the Council confirmed that Judge Joaquín Canivell could keep sitting in the Krajišnik case beyond April 2006 until it ends. His total service would thereby pass the usual three-year limit for judges of his class, which the Council set aside for this case.

An acting Secretary-General for the United Nations is recommended on 3 November 1961. The office had fallen vacant, and the term fixed by the General Assembly ran until 10 April 1963. The Council recommended that the General Assembly appoint U Thant as acting Secretary-General for the unexpired portion of that term. Under the Charter, the Assembly appoints on the Council's recommendation, so this short text is the step that put him in the post.

Resolution 1768, adopted on 31 July 2007, extends Congo's arms embargo by just ten days. The experts monitoring the embargo had filed their final report, and the Council again condemned the illegal flow of guns into Congo and around its east. Militias in North and South Kivu and Ituri kept the whole region insecure.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the arms measures, first imposed in 2003 and widened several times since, until 10 August 2007. A renewal this short is a scheduling device, not a policy shift: members needed the measures kept in force while they finished negotiating the regime's next, longer phase. The Council also noted its mission's June visit to Kinshasa.

Afghanistan's assistance mission, UNAMA, is extended until 23 March 2010 on 23 March 2009. There is no purely military answer to Afghanistan's problems, it is stressed, and a broad approach is needed. A Council mission to the country in November 2008 informed the renewal, and elections were due later in 2009.

UNAMA's mandate is kept, and the mission and its head will keep leading world civilian efforts, under Afghan ownership. Priorities include support for elections, governance, aid coordination, counternarcotics, and regional cooperation. All Afghan and international actors are called on to work with the mission and to protect United Nations staff, whose freedom of movement is treated as essential.

Children in armed conflict are the focus of Resolution 2068, adopted on 19 September 2012. The Secretary-General's April 2012 report showed progress — thousands of children demobilized, action plans signed, some parties delisted. But in several conflicts parties kept recruiting and using children, killing and maiming them, and committing sexual violence, in open disregard of the Council.

The Council strongly condemns all such violations and demands an immediate end to them, including attacks on schools and hospitals and denial of humanitarian access. It tells states to bring perpetrators to justice at home or through international mechanisms. It repeats its readiness to adopt targeted, graduated measures against persistent offenders. Its Working Group on Children and Armed Conflict must, within one year, weigh a broad range of options for increasing pressure on those offenders. Annual reports continue, the next due by June 2013.

Portuguese forces bombed a village in Zambia in 1969, and the Council answered on 28 July that year. The village was Lote, in the Katete District of Zambia's Eastern Province. It stood near the border with Mozambique, which Portugal then ruled. Zambian civilians were killed in the attack, and property was destroyed.

The Council strongly censured the Portuguese attacks. Portugal was told to stop violating Zambia's territory and to end unprovoked raids at once. Zambian civilians kidnapped by Portuguese forces had to be released and returned. Those forces operated from Angola and Mozambique. Property taken from Zambian land also had to be given back. If Portugal failed to comply, the Council warned, it would meet again to consider further measures.

The Sinai buffer force gained just three months in the spring of 1975. On 17 April, the Council adopted Resolution 368. Thirteen members voted yes and none voted no. The force had been built by Resolution 340 in October 1973. It kept Egypt and Israel apart after the Yom Kippur War. Tension still hung over the area, the Council noted.

The text calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 at once. That 1973 order pairs a truce with peace talks. The mandate then runs to 24 July 1975. A report from the Secretary-General is due at the end. The short term fit the moment. Shuttle talks over a fresh pull-back in Sinai were then at their peak.

On 20 September 1990 the Security Council unanimously endorsed a framework meant to end the conflict in Cambodia. Five permanent members of the Council had drafted the plan after the 1989 Paris Conference stalled short of a full settlement. Cambodian parties accepted the framework at a meeting in Jakarta earlier that month.

Under the plan, a Supreme National Council would speak for Cambodia while the country moved toward free elections run by the United Nations. The resolution welcomed the parties' pledge to turn the framework into a complete political settlement through the Paris Conference. It gave UN backing to the blueprint that soon produced a transitional authority and Cambodia's first UN-run elections.

Arms control filled much of the UN's early agenda. Resolution 68, adopted on 10 February 1949, is a short housekeeping text on that effort. Nine members voted in favor. The Ukrainian and Soviet delegations abstained. The General Assembly had passed its own arms resolution the previous November.

The Council simply sent that Assembly text onward. Assembly Resolution 192 asked for work on conventional weapons. The file went to the Commission for Conventional Armaments. That body handled plans for limiting non-nuclear forces. The resolution shows how the two UN organs passed disarmament tasks between them in the Cold War's first years.

Civil war in Tajikistan is the setting for Resolution 968, adopted on 16 December 1994. The government and the Tajik opposition had signed a temporary ceasefire deal in Tehran that September and had just agreed in talks in Islamabad to extend it. A joint commission was set up to watch over the truce, and talks on settling the conflict were set to continue in Moscow.

The Council sets up the United Nations Mission of Observers in Tajikistan, called UNMOT, for up to six months. Its observers help the joint commission track the ceasefire, look into reported breaches, keep contact with both sides, and back wider peace work. The mission lasts past 6 February 1995 only if the truce is extended and both sides stay committed to peace talks.
vera-clavicola-1868:
La Vera Clavicola, the True Little Key, was printed at Milan in 1868. It is the Italian edition of the Grimorium Verum tradition, Italy's own true grimoire. Seventy-six sections set out its spirits and operations, rite by rite, for the magicians of the peninsula.

The Italian text follows its French sources while wearing a local cut. Conjurers get lists of spirits, their seals, and the hours and tools each rite requires. The Milan printing shows the grimoire trade alive in nineteenth-century Italy. Complete and unabridged, the Vera Clavicola served practitioners who wanted the Verum in their own tongue. It pairs naturally with the French True Grimoire.
welsh-triads-skene-1868:
Welsh lore was kept in threes: three names, three deeds, three fates bound in one short saying. Trioedd Ynys Prydein, the Welsh Triads, gathers hundreds of these brief groups. Two Victorian versions stand here, William Skene's of 1868 and the Rhys and Evans text of 1887.

The triads name heroes, battles, bards, and wonders of old Britain in terse, packed lines. Bards used them as hooks on which long tales and poems could hang in memory. Read in bulk, they map the whole world of Welsh legend. The paired translations let readers test one rendering against the other.
